All performance data should have been reviewed in the FMC for the runway change.

CRJ-200 flight Captain reported an uneventful landing at destination after experiencing ADC1 failure during flight and successfully overcame failure.

I was called out on a reserve callout to deadhead to ZZZ to pickup an airplane that needed to be repositioned to ZZZ1. I noticed in the Maintenance log that Maintenance had been working on the standby Airspeed Indicator/Altimeter. I assume that this is why the airplane was stranded in ZZZ. First Officer and I completed our preflight checks and briefings to include the Non Routine Flight Operations task cards per normal; with nothing unusual occurring. We taxied out to ZZZ Runway XX; and departed normally via the ODP. The winds on takeoff were a strong gusty crosswind to about 30 knots from the right. The takeoff roll was normal with no abnormalities. We called positive rate; and then I called for 'Gear Up'. Shortly after selecting the landing gear up; all of my air data instruments went blank; and displayed Red IAS; ALT; & V/S flags. The autopilot was not engaged; and my flight director did not indicate with the loss of air data indications. I told my First Officer that I lost my airspeed and air data; and left the power set for takeoff and pitched for 10 degrees nose up. My First Officer read out the speeds on his speed tape and the standby gauges. While I had a hunch that his indications were correct; due to the Maintenance write-ups and recent work; and the unusual and immediate failure; we elected to initially diagnose this as an unreliable airspeed emergency; at least until we could verify that both the First Officer's ADC and the standby gauges were correctly indicating. I suspected an ADC 1 failure of some sorts. After reaching a safe altitude and completing the After Takeoff Checklist; I transferred the flight controls over to my First Officer; and told him to climb on course initially while we could work to verify that the airspeed indicators on his side were correctly indicating. ATC was notified of the instrument failure and of our request to climb on course for the time being. We were in VMC conditions and felt it was safe and prudent to continue to climb away from the terrain around ZZZ. As the airplane was empty; it's climb performance was exceptional. After verifying our speed; power settings; and pitch attitudes using the charts from the Unreliable Airspeed procedure we were able to affirmatively establish that both the First Officer's indications along with our standby instruments were indicating correctly. We at this point elected to abandon the unreliable airspeed procedure; as we still had two functioning airspeed indicators and instead address this as an ADC 1 abnormal procedure and failure. I felt that the unreliable airspeed procedure; while providing us with good situational information to verify that our other two indicators were functioning correctly; was irrelevant because we didn't have varying unreliable airspeed indications; but rather a complete loss of air data information. Although I suspected it was simply an ADC failure initially; due to our low altitude and critical phase of flight; we elected to initially treat the failure as an unreliable airspeed situation to assure that we were flying a safe pitch and power setting regardless of airspeed to reach a safe altitude clear of the terrain. ATC was updated that we suspected an ADC 1 failure. An emergency was never declared with ATC. We spoke to Dispatch and agreed that with the ADC 1 failure a diversion to the nearest suitable airport was not necessarily required; which is an important difference from the unreliable airspeed procedure; although we did discuss as a crew and with Dispatch the possibility of a diversion to ZZZ2 or another nearby airport along our route. We agreed that with the situation stable and well diagnosed; we felt it was pertinent; legal; and safest to continue on to ZZZ1. We landed in ZZZ1 where the ADC failure was written up in the Maintenance log as a discrepancy; and Maintenance was briefed on the phone. I called the Flight Dispatcher and debriefed with him as well; and he assured me that he was in agreement with our decision making and the [Dispatcher] was aware of the situation; and no further calls or reports were required. Maintenance later removed; and replaced ADC 1; prior to dispatching the aircraft on it's next flight. The cause of this event was a failure of ADC 1. I am curios as to whether or not the Maintenance work done on the standby airspeed/altimeter could have contributed to the failure of ADC 1. In terms of recurrence; and preventing this; from a flight ops standpoint I'm not sure what to recommend. However; I will say that this is the 2nd time in a month I have dealt with an unreliable airspeed issue; pitot/static issue; or ADC issue on the CRJ. Maybe I'm snakebit; but I have taken notice to the increase in frequency with these events. We train for this; and just a week ago I went through [training]. In our training we ran through the unreliable airspeed procedure. Because of this; I was familiar that if an initial climb is required; or just after takeoff; in the CRJ200 the checklist tells you to pitch to 10 degrees nose up at takeoff power. Fortunately; the recent familiarity with that procedure 100% helped; and was highly effective through the initial diagnosis and trouble shooting of our abnormality. There isn't a great checklist for 'loss of airspeed' in the QRH; you have to pick between unreliable airspeed; and an ADC failure. We used the Immediate Action Items from the unreliable airspeed checklist; along with the pitch/thrust reference tables; to help assure that we were climbing in a safe flight path state; and that our remaining operational airspeed indicators were properly functioning; however; then rediagnosed the issue as a full ADC 1 failure; and felt it was more prudent to treat this as an ADC failure as opposed to an unreliable airspeed emergency. I realize today though that in real life...It could be difficult to truly distinguish between the two. As a crew; we elected to start with the ultra safe option; and then once we gathered more information about the problem; were able to move into a different; and more accurate checklist; that more appropriately addressed the problem. If I could make a recommendation; I think that we need to add both memory items; and a QRC checklist for a suspected Unreliable airspeed or loss of airspeed immediate response. The immediate action items in the QRH; should absolutely be committed to memory; and probably be backed up by a QRC. While I was fortunately familiar with these; should we have a new Captain/ First Officer pairing on the aircraft in the future; that maybe isn't familiar with the aircrafts normal performance; this could potentially be an unforgivable consequence. Just a recommendation after taking some time to look back at the events of today.

B737 flight crew reported inflight shut down and diversion due to hydraulic system failure.

Captain and I [deadheaded] to ZZZ to pick up a 737-800 to ferry back to ZZZ1 due to a loss of system A hydraulic fluid. Preflight showed no leaks and everything ok with the aircraft. I was PM and upon takeoff the Master Caution light came on for engine driven hydraulic pump for system A. The light went out and continued. Abeam ZZZ2 the master caution came back on for engine driven hydraulic pump number 1 system A. I pulled out the QRH and ran the Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure checklist which had us turn the pump switch off. With quantity and pressure still good using the electric pump we decided to continue to ZZZ1. Maintenance techs on the aircraft agreed with the decision. Soon after passing ZZZZZ intersection the number 1 Engine Oil Filter Bypass indication on the upper engine MFD illuminated. I pulled out the QRH and we decided to request a lower altitude since we knew we could not maintain level flight with one engine at idle. We asked for a descent to FL 200 and told them we were working on a problem with our left engine. Since the OIL FILTER BYPASS indication remained illuminated the next step per the QRH was to shut the engine down. As a result we had to land at the nearest suitable airport. We decided that ZZZ3 was the best choice since it was close the weather was good and we were both familiar with the airport. I continued with the checklist as [the Captain] flew the aircraft; [requested priority handling]; and requested the diversion. We were cleared direct to the airport and a descent to FL 70. Shutdown and descent proceeded normally with me accomplishing the shutdown and [the Captain] continuing to fly and maintain communication with ATC. We then moved to the one engine inoperative and landing checklist which included calculating single engine landing distance. Hydraulic system A at this point had gone down to 25 percent. We prepared for the possibility of losing total system A pressure and a manual gear extension but was not a factor as the gear operated normally; [the Captain] performed a visual approach and landing with a safe landing in ZZZ3. We then sent a message to dispatch via ACARS that we were safe on the ground.

First Officer and I deadheaded to ZZZ to pick up a 737-800; which had been down for maintenance due to failure of the number 1 engine driven hydraulic pump failure and loss of system A fluid. Upon arrival we did our normal preflight and found no problems with the aircraft. The 3 Tech OPS employees who fixed the aircraft were embarked and we prepared to fly.Start up; taxi; and takeoff were normal. I was flying pilot and [First Officer] was monitoring. Early in the climb master caution light for the hydraulics came on and [First Officer] noted that the low pressure light for the engine driven hydraulic pump on engine 1 was on then quickly went out. Thinking it was anomaly with sensor and hydraulic quantity and pressure normal we continued. We were abeam ZZZ2 and the master caution for Hydraulics once again illuminated and [First Officer] noted the Low Pressure light for engine driven hydraulic pump on the left (number 1) engine was illuminated and stayed on. [First Officer] pulled out the QRH and proceeded to run the Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure checklist which lead to the pump being turned off. With quantity and pressure still good using the electric pump we decided to continue. We did get one of the Maintenance Techs to come to the flight deck and we showed and conversed with him about the issue. Nothing changed our thought process so we continued.Soon after passing ZZZZZ intersection and headed directly to ZZZZZ1 intersection; the number 1 Engine Oil Filter Bypass indication on the upper engine MFD illuminated. [First Officer] once again pulled out the QRH and we decided I would continue to fly and talk and he would run the checklist. We were at FL300 and decided to request a lower altitude as we knew we could not maintain level flight for long with one engine at idle. We asked for and received a descent to FL200 and told him we were working on a problem with our left engine. [First Officer] worked our way through the checklist resulting with the OIL FILTER BYPASS indication remaining illuminated. Per the checklist the next step was to shut down the engine and as a result of that we would need to land. We chose ZZZ3.[First Officer] continued the checklist as I [requested priority handling] and requested to divert. We were cleared direct the airport and a descent to 7;000. Shutdown and descent proceeded normally with [First Officer] completing the shutdown checklist. With the engine secured we moved on to the one engine inoperative and landing checklist to include the non-normal single engine landing distance. As we got closer to ZZZ3 the hydraulic issue took another turn. The quantity began to change first climbing to 106 percent and then slowly starting to decrease to mid-70 percent and then working its way down slowly till as we were coming down final it was in mid-20's. [First Officer] brought up the possibility of losing the 'A' system; so both of us were both prepared should that happen. Fortunately we did not have to run that checklist. Visual approach and landing was uneventful and normal. Landed and taxied to parking spot.We sent a message to Dispatch using ACARS that we were safe on the ground. The call I got after we had been on ground for 15 min. or so from the FODM gave me the feeling that it didn't go through but it was sent. It was confirmed by maintenance that in fact the 'A' system was depleted to about 25 percent and still leaking.

C310 Flight Instructor reported striking trees during go around.

A friend who has a multi engine and instrument rating was interested in possibly buying my Cessna 310 so we flew to breakfast in IMC with me in the left seat acting as PIC. I suggested that on our return; he sit in the left seat and we fly to ZZZ where they had longer runways than our home field and he could practice some landings. While he was rated; I was still PIC from the right seat as he was not multi engine current and I was a multi engine CFI.We flew down and executed an RNAV/GPS (Area Navigation) approach to Runway XX in VMC conditions. I said that our first landing exercise would be to take the plane almost down to the runway and just fly a foot or so off of the deck to help visualize the sight picture; before cutting the throttles and landing. We'd then taxi back for more pattern work.The approach was very successful and everything went well until about 50 feet when he started to flare. I said we needed to keep coming down; we were nowhere near the altitude we needed to be at to begin the flare; but he leveled off; seeming to feel for the runway from that point. We quickly reached the midpoint of the runway and I began thinking that a go around would be necessary but I let him continue a bit further. Shortly thereafter I called for a go around but he cut the power; raised the nose; and landed firmly; about 2/3 of the way down the runway. I did not think we had room to stop on the remaining runway and at 80 knots we were close to flying speed. He told me to take over and I applied full power. At the end of the runway we still were slower than I would want to be but I raised the nose and we were airborne in ground effect. The plane was very slow to accelerate or climb and I felt my friend pulling back on the yoke. I pushed forward not wanting to stall or leave ground effect. At this point I realized that our gear was still down and that we had landing flaps. I knew that if I retracted landing flaps we had a very strong potential to sink into the ground so faced with that option I left the flaps down. I was not sure of the drag effect from gear retraction so I left it down as well. Again I felt him pulling back on the wheel while I yelled 'stop pulling' and pushed forward.Soon there was a row of trees in the windshield and I gathered we had gotten all of the speed we could for the time being and I pulled back on the yoke. The tower controller had seen what was going on and asked us if we were ok; did we need assistance; and did we see the trees. He also asked if we would be avoiding the trees. These calls were a distraction and I did not answer as my first priority was to fly the aircraft.We climbed out; retracting the gear and flaps. The controller asked if we wanted him to cancel IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) and for us to resume our pattern work. Shaken; I was not interested in pattern work and I asked him to cancel IFR and we would leave the area. Since he had questioned if we had hit the trees I decided to fly about 5 miles to an airport where I have maintenance done to have the plane inspected. Apparently we had made contact with the very top of the tree line as evidenced by some leaves on the nose gear. The mechanic came out to inspect the plane and could find no damage at all after inspecting the gear; flaps; wings; fuselage; and general condition.In retrospect; I had put my friend in a bad position. Even though he had watched me land many times; and had landed himself in the past; I should have demonstrated the first landing. I know better than to land outside the touchdown zone and yet we did. At the midpoint of the runway with limited runway ahead of us; I should have had an aggressive transfer of control and taken the plane around myself. If I had done that I have no doubt I would have raised the gear and flaps allowing a successful climb out; but in the uncertain transfer of control with the pilot monitoring suddenly and unexpectedly becoming the pilot flying; the sequence of a successful go around were lost.I can't help but think that I put the pilot flying into a bad position by not doing the go around sooner and not having the plane in proper climb configuration was a bad error. I have replayed this many times and reminded myself that in this situation; even though you are not the flying pilot; you have to stay on top of things mentally and be prepared to take over at any point.The better decision after the touch down would have been to get out of the mental go around mind set and just kept it on the ground. A couple of blown tires and a plane in the overrun would have been nothing compared to the threats of staggering into the air in a bad configuration with trees ahead.

Air Carrier flight crew reported the FMS produced duplicate fixes during an arrival and runway change.

It was from ZZZ1 to ZZZ IFR flight. Our flight plan and clearance was from ZZZ1..ZZZZZ5. ZZZ. On the ground; [the] Captain; and I reviewed the route including every fix in the arrival and programmed [the] FMS for Runway XXL in ZZZ. From takeoff until descend via ZZZZZ 5 Arrival; flight was uneventful. Captain and I took off from Runway XXL at ZZZ1 and then instructed to go direct ZZZZZ shortly after instructed go to direct ZZZZZ1 which is [the IAF] of [the] arrival. We were instructed to descend via ZZZZZ5 Arrival in to ZZZ with both altitude and airspeed restriction as stated in the STAR. During the descend; the ZZZ Approach Controller gave instruction to switch our runway to XXR. Captain and I programmed [the] FMS and switched our planned runway to XXR as well as review the fixes along the route. However; as we approach the fix ZZZZZ2; LNAV autopilot was switched to lateral mode [and the] airplane was late to turn to [the] final [approach] fix which is ZZZZZ3. As soon as Pilot Flying noticed the mode change in autopilot; Pilot Flying used heading bug to make a left turn to rejoin the course for the rest of arrival. After the arrival; flight crew flew rest of flight uneventfully and land safely at Runway XXR. Next time; we will review the fixes more carefully after making any changes on the runways or arrivals and make sure if there are any fixes that are duplicated; we will deleted it.

On arrival to ZZZ we were descending via ZZZZZ5. Our dispatch release had planned [Runway] XXL and we had already briefed our approach prior to the beginning of the arrival as is common for preparation and safety. As an LCA (line check airman) I have been flying our route structure for over X;XXX hours in the left seat and this is common practice for myself. However; I am still trying to understand the traffic flows in ZZZ and as time progresses I am positive the other crews and I will get better at selecting runways based on flow and approaches utilized over time. ZZZ Approach Control gave us instructions for XXR somewhere after ZZZZZ5 I believe. I was the pilot monitoring. So I immediately went to work resetting FMS verifying ZZZZZ3 had now changed to ZZZZZ2. Altitudes were correct at said waypoint. Getting new landing data. Resetting both navigational aids for the correct runway. And since my FO (First Officer) was fairly new to the plane I began briefing his approach to him out loud; highlighting changes and re-briefing all pertinent information. It was in the middle of this brief that I heard the lateral NAV disconnection chime. The plane had entered ROL mode and within a second I and the FO were both reaching for the heading bug. He made the correction on the FGC (Flight Guidance Computer) about as quickly as anyone could. We recaptured the LNAV course to ZZZZZ2 and were given a number to call.I have been operating with this company for over X years; almost Y are as an LCA. In all my time I have never seen what I described above. After the fact I am aware of exactly what happened and I will explain and make suggestions to correct. Upon loading the runway change to XXR the FMS duplicated the ZZZZZ fix. I know this because the pilot observing told us when we got on the ground what he had witnessed and told us it was a current trend within our airline and they were trying to troubleshoot. I understand why that might happen in the mind of the FMS as it is trying to separate the arrival into parts. Initial arrival segment versus approach segment. However; reloading approaches or fielding runways changes are common in our route structure and not once in four years has this happened anywhere else. ZZZZZ4 in ZZZ2. Landing north transitions to ZZZZZ6 at 7000. Landing south your next fix might be ZZZZZ7 at 7000 for XXC. But never in four years has a reassigned runway and a reload of the approach caused ZZZZZ4 to duplicate. This is specific to ZZZ2. This is why we are just now seeing this throughout the pilot group in this airspace. I know there is verbiage within our books that states duplicated points must be removed for this very reason. However; in this event I was unable to catch the duplicated fix due to workload and I had never seen the issue before so my mental radar so to speak was focused on threats I have seen: monitoring our descent rate; monitoring speed control for arrival compliance; re-briefing navigational aid frequencies; briefing go-around and missed approach for the new runway. All the things I have seen cause errors in our flight on a normal day. So when this lateral break happened I was as stunned as the FO. I will say to his credit he corrected in the quickest fashion and made the correct adjustment for the situation. There was nothing more we could have done. I did not feel safety was at stake nor that the violation was hugely significant. I however do see that as a systemic issue the implications of this are massive and need to be corrected ASAP which is why I have my recommendations. I spoke with a sim pilot who was able to recreate the event and he confirmed what I had already suspected. Pilots need to be aware that this is common in ZZZ2. When receiving a new runway or a change to the approach. Look for duplicate fixes!

CRJ200 flight crew reported a #1 IDG light illuminated on takeoff and elected to continue; subsequently turning off the #2 IDG; causing the deployment of the Emergency Air Driven Generator and resulting in an air turnback.

The first 3 flights were uneventful and on arrival in ZZZ we were swapped into Aircraft Y - a broken airplane for ZZZ - ZZZ1. We were then swapped into Aircraft X - an airplane coming from the hangar that was a first flight and had a deferred APU. There was no ground air available at the gate and we were now an hour late. We boarded 30 passengers and had a Company Dispatcher Jumpseater. We started one engine at the gate and taxied out and performed a cross bleed engine start for #1. ATIS was reporting wind shear and we used wind shear numbers for takeoff on XXR; [Taxiway] XX; with ignition ON.On the takeoff roll I noticed an intermittent IDG 1 caution message; followed by an intermittent CONFIG SPOILERS warning message; a BTMS 3 that was dashes and two probe/window heat messages. I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. I believed the message to be associated with a MEL on a previous flight; and I said; 'Associated; continue;' and continued the takeoff. The winds were very gusty. After takeoff we had a GEN 1 caution message and I ran the QRH for GEN 1; and in the process I accidentally switched off GEN 2; resulting in the ADG deploying. We [requested priority handling] and returned to ZZZ; landing on XYR. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) was there and escorted us to Gate XXX. No injuries or complaints were reported. We were met by Maintenance and then had a 5-way call with Company; Maintenance; [another person]; and one or two other people. I explained what had happened and told them of my mistake. I and the First Officer said that we were done flying and we were taken off our schedules. We then had a call with Maintenance and wrote up the airplane; including the #1 IDG; ADG deployment; and spoiler warning message.I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. Once airborne; and running the QRH; I should have confirmed that the GEN1 switch was selected and confirmed with the flying pilot prior to actuating the switch.

The day began early with an XA45 wake up to accommodate an XB45 van and [an] XC15 show. We completed the first three flights of the day without issue. Upon landing in ZZZ and swapping our good airplane for the plane we were taking to ZZZ1; we found out that that aircraft had maintenance issues and would require us to swap aircraft again. We were informed that there would be a delay in getting a new aircraft from the hangar. After waiting for about an hour the aircraft was finally coming from the hanger and we found out that it had an inoperative APU and it was its first flight of the day. Additionally; we would be having a Company Dispatcher in the jump seat. We were able to complete our first flight of the day items; acceptance checklist to include the first flight of the day items; complete an air start; push back; single-engine taxi out; and complete the cross bleed start without incident. We were set up for a wind shear takeoff with continuous ignition on.We were given a lineup and clearance and taxied onto the Runway of XXR at [Taxiway] XX. After a momentary wait; we were then given the takeoff clearance with a turn to the north. I was the flying pilot at the time; so I was given controls upon completion of the takeoff checklist. I pushed the thrust levers up and commanded for thrust to be set; the CA (Captain) confirmed thrust set and guarded the thrust levers. Shortly after this; a caution message appeared and the CA called out 'IDG 1' and called for the abort initially; but then said; 'Wait; that's associated.' The CA did not perform the abort; so I continued to fly the plane to ensure the positive control of the aircraft. Shortly after this; a warning message appeared momentarily; and the CA called out; 'Config Spoilers;' and the message disappeared. We continued the takeoff normally and began our turn to the north per ATC instructions.I was initially hand flying but shortly after reaching acceleration altitude; I called for the autopilot to be engaged. I called for the after takeoff checklist and noticed the caution messages that were present and called for the QRH. The Captain began to run the GEN 1 caution message QRH for the caution messages that were present. We noted the associated probe and window/windshield heat messages. While he was running the QRH he called out; 'GEN 1 off/reset; then on;' and reached up to perform this action. It appeared that he accidentally reset GEN 2 and the aircraft went dark momentarily; our EICAS and instrumentation screens went dark momentarily; and we heard the ADG automatically deploy. The CA immediately acknowledged his mistake and I continued flying by hand to maintain positive control of the aircraft while we sorted out the generator issue. The CA turned GEN 2 back on and communicated with me that we should return to ZZZ; I agreed.The CA then communicated to ATC that we needed to return to ZZZ and [requested priority handling]. The CA then communicated to Dispatch; the FA (Flight Attendant); and passengers that we were returning to ZZZ and to expect a normal landing. He did mention that there would be emergency vehicles near the aircraft; but that they were just a precaution and not to worry. We were then given vectors for the approach to Runway XYR; giving us time to brief our approach and landing; complete our in-range; approach; and landing checklists. We completed a normal landing; taxied back to our departure gate of XXX with an emergency escort; and arrived at the gate without issue.It would have been wise to perform the takeoff abort procedure at the earliest possible indication of an abnormal situation while the airspeed was still low and safe to do so. This would have prevented handling the aircraft issued in the air. Additionally; it is important to always confirm guarded switches with our fellow crew members to avoid making a stressful and abnormal situation worse.

E-175 flight crew reported an uneventful diversion due to Hazmat loading issue due to missing NOTOC at departure.

After sorting out an issue in ZZZ of not getting a cargo load report (CLR) notes on ACARS on any live animals. The flight crew simply asked [the] ramp agents to resend it. They were unable to do so so we simply asked for a paper CLR. The Ramp Lead became flustered with his scanner and went to go ask a manager for help. The manager came back about 10 minutes later after we had closed and gave the flight crew the notice to Captain form (first time we discovered there was dangerous goods onboard) and resent the CLR with the notes on DG (Dangerous Goods) and live animal (I noticed the bird and medical boxes on my walk around but didn't notice any markings on the medical boxes pertaining to DG). Already delayed pushing back we then became saturated with a runway change. Reaching cruise we became talking more about the lack of NOTOC (Notice to Captain) and an impending incident report. After talking for a few moments at cruise. I realized that we are not allowed to be carrying both dry ice and any live animals in the forward cargo bin together. After bringing that to light I began inquiring about possible diversion options. Including the destination of ZZZ1 40-45 minutes out. After the Captain messaged with Dispatch we decided to divert to ZZZ2 as that was the fastest option to separate the dry ice and live animal. Landing and taxing in we made sure we had a ramp crew that was informed of the situation and needing to open the fwd cargo door asap and remove the live animal. As well as a gate in ZZZ2. I went down to check as soon as the jet bridge was pulled up. And when I got down there the bird was out of the fwd cargo and in good health. The live bird was ok and the ramp agents took the bird into the office to be in the air conditioning and off the loud ramp environment while the ramp crew and flight crew figured out a new bag count. Cargo count. And any other required paperwork. I began calling for fuel. Loading in the new flight plan from the release while the Captain went down to talk to ramp managers as to what cargo is staying or going. A new and confirmed bag count after ZZZ2 rampers recounted bags and cargo (which did not match the original bag count out of ZZZ even though we only removed the DG) was received.After getting everything all figured out in ZZZ2 we calmly talked to the passengers and gave them a timeline of when we would expect to be pushing back and going to ZZZ1. After getting to ZZZ1. And finishing the flight. Deplaning. And; making sure the live animal was ok and in the possession of ZZZ1 Ramp Operations. The Captain and I began debriefing today's events. We reconstructed a timeline. No cargo load remarks. Called OPS. They began to get flustered about their system. We then just asked for a paper cargo load report to remedy the glitch in the system. The Ramp Manager came and threw though the window a notice to Captain. This was the very first time we realized we had any DG onboard. We then hyper focused on the problem of closing without a NOTOC and making sure to talk to OPS and Ground. When talking about this in the air. I realized the problem of the DG and live animal in the same compartment. We quickly then realized that this was not a situation that could continue. We began looking at diversion options. Talking to Dispatch and ZZZ2 OPS. We diverted and handled the situation at hand going forward. We talked about how there are numerous safeguards to never let a situation like this happen before it even gets to the airplane or airport/cargo processing counter for that matter. And how this is a prime example of reasons [for the] swiss cheese model. Starting early this morning with 3 runway changes and a wrong turn on a taxiway resulting in the first ASAP. Airline's ramp scanning system and software letting these be scanned together or a safeguard overridden to let this happen. Us hyperfocusing on discovering DG was onboard after closing with no NOTOC. And resulting in missing the combined DG and live animal in the same cargo compartment until cruise flight. Going forward and learning from this. This is a prime example of how to simply complete tasks and move on without hyperfocusing on the previous threats or errors.

Today I; while operating Aircraft X from ZZZ-ZZZ1; made a grave mistake and allowed myself to depart ZZZ with dry ice and a parrot in the forward cargo bin. Upon discovering my mistake I contacted Dispatch and subsequently diverted to ZZZ2. The parrot was alive and we got some gas and continued onto ZZZ1 without further incident. While in ZZZ my FO (First Officer) noticed a big parrot and some medical looking boxes sitting outside cargo bin during preflight. He brought it to my attention. I was focused on making sure we had one or the other listed on load remarks. We got our baggage data but it did not generate a load remarks message. I released parking break while talking to [the] Ramp Lead via interphone. I inquired as to why we did not have a load remarks message. I asked if he could resend it. He was unsure of everything and went to find his supervisor. At this time I could not confirm if we had an animal or DG or both. I called Dispatch to see if he could look at stuff for me and he confirmed we got bag total the weight of some cargo thru close out but no load remarks. As a side bar I spoke with Name1 on the Hazmat hotline and he stated that company had to manually override scanner to allow for DG and animal at same time. Could this be why we didn't get load remarks? After about 10 minutes; [a] ramp agent returned but paced. He did not get back on intercom during most of this but when he did I explained he had a couple options. We could do a return to gate or they could give me a paper CLR (Cargo Load Report) thru [the] window if they could not fix it with [the] scanner. He radioed someone and a minute or so later a supervisor came out of an office and did not look happy. He had a wad of paper. He came to FO side and tossed the wad of paper thru window which ended up being the NOTOC for the dry ice. At about the same time we received the load remarks and I was focused on the DG the live animal got past me. I did not do this on purpose. At the time I was more upset with blocking out without the knowledge of DG on board and focused on making sure I had all my correct paperwork and it matched since I had DG. We also had the remark 'EXST:9A'. This threw me for a loop because I didn't know what it meant. We figured it out to be that a passenger had bought a seat onboard a raft for an animal which I already knew about because of gate agents and flight attendants. We had wasted enough time so I decided to continue with the push. We had a runway change on taxi out so I focused on getting thru that and we as a crew focused on operating safely until we were in a low workload environment to talk about it again. At cruise I was filling out incident report for not getting NOTOC when I was talking my narrative out loud the FO was looking at [the] FOM and said we have both an animal and DG on board and he just realized it as he was reading and telling me. We immediately contacted Dispatch who advised us to go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 and divert. I chose ZZZ2. I alerted [the] flight attendants and we landed in ZZZ2 without further incident. There was confusion on [the] ground in ZZZ2 as to which item should continue with us. The bird or dry ice. I called Dispatch again and they chose the dry ice and while I was talking to ramp they said company wanted to keep bird to ZZZ1. While checking packages manually in cargo bin I discovered the DG also contained Blood. UN3373. After OPS and company agreed; we departed to ZZZ1 without further incident. After landing I called Hazmat hotline and submitted pictures of bird and DG and ACARS remarks to company.I did not purposefully depart without NOTOC or depart consciously knowing we had dry ice and a bird in same bin. I know it's one or the other. I was just hyper focused on being legal that I missed connecting the two together. I believe I realize now that I can take as much time as I need to make good decisions. No need to rush. I did and it got me nowhere. I hope someone can imagine getting a wadof paper thrown into flight deck and the distractions of finally realizing the gravity of I had almost departed without knowing what was in cargo bin. I had always believed there were safeguards in place to prevent this from happening. This is the first time in 15 years of safe flying I've had to divert for a bad decision I made. I feel horrible and I'm glad the animal was still alive. I know it could have been much worse. I believe this flight had a happy outcome because of Dispatch and my crew. I tried to thank them but I cannot thank them enough.

TRACON Controller reported working a RADAR Positions in the TRACON combined and having too many aircraft resulting in a sequence that was not desired and a possible loss of separation.

I'm not sure if; or how many errors I had; but I'm submitting this report for consideration. Everything described below happened within about 3 minutes and it wasn't until the dust settled about a half hour later I had time to reflect on things and wonder what just happened. I took [position name] Radar at or around XA:57z. I was working all TRACON airspace combined; no hand-off; no radar split and no CIC to help. I was all things TRACON. Sector was busy with; I don't know; 12; maybe 15 flights of aircraft talking to me. Everything fell to pieces 5 minutes after taking the position.Aircraft X [flight of 2 VFR] were returning from the Range Complex from the south; set up for about a 10 nm left base; coming fast; at 310 kts to beat Aircraft Y straight in for RWY XXR. I vectored Aircraft Y on a 270 Hdg down to 7000 (6500 mva) for sequencing to follow the Aircraft X [flight]. At or around XB:02Z; Aircraft Z in the southwest practice area; about 12 - 15 nm southwest of ZZZ called me but was blocked. He called again and stated he is 'Priority inbound; my engine just let go'. I told him to enter left traffic RWYXXR; I called Ground Control on the override; told them to roll the equipment for Aircraft Z emergency inbound had lost his engine. I tagged Aircraft Z as an emergency and then started issuing traffic to Aircraft Z to follow the Aircraft X flight; about 8nm straight in. I knew I needed to slow the problem down; and began by slowing my Aircraft A on north downwind to 180kts. I slowed Aircraft Y and all the other traffic in the queue to 180 kts and began vectoring people wide for sequencing. I looked about 15 nm east and realized Aircraft Y was at 6100 in my 6500 MVA; and descending! I told him to maintain 6500 (forgot to say low altitude alert). He acknowledged and descended to 5700. I told him to climb immediately to 9000 no delay through 8000. I needed to break him out to the south because it was going to be a three-way tie with him; Aircraft X and Aircraft Z. I had to get him above my MVA's to break him out to the south for re sequencing.Without benefit of reviewing the tapes to hear the audio; I'm very sure Aircraft Y was never cleared for a visual approach; but maybe I did and that was why he was so low. Again; I don't have tapes to listen to and there's no management in the building to help me answer that question. Did I miss him read-back a wrong altitude? At some point in this fiasco; I realized the Aircraft Z way too fast (280kts) and catching the Aircraft X flight and told tower to move the Aircraft X flight to the south runway; 'Aircraft Z does not have them in sight'.By now; Aircraft Y was at 6000 slowly climbing but still in the face of Aircraft Z; 5 nm opposite direction at 6000; talking to tower with the Aircraft X flight are on short final. Next thing I know Aircraft Z is basing at 5000 and the Aircraft X flight are in the flare. Aircraft Z had his hands full and mis judged his approach so he made S-Turns or a right 360 on final to get down and land. I got Aircraft Y out of 7000 and turned him Heading 230 for sequencing following another flight of Aircraft X flight on a dogleg to follow the Aircraft A on the north downwind and another commercial aircraft straight in. All the fighters and air carriers parked north side and wanted RWY XXR; but I knew it would close behind the Aircraft Y so I changed them all to the south runway. I got everyone in line; speed controlled; cleared and visual separation applied.I switched Aircraft Y to the tower earlier than I would normally when I saw the Aircraft Z starting to base to about a 3 mile final and put him on the tower for landing clearance. I don't think I ever got a response from him that he had Aircraft X flight in sight. I was very rattled; in damage control mode and trying to fix the air carrier too low on final where I didn't expect him to be.Now that I had time to think about what just happened. Here's what I don't know:1.) Did Aircraft Z have Aircraft X in sight and pilot applied visual separation? He flew around a bit on final and maybe even 360'd; was above the Aircraft X flight altitude at all times; was never behind them on final but did overfly the south final to maneuver north of it for XXR. 2.) Did I clear Aircraft Y for Visual approach? I don't think so because I was intending to have him follow Aircraft X flight and I didn't even have time to try and tell him about Aircraft X flight yet. Did he read-back an incorrect altitude when I told him 7000? If he did; I didn't catch it. Did he bust his altitude assignment? I believe he did because I wouldn't have issued such a low altitude in that 6500/7100/8000/9000 area on our final extending out from 20 nm. What was he doing so low in there? Well; for starters; I should have said 'LOW ALTITUDE ALERT' to Aircraft Y when he was at 6100' in my 6500 MVA. It was just unreal; I couldn't believe what I was seeing. What was he doing below 6500 there? I didn't clear him yet! I told him to climb; he acknowledged yet he descended further to 5700'! I was incredulous and told him to immediately climb through 8000 to maintain 9000. He finally understood that and did what I instructed. Once Aircraft Z dropped his situation in my lap; I immediately and with out delay coordinated with the tower; did an 'EM' Slew/Enter so they could see he was the emergency and modified the SPAD for the north runway. I had data tag over-lapage (multifunction O/E doesn't work at TRACON so our auto-offset feature didn't do anything to keep data blocks from overlapping) and I didn't realize Aircraft Z was SO fast on a 2nm downwind. With the Aircraft X flight on a 5 nm straight in that math wasn't gonna work. He was catching them FAST and I pointed out traffic; he said 'looking'. I know he was busy and in a bind and I needed him to see those Aircraft X flight. I tried to fix it; saw that Aircraft Z was in position; already basing; needing a landing clearance; not going to physically catch the Aircraft X flight so I dumped him to the tower so I could try and fix the Aircraft Y who was not doing anything I wanted; needed or expected him to do. Plus; I had 12 other pilots going places and calling me all this time too. Everything transpired in 3 minutes; from the time I understood Aircraft Z was in trouble to the time where he was on final and I could deal with the other traffic.There's nothing that can be done 'to prevent a re-occurrence of this event'. You can't anticipate emergencies. That said; I should have issued a low altitude alert; and I should have had the Aircraft Z call the Aircraft X in sight or break the Aircraft X flight off final; sterilize everything and let the Aircraft Z do his thing. Also; this very same Aircraft Z has pulled this stunt on me in the past. He called with an engine failure; bombing into the left downwind at 280-300 kts. Prior to this incident; I didn't have other traffic to conflict with him. This was a rapidly devolving situation I did my best to manage and in retrospect realize a couple lapses in my control actions. I was just working the problem in the moment; trying to make planes miss and not overly concerned over 'words'.

EMB-145 flight crew reported rolling off the end of the runway after struggling with directional control while rolling out on the snow-covered runway.

Prior to landing; ATIS received reported winds at 060@06KTS; 3/4SM -SN OVC004 with braking action good. Upon talking to Tower; the controller also stated that an aircraft landing approximately an hour or so earlier reported braking action good with no further reports. Upon starting the approach; we had ground contact at 3;000 ft. On about a 6-mile final to the runway the snow and rain mix got very heavy. At approximately 700 ft. we broke out with the runway in sight. Upon touching down and applying the brakes I felt and saw the aircraft begin to skid to the left as if the main wheels were sliding. Upon releasing brake pressure gently and using rudder inputs we regained directional control. Upon applying the brakes again and now the thrust reversers spooled up; the wheels slid again and abruptly caused the tail of the aircraft to yaw to the left again in a skidding motion. I then regained directional control of the aircraft with rudder inputs to regain centerline. Once I regained directional control and gently getting the brakes to work without locking up; reverse thrust was activated again with some effect and slowing the aircraft down. Upon reaching 500 ft. of runway remaining I had positive brake control. However; as slippery as the runway was; I could not make the right turn at the end of the runway onto the taxiway which would have been a 45 to 90-degree turn. making that turn with still some speed I believe would have caused the aircraft to go into an uncontrolled lateral skid causing damage to the aircraft and/or injury to passengers. The aircraft then gently departed the end of the runway about 20 ft. the aircraft did not sink or bog. We immediately contacted the Tower and the Flight Attendant. The Flight Attendant stated that everyone was ok with no injuries. Afterwards we contacted Dispatch; Operations; and the Chief Pilot. Every five minutes or so I updated the passengers with what happened and that we were working on getting them off the aircraft. The Flight Attendant did an excellent job assisting the passengers. Operations transported the passengers to the terminal. During the deplaning of passengers; Contract Maintenance inspected the aircraft and found no damage to the aircraft. Braking action was not reported correctly. Under no circumstances was that runway good as reported. The aircraft that landed an hour or so ahead of us may have had good braking action but how much snow and rain fell within that hour? Contract maintenance told me that the reason he was on the field was due to [another] flight; which had a flap failure after landing due to the amount of snow; ice and slush trapped in the flaps after landing.I suggest runway inspections every hour.

As we approach to terminal segment of the flight; I submit a WX request through the ACARS and confirm it with the current broadcasting ATIS. The ATIS was reporting wind at 060 @ 6 kts; 3/4sm -SN OVC 400 with a braking action reported as 'good'. Also took notice at the Notam indicated the Ficon as 5/5/5. While checking in with Tower the Controller was very vague on the runway condition stating a past aircraft was able to land. At about 3;000 ft. I told the Captain that I could see some residential lights in the distance just for situational awareness. At around 700-800 ft. I was able to spot the runway approach lights; calling 'continue'; and about 3-5 second after I was able to see the runway and runway edge lights calling 'runway in sight.' The flare to the round out part of the landing were standard in nature: On speed; on centerline and on glidepath.As we touched down the Captain started applying brake and the aircraft skidded to left of centerline as if we were skidding on locked wheels. Soon after; I saw the Captain making adjustments and bring the aircraft back to the center line. Additionally; as I looked down the runway I saw with my peripheral [vision] when [the Captain] was deploying the thrust reversers and seconds after I saw them spool up. As I felt that neither the reverse thrust nor the antiskid were helping us to come to a full stop; I looked down the runway then over to the yoke just in case the Captain needed me to take over the yoke to use the tiller. This wasn't the case. On the rollout the brakes kept locking up several times and the plane kept veering to the left. [The Captain] kept applying the correction to keep on centerline. [He] kept repeating that process until he was able to regain efficient braking from the brake while keeping directional control of the aircraft.Although there was a turn at the end of the runway the Captain made the decision on keeping the aircraft [aligned] with the runway to avoid an uncontrolled spin or ground loop due to the momentum we still had and the runway condition. The aircraft then came to a full stop at the end of the runway with both main and nose in the grass and tail and rudder were still over the runway (about 20 ft.). We both coordinated with the Tower Controller; Operations; Dispatch and Flight Attendant to ensure that all the passenger were safe. The braking action was not reported correctly on the ATIS. As we locked wheels a couple of times it became apparent to us that the runway condition was 'poor.' Even thought it was reported 'good' and Ficon 5/5/5 we got little to no braking action from the runway. Also; the constant locking and sliding of the wheels made it a lot harder to come to a full stop. Lastly; it didn't seem as it was light snow although that was reported. As far as correction the airport should be more specific on the runway condition. Plow more often when the intensity of the snow increases. This event could have been avoided if we had known the actual condition of the runway.

SCT TRACON Controller and a GA pilot reported evasive action by GA pilot caused an RA for opposite direction traffic.

The VFR Aircraft; Aircraft X; was cleared on the [published VFR route] to maintain 5;500 feet. He was southbound and converging over the VOR with Aircraft Y who was IFR and descended to 5;000 feet and told about the 5;500 feet traffic that was at the time 4 miles north of the VOR. Everything was fine and it was a normal everyday situation. I was cleaning up some loose ends giving headings to other aircraft and traffic advisories; many traffic advisories. I had an aircraft report getting an RA but its resolution told him to stay where they were because there were just so many VFR's. Then I hear the Traffic Alert start which isn't uncommon for aircraft 500 feet apart in this airspace and as I look up the Aircraft Y tells me he's responding to an RA and his voice is clearly strained.I incorrectly said what I was thinking which was 'Aircraft X what are you doing! Climb immediately to 5;500' as I'm watching him descend through 5;200 feet right on top of Aircraft Y. He responds that he 'thought they were on a collision course'. To which I informed him that his actions caused the collision course. He also turned right which would have been fine if that's all he had done and stayed at 5;500 feet; but the descent made it a near or for sure mid-air if Aircraft Y hadn't taken evasive action. I issued a Brasher Warning to the pilot of Aircraft X because he 100% cause a perfectly separated situation to become a very ugly situation. Both aircraft were in the Class Bravo airspace and the VFR aircraft had no right or reason to descend at all.Over the top of LA is just a busy place where aircraft are routinely separated by 500 feet; that's just life. If they move the VFR areas where Special Flight Rules is to somewhere else then we would definitely have more altitudes to use to separate people by greater than 500 feet. but; until that happens it's just going to be what it's going to be.

While on a Class B clearance through the Class Bravo airspace on published VFR Route southbound at 5;500 feet; I received a traffic notification from Approach for traffic at 11 o'clock; opposite direction; at 5;000 MSL a conflict for traffic that was approaching nearly head-on. I continued to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; and when I finally spotted the oncoming traffic it was at my 11 o'clock to 11:30 position in my windscreen; at eye level. I was unable to discern any relative motion of the target relative to my windscreen. The only change I could see in the target was that it was getting larger in my field of view; and that it appeared to be some type of small jet aircraft. I immediately initiated a turn to my right in order to avoid the oncoming traffic. The turn that I initiated was done very quickly; and was probably on the order of a 30 to 35 degree angle of bank. As a result of this turn; I lost approximately 250 feet of altitude from my cruising altitude of 5;500 feet. My change in heading was approximately 45 degrees; and once my turn was completed I was able to discern relative motion of the target with respect to my windscreen and left side window. The traffic was now moving to my left; and the separation between the two of us was increasing.The opposite directly traffic passed well behind me. At that point the TRACON Controller called me and admonished me for deviating from my assigned heading and altitude. I responded to the controller with an apology; and explained that the opposite direction traffic appeared to be on a collision course with me; and it required me to take evasive action. The controller provided me with a toll-free number to call after I landed. After landing I called the toll-free number and spoke to an individual at SOCAL who asked me to describe the occurrence from my perspective. I described the occurrence in an identical manner to what I have written here. The individual was very courteous and listened carefully to my explanation; and thanked me for calling. The call ended with no indication to me that any further action would be forthcoming.It is extremely difficult to estimate lateral and vertical separation of traffic; especially when a target has no apparent relative motion and is approaching head-on. Any vertical separation that does exist between two aircraft in this situation will not be perceptible until the aircraft are very close together; when there is very little time to take evasive action if it is required. In this particular case; the opposite direction traffic was probably traveling at least twice as fast as my aircraft; resulting in an effective rate of closure of at least 400 MPH. A vertical separation of 500 feet is very small; and when possible sources of altitude error are included; it is possible that the actual vertical separation between our two aircraft was less than 500 feet. Approximately ten minutes after this occurrence; I was in the vicinity of another airport and was in contact with another sector of the TRACON. This Controller provided me with a traffic advisory regarding jet traffic inbound from the west at 5;000 feet; and gave me instructions to climb and maintain 6;000 feet for separation purposes. I initiated the climb and leveled off at 6;000 feet; and observed the jet traffic passed well below me. After the jet traffic had crossed my flight path; the Controller cleared me back down to 5;500 feet. I have included a description of this action on the part of Approach as an example of prudent traffic management.In summary; I should have been more diligent in maintaining my assigned altitude of 5;500 feet during my turn to avoid the oncoming traffic. However; it was my belief that there was insufficient separation between the flight paths of our two aircraft; and seeing no relative motion of a target that was at eye-level in my windscreen; as pilot-in-command of the aircraft I took evasive action in the interest of collision avoidance.

A Glider pilot reported a NMAC with a fixed wing aircraft while in a published glider flying area that is close to a busy airport on one side and a mountain range on the other.

I experienced a near midair collision while flying a glider south of the ZZZ airport. Purpose of the flight was currency since the soaring season is mostly over apart from mountain wave flying. Typically; I take a tow into the mountains to connect with the excellent soaring conditions. The plan was to stay close to the airport and perform a short pattern flight. Before the flight; I thought about the extra vigilance required due to the flight in congested airspace. Flying in the mountains presents it's own set of challenges; but from a traffic perspective it's much less stressful than flying close to the ZZZ airport. Takeoff and climbout were normal; and we were established on an easterly heading in the 'glider box' climbing through 7;200 feet when I released from the tow plane. Normal release procedure is to clear right; release from tow; and perform a slight climbing right turn to deconflict from the tow plane while the towplane performs a descending left turn. This was accomplished; and I kept the turn going to a 270 heading. Once rolling wings level at 270; I was presented with the image of a blue and white Piper Cherokee rapidly filling my windscreen head on. Time from recognition to action was within a second and I dumped the nose to build airspeed/separation and rolled right to deconflict. The Cherokee seemed to pick me up at the last minute; and I observed him making a slightly delayed climbing right turn. I estimated separation at between 100 and 200 feet. It was too close! If I remained on tow on an easterly heading; there is a very good chance the Cherokee would have flown directly into me at my 6 o'clock. Very similar to a fatal midair accident that happened 10 years ago at ZZZ between a towplane; glider; and Cirrus transitioning the area. I was on the ZZZ CTAF with the tow plane; and neither me or the tow pilot heard the Cherokee making position calls. The Cherokee continued it's flight eastbound and I made an announcement about the near miss and called his position to anyone else on frequency. Technically; nobody did anything wrong. The Cherokee was not required to make position calls. However; in the busy airspace around ZZZ this is common sense. See and avoid worked; but just barely. I was squawking 1202 (glider transponder code per Letter Of Agreement with TRACON) with a Mode S transponder. I confirmed the transponder was on during my before takeoff checklist and directly following the incident. I had a FLARM collision avoidance system installed in the glider. This picks up Mode C; Mode S; and other Flarm traffic. In the event of a conflict; there is an audible warning and the screen on the S100 variometer displays the clock position; distance; and altitude above/below of conflicting traffic. Very similar to a TCAS. It does not display resolution advisory/vertical speed required for deconfliction. The FLARM alarm did not activate; and I didn't even look at the instrument. My eyes were outside the whole time and I was very lucky they were. This comes down to solid training and a good scan. The World War II pilots had it right. 'Keep your head on a swivel'. Don't trust your traffic avoidance system to show or alert you to everything out there. TCAS; ADS-B; TIS; FLARM; etc. all offer an absolutely incredible advantage in situational awareness and safety. However; it's not a 100% solution. Many gliders and older powered aircraft don't have transponders; and a traffic avoidance system won't pick up something they can't see. You still need to look outside the cockpit.The FLARM/S100 system has certain configurations that can be set by the pilot on when to audibly and visually alert on a potential conflict. Due to flying in close proximity to the tow plane on tow; I believe it's a possible setting to inhibit warnings while on tow. Since this happened within seconds of release; it's possible that is the reason I didn't receive an alert. I'll need to do some reading of the manual and also investigatethe configuration of the S100/FLARM system installed on Aircraft X to further understand this logic. It's very possible this is my fault; and by configuring the system differently I could have avoided a slice of swiss cheese or two from lining up. It's not the people talking on the radio that will hit you; it's the people that aren't. A good scan is critical. Keep that head on a swivel and outside. When releasing from tow in the future; I'll start clearing not only my 3 to 4 o'clock but all the way to my 6 o'clock. It's unlikely I would have spotted the traffic doing that due to the headrest blocking my view directly backwards; but it's a good idea none the less. The local terrain and airspace setup cause a bottleneck between the mountains to the west and the Class B to the east. You have a lot of airplanes flying VFR in a fairly small corridor. That ups the chances for these types of incidents occurring. More education for pilots that not all traffic will be presented or presented accurately on their traffic displays. This is a perfect example. Many pilots think everything out there that can hit them will show up on Foreflight; TCAS; etc. That's absolutely not the case. Better education about the 'glider box' at ZZZ. There is a note about it on the ZZZ airport website; and in the Chart Supplement. It's buried; and realistically not many pilots read those materials for airports they will overfly. There should be a note on the Sectional about the specific dimensions/locations of the ZZZ glider box.Even better; the FAA should make a database of this type of airspace and it's dimensions and allow it to be displayed as an overlay on tools like Foreflight. Just like they do with TFRs. While the Chart Supplement is an awesome resource; my honest experience is nobody looks at it unless they are taking a checkride. Everyone uses Foreflight these days. By presenting this type of airspace as a graphical overlay on these types of moving maps/apps; you have a much higher likelihood of awareness and compliance from the pilot population. This would increase safety tremendously! This wasn't a causal factor in this incident; but easily could be in a future one. All gliders should be required to have transponders. There are plenty of people flying gliders at 17;999 feet. In busy terminal arrival and departure corridors without a transponder. The battery technology exists for this to not be a problem anymore. I can fly all day with my transponder; radio; electronic variometer; and two moving map displays without running out of battery power.

Air Carrier flight crew reported thinking they were cleared for takeoff; but were only cleared to line up and wait.

The FO told me upon our initial meeting at the gate that she had been off for the past 7 months; that she flew for the first time 'yesterday' (a ZZZ1 turn); and that this was her second day back after 7 months off. While pre-flighting and briefing on the flight deck; at Gate X; Runway XXL auto-populated for departure when the FO loaded the FMC; as it usually does for a destination airport to the west (ZZZ2 in this case). I told the FO that; during COVID; we often get east side departure runways (ie; [Runway XXR in this case) when we depart from east side gates. So; I told her; she could change it to XXR now; if she wanted to; or we could leave YYL in the box; wait for our runway assignment; and I would taxi very slowly while she loaded the box if we got the east side. We left YYL in the box. We departed the Ramp from Spot X and Ground assigned XXR; which was a very short taxi from Spot X. I made the Takeoff PA; and; as I said I would; I taxied very slowly while the FO loaded the box with the new data; read the Legs page aloud (from the new runway) as I followed along on the ZZZZZ 3 Dept on my iPad; and briefed the Takeoff Data. As we were in the middle of the pad; northbound on taxiway; still fairly far from the departure end of the runway; Tower asked if we were up. The FO said we were. Tower then asked if we would be ready at the end. The FO and I briefly checked with each other and acknowledged that; yes; we would be ready at the end. In my recollection; I then heard 'RNAV to ZZZZZ1; Cleared for Takeoff; XXR.' I chimed the flight attendants and turned on my two Landing Light switches; which is something I purposefully only do once Cleared for Takeoff. The FO finished the checklist with plenty of time (everything was properly set up before she began it); and prior to crossing the hold short line onto XXR; she said something like; 'I'm pretty sure I heard Cleared for Takeoff; but do you want me to verify with them?' I looked at my Landing Lights; saw that I had moved them to the ON position; which I 'only do' once cleared for Takeoff; and thought I specifically heard 'RNAV to ZZZZZ1; Cleared for Takeoff.' So; I said to her; 'No. I don't need you to verify. I heard Cleared for Takeoff; too. ... But please ... verify if you want to! Do you want to?' She said something like; 'No; I think we're good. We both heard the same thing.' I said something like; 'I specifically remember hearing 'RNAV to ZZZZZ1;' which they never say until they clear us for Takeoff. We're okay.'While on the Takeoff Roll and prior to V1; Tower called; 'Aircraft X?' We did not answer. They called again once we were airborne and told us to fly Runway Heading. I pretty much knew at that point that we either were NOT cleared for Takeoff ... OR we WERE cleared for Takeoff and the Tower Controller forgot that he cleared us. Shortly after that call; the Tower Controller said something like; 'Aircraft X; Possible Pilot Deviation; Advise when ready to copy.' And of course; at this point; I had a very sinking feeling. We copied down the number for Tower. Once clean and on our way; I sincerely apologized to the Tower and told him that; in my recollection; he asked us; while we were still fairly far back in the pad; if we would be ready at the end; we said we would; and then he cleared us 'RNAV to ZZZZZ1; Cleared for Takeoff.' He apologized as well; for any confusion; and we went on our way to ZZZ1. Naturally; I had a sinking feeling that perhaps I was at fault ... but I also thought my memory of it was clear ... and I felt just a little hopeful by the fact that the FO and I both independently thought we were cleared for Takeoff. Once at the gate at destination and off of the aircraft; I called the number for ZZZ East Tower. I spoke with a very professional; very kind gentlemen who said he had listened to the tape 3 times and that we were only cleared to Line Up and Wait. I felt so very disappointed with myself at that point.I see several causal factors in thisevent. The number one Causal Factor in my mind was that I should have immediately said to the FO; when she asked me if I wanted her to clarify while crossing the Hold Short Line; 'Yes! Please clarify. Thank you!' If there's ANY doubt in ANYBODY'S mind; then clarify! There were other Causal Factors as well. Two: the FO was on her second day back from a 7 month leave. She was a good stick and has good general knowledge; but she was very understandably 'slower in hearing' and 'slower in doing' than she otherwise would have been had she been more current. Reduced currency of either party in a two-person cockpit; particularly on the first leg of a trip; often results in a more cumbersome; somewhat disjointed crew coordination experience. And that is how I experienced the beginning of our first leg together -- less coordinated than usual; but understandably so. I say this with no disregard or criticism of the FO; who does very good work; and is clearly a sharp; experienced; very good pilot. Three: this was our first leg together of our first day together. We were just getting used to working together as we pre-flighted and taxied out. Four: For many months now; with fewer operating flights; we are often assigned east side runways when departing from east side gates. This is something that is fairly recent in ZZZ; presumably because of reduced operations during COVID and because of runway construction on the west side. However; particularly when departing from Spots X; Y; or Z; and no other aircraft in sight (as was the case this morning); a runway XXR departure often results in a crunch period while the FO re-loads the FMC and re-verifies the departure LEGS page while I cross-check the chart. Though I did not personally feel rushed; and though the FO said she did not feel rushed; a last-minute runway change is just one more thing to do on a short taxi. Five: I long ago established in my mind that I would not turn on the Landing Lights until Cleared for Takeoff. But today; I clearly; for some reason; turned them on anyway when we were apparently NOT cleared for takeoff ... and then I fairly comfortably relied on the fact that I turned them on as further evidence that we WERE cleared for takeoff. Six: It was fairly unusual in ZZZ to be cleared for Takeoff OR Line Up and Wait; from such a distance from the runway. Today; we were still fine-tuning our crew coordination and were working in a more disjointed way than usual. I was taxiing very slowly; and while time didn't consciously seem to be a factor to me (the FO was done with all duties well before we crossed the Hold Short line and entered the runway); I was aware that the FO was briefing me; checking the box; and starting the checklist; at the time that Tower called us ... AND that we accepted an important clearance in the midst of what was actually a very busy time. It is my guess that the distractions of our work at hand; at that time; interfered with the way we each interpreted the clearance. And we later learned that we interpreted it incorrectly. I have no other explanation for the misunderstanding and am still surprised that both the FO and I jointly misunderstood. I have several suggestions ... mostly for myself ... as to how I will prevent this type of event from occurring in the future. Starting from the beginning; in point of time ... ONE: Over the next few days I am going to give strong consideration to the idea of directing the FO to change the auto-populated runway in the FMC RTE Page AT THE GATE; to match the runway that I'm expecting for departure; or at least to match the runway that is closest to the departure gate. It will be less disruptive to change a runway during taxi out to a runway that is FARTHER AWAY from us; than it is to change a runway during taxi out to a runway that is much closer to us. TWO: As the FO loaded the runway change; briefed the takeoff data; ran the checklist; and answered the Tower's call and clearance; despite the fact that there was plenty of distance and time between us and the runway; and despite the fact that I knew I was in control of how fast I taxied (two factors I considered while all this was going on); it would have been so much wiser to tell the Tower controller to Standby rather than taking on One More Thing while on the taxi out. Perhaps if we were not so busy during that particular time when Tower called; we may have heard the proper clearance exactly as it was issued! THREE: It would have been wise to simply say to the FO; 'Don't worry about time at all. We will plan on stopping short of the runway and taking a close look at all of this together.' Particularly under the circumstances (the FO's lack of currency); that would have been the smart-and-considerate-Captain thing to do. I regret not making that choice. It would have removed all pressure. I will be particularly vigilant with less-current and/or new FO's; but I will also try to be mindful of this option in all circumstances. I fear that I may have rushed the FO. FOUR: It was extraordinarily foolish of me not to take the FO up on her suggestion that we clarify the clearance! She asked me if I wanted her to. I should have simply said 'YES! PLEASE! And THANK YOU!' For this; I am most regretful. The answer; ALWAYS; when there is ANY doubt from ANYBODY is to say; YES; Please Clarify! FIVE: And on that note; I will no longer let my own habits lull me into any false sense of security. I have the habit of turning on the Landing Lights ONLY AFTER I have been Cleared for Takeoff. I turned on the Landing Lights while still taxiing north on taxiway; and then I allowed my own habit to lull me into a sense of security that I HAD BEEN cleared. But that was foolishness. I apparently misheard the clearance while distracted by several other obligations. The fact that I turned the lights on; or participated in any other habit of my own; does not necessarily mean I heard or interpreted anything correctly. I will be more vigilant in the future.

Our flight was cleared to taxi to [Runway] XXR in ZZZ. We were taxiing on a parallel toward the end of XXR. There were no airplanes in line and about 200 yards from the end of runway Tower asked if we were ready at the end. I acknowledged we were. We both believed he then cleared us for takeoff. As we turned the corner toward the runway I questioned myself and asked the Captain if we were indeed cleared for takeoff. The Captain said yes; but also added I could verify if I wanted too. I felt almost sure we were cleared for takeoff; so I felt comfortable not asking tower. On takeoff roll we were told of the deviation.This was my second day of work coming back from a 7 month leave. Although it was a short taxi I felt comfortable and prepared for the takeoff. Just prior to the 'clearance' I was busy; but felt we had caught up with everything when he asked if we were going to be ready at the end. I do not know how both the Captain and myself felt certain we were cleared for takeoff. It was quite shocking to find out we were wrong. Even though I questioned myself; I really thought we were cleared to go.My biggest takeaway is whenever I question myself on a clearance just ask ATC to clarify. That would have been the best option. In the future if I doubt myself I will do this first; if possible. Now that I have had this experience; I will most certainly never accept a -- 'TO clearance' -- so far from the end of a runway without clarifying with Tower before TO.

EMB 175 flight crew reported brief heading deviation that resulted from a non-existent waypoint entered into the Flight Management System.

We were departing from Pittsburgh Airport. We took off on runway 28R and were assigned runway heading.Our flight plan first fix was AHTIY (then to BURGS). We briefed the route during preflight and of course verified that the course looked like it should.Shortly after takeoff; we were given a turn to the left to 'eighty' which I know from prior experience is how they pronounce that first fix; AHTIY. We brought that point up in our flight plan; inserted it into the FMS (Flight Management System) direct; agreed; then activated. The turn was a very sharp left. Once we realized we were turning toward the airport and away from our course; we briefly discussed amongst ourselves that the seemed strange. I immediately called up to verify that our clearance was a left turn direct 'eighty' (or AHTIY.) ATC (Air Traffic Control) confirmed but immediately told us to turn right to a heading of 180 'one eighty'. We started a turn to 180 but it only added to the confusion because now I thought that perhaps when I had heard 'eighty' earlier maybe I misunderstood and it was actually a heading of 'one eighty'.Once we were on that heading; we were cleared again 'direct AHTIY'. I read it back very slowly and asked to confirm that we would make a right turn direct to the fix. He said; 'Affirmative... Direct Alpha Hotel Tango India Yankee.' It was then that I realized that the point I had on my flight plan in the FMS had the T & the I switched... AHITY. I proceeded to type in the correct spelling; we agreed and flew toward AHTIY. At this point; I thought that the point AHITY actually existed over the top of Pittsburgh Airport. I found that to be a really strange placement for such a closely spelled GPS (Global Positioning System) fix to AHTIY. Upon beginning this report; I looked at my charts to verify where that fix was located. The fix doesn't seem to exist. I racked my brain to try to figure out how the fix existed in that plane but not on my chart. Then I remembered that pilots can create their own waypoints. Normally; if a fix does not exist; the FMS pulls up an option to create a pilot waypoint. I can tell you with 100% certainty but this did not happen to me when I was entering the flight plan. However; because it took my false waypoint without the prompt to create it; I can deduce that someone created that way point in that database prior to my typing it. At this point; someone must have created a misspelled version of AHTIY as AHITY. It was then that I remembered a detail that I had deemed unimportant prior to this. When we began entering the flight plan; the First Officer was holding the paperwork. He had started to enter the flight plan and then stopped. When I asked if he was doing it or if he wanted me to; he said that he decided to stop and get the ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) first so I could do it. He spelled the first point for me as AHITY and I typed it. I then picked up the other copy of the flight plan and told him I would use that for the routing if he wanted to get the ATIS. I continued with BURGS and so on. I wanted to confirm my suspicions about this waypoint so I looked up the crew for the outbound flight on that aircraft. The First Officer happens to be a friend of mine. I called her and I asked her to pull up the pilot created waypoint list. She did; and sure enough there was a fix called AHITY. I had her take a photo of the coordinates for that point and send it to me. I also asked her to please delete the point from the database. I spoke with my First Officer today about user created waypoints. He says he did not create AHITY. Either way; it was a point in the pilot waypoint database and thus allowed me to use it in my flight plan.An unfortunate series of events seems to have led up to us turning toward a non-existent point. Luckily there was no mention of pilot deviation or loss of separation with any aircraft; but a mistake was still made.In the future; I will make apoint to double check the spelling of all waypoints along the route myself. We did not catch it on our verbal route review because we read it as the first fix despite the 2 letters being switched. It didn't look much different. I have certainly learned a lot from this experience; and will do my best to ensure that this does not happen again to me or anyone that I fly with. The only suggestion I have is perhaps to request that the company send a reminder to the pilot group to refresh everyone about pilot created waypoints.
