I would emphasize that if you do create a waypoint; you should only do it if you are doing it purposefully and using the coordinates on your chart. Then; after the flight; you should delete that point so that we don't have non-existent points in our database.

Flight crew reported receiving an obstacle alert on a night visual approach to OKC.

During vectors into OKC from the east; the Approach Controller assigned us Runway 17R differently from the one we had setup (17L). After re-configuring for the ILS 17R; I asked the Pilot Monitoring to brief the approach so I can concentrate on flying (Approximately 14;000 feet MSL and descending to 4;000 feet). During the brief a bright shining white light; like a spotlight shined at us; caught our attention and cause a distraction. We still conducted the briefing; including the highest elevation figure. As I kept flying I was paying attention if the light shined us again; in the event it was a laser that needed to be reported. I had the terrain page setup from the previous briefing and both pilots were aware of the obstacle northeast of the airport (Antenna 2758 feet MSL). After the briefing was complete; we were given a vector (a 90 degree angle) for the approach within a close proximity of the Final Approach Fix (minimum altitude at FAF 3;000 feet MSL). This vector would have flown us south of the obstacle depicted in the plan view section of the approach chart. Approximately 18NM from the airport the Approach Controller queried the visual contact of the airport. Pilot Monitoring told me he had contact with it and after I picked it up in sight I asked to call for it if he still had it. At that point the Approach Controller cleared us for the visual approach for [Runway] 17R. Slightly after; the Approach Controller notified us of traffic on the approach to the parallel runway. Both pilots were trying to ID the traffic since it was below our altitude and we had to cross his approach path. We seemed clear of the traffic; but a strong wind from the south was drifting us north which cause a concern for us due to the known obstacle. The aircraft was just approaching 4;000 feet of altitude and started to level off; when I set 3;000n in the Altitude Select box. The aircraft transitioned into a shallow descent instead of holding 4;000 since it wasn't fully captured. While having a discussion about the wind I adjusted my heading and kept the descent to 3;000 feet so we could be close to level and slow when we intercepted the course outside of the FAF. Around 3500 feet we both remembered the obstacles when we saw its lights ahead and below us. I already started a transition into a climb when the Pilot Monitoring verbally reminded me of the obstacles. During the climb we got a 'Caution Obstacle'; due to the projected descent; which was removed shortly since we were already compensating. We were 500 to 700 feet above the highest obstacle. The obstacle represented on the MFD was not the highest elevation figure on the IAP chart. This depicted obstacle was part of another group of towers not depicted on the chart but they can be seen on the VFR chart in the Jeppesen app. Since it was a visual approach; I had focused on maintaining the airport inside; and started to descend and slow down so we could be on a good position for the stable approach. Following the event; we landed with no issues and had a discussion at the gate on how we could have mitigated our error. We were below the MSA and had loss awareness of the obstacles due to other distractions and the tight vector to the approach with the visual approach. Several factors played key roles for the loss of situational awareness that led us to be at a lower altitude for our location. Flags:-A night Visual approach into an airport were an obstacle is a threat.-A night Visual approach to an airport were the elevation of the airport is higher than we are normally used to.-An arrival consisting of an extended base into a visual approach rather than a downwind arrival.-The change of runway that led to a new setup and briefing.-The distractions caused by the wind-drift; traffic; and the bright light.-The tight vector given and accepted for the original approach. Our error was the premature descent to 3000 feet with the goal of not being high once we intercept the final course with short distance to the final fix. Although the setup for the approach included the awareness of terrain and using the terrain displayed as an aid; we should have use TEM to establish a plan to avoid the premature descent. A briefed plan of using the last assigned altitude of 4;000 feet until intercepting would have avoided this. During the approach brief; I should have asked my Pilot Monitoring to intervene in the event I set a lower altitude while maneuvering for the visual (mitigation plan in the vent of losing SA). I realized that our briefings cover informational items that could be threats but we should discuss mitigating plans for them. Other actions that could have been taken are: 1) denying the visual at night due to the obstacle; 2) requesting a vector for the visual; and 3) querying if a lower altitude was needed which would have led the Controller to keep us at 4;000 feet.

I was Pilot Monitoring. Approximately 20min out we were giving the option to change our landings intentions from [Runway] 17L to 17R which we took. Captain asked me if I could brief the approach which I did and then we performed the runway change items from the checklist. During this briefing moment we both noticed a bright light from about a 12 o'clock position which caught our attention. Captain was aware of the obstacles to the northeast of the airport (antennas) and turned on the terrain. At approximately 18 miles out we were asked if we had the airport in sight. We both saw it and were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17R. Winds were out of the south at approximately 26kt pushing us to the north since we were coming from the east. We were at 4;000 ft. and began a gradual descent. ATC advised us of traffic at 11 o'clock landing on the parallel runway. Looking for the traffic we began to noticed the red lights of the obstacles (towers) on the northeast of the airport. I pointed them out as [did] the Captain. The altitude window was set for 3;000 ft. we were currently at 3;400 ft. Captain turned off the autopilot and began a climb. As we were climbing we received a Caution for the obstacle but it cleared quickly since the Captain had already began the climb. Once cleared we continue to intercept the final approach course and perform a normal landing. We both had a long discussion after the flight and both agreed that we should had mitigated this by simply staying at 4;000ft when cleared for the visual approach since we knew about the MSA which is 3;800 ft. Also the parallel traffic played a role on this since we started looking for it due to it being in our path for intercepting the final approach course of [Runway] 17R. As a Pilot Monitoring I should had advised the Captain that selecting 3;000 ft. and continuing the descent once cleared for the visual would had put us close to the highest obstacle stated in the approach plate. I will keep this in consideration for future flights to come ensuring we are not at a lower altitude than the MSA not established on a final approach course as well as keeping in mind obstacles around us at all times.

Flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC departing MSO when they had a track deviation following communication difficulties.

We briefed the route and departure; to include the [engine failure] procedures. We confirmed the route in the FMS. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; We turned to heading 189 and hit moderate or greater turbulence and mountain waves; which significantly affected us. I had trouble communicating with ATC and performing cockpit duties due to turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 AGL; Tower said switch to departure. Upon contacting departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to a fix'; but the radio quality of the transmission was poor and we couldn't clearly hear the name of the fix. I realized the mountain was on our path and for an immediate left turn to avoid terrain. The Spokane Departure Controller cleared us direct to a fix by name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling; which I couldn't understand due to significant turbulence and poor radio quality. We continued normal flap retraction callouts and takeoff profile. We were given heading a 120; to which we turned; and it took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. We were mistakenly trying to navigate to ENY VOR which caused us to be confused and task saturated. Once we got the correct identifier for HIA and entered into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. This caused the controller to get a low altitude alert although we did not receive any terrain avoidance warnings from our aircraft. In retrospect; the controller admitted on our phone conversation afterwards that this situation is very common. There are a lot of risks and stressors associated with this MZULA.MSO RWY12 and I feel like our outside resources did not help the flight crew. We accept full responsibility for allowing this situation to develop; but changes to this procedure will greatly increase safety in the future.First our Jeppesen charts had no verbal narrative and left us needing FAA charts to understand the procedure. It would be a great help if the procedure could be simplified or the controller's expectations that are outside the procedure could be communicated before we hit significant turbulence. The controller was clearly frustrated with us which only made our situation worse by trying to give us a phone number during a high stress and high workload phase of flight in significant turbulence. This shows the controllers are not fully aware of what human factors the flight crews have and how to help safety of flight. Having poor radio transmission quality was also a significant factor.

I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying departing MSO. I received and read back the clearance from ATC which included the MZULA5 Departure MSO transition. I programmed this into our FMS and the Captain and I thoroughly reviewed the route in the FMS and on our Jeppesen plates. We also briefed the procedure for engine failure departure. In my takeoff briefing I again described the departure we were assigned. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; I turned to heading 189 as charted. Immediately we began to encounter moderate turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 ft AGL; Tower said switch to Departure. Upon contacting Departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to ________ ' but it was very turbulent and we did not clearly hear the name of the fix. I immediately realized the flight director was not commanding a left turn in accordance with the charted procedure. The Captain asked to say again the fix; and the controller said the name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling. At 1;000 ft AGL; I called out 'flight level change'; followed by the normal flap retraction callouts and told him we needed a left turn since I knew from the charted SID that's what we were supposed to do. Meanwhile the Captain was trying to get clarification on the fix to which we were to proceed. We knew it would be a left turn so he asked for a left turn and we were given heading 120; to which we turned. During this entire time it was very turbulent and took a lot of effort and concentration to focus on safe flying. It took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. Once we got the correct identifier and entered it into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However; this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. During this time; we had terrain radar displayed on our MFD and were well aware of our surroundings and the location of rising terrain; and at no time did we ever get a terrain caution or warning.Although the SID was correctly programmed into the FMS; for unknown reasons the Flight Director did not command the left turn to intercept the MSO 159 radial. The extreme turbulence and difficulty understanding ATC instructions caused a delay in turning to the assigned fix; resulting in a course deviation. First of all; given our route of flight; it would have made much more sense if; in the pre-departure clearance; we would have been given the Salmon transition. This fact was even stated by the ATC supervisor on the phone when I called him after we landed. He further stated they have had frequent problems with pilots and aircraft not following the procedure we were assigned. Second; I could have anticipated a potential issue; and tuned the MSO VOR in NAV 1 and 2; along with the radial to intercept prior to takeoff. If I return to MSO in the future; I will definitely do that as a backup in case this kind of thing should happen again. I realized we were supposed to be turning left; which is why we asked for a left turn in the interim while trying to get the identifier for the fix and get that loaded in the FMS. The significant turbulence and the communication difficulties with ATC were definitely contributing factors in this temporary deviation. Nonetheless; as a pilot it is my responsibility to safely and correctly fly the plane; so I will ensure I have a backup navigation source programmed and ready in the future. And if I go back there again and get assigned that same SID; I will ask for the Salmon transition rather than the MSO transition; as suggested by the ATC supervisor. Finally I will brief my Captain on what happened previously so we can be vigilant and prepared.

C150 pilot reported multiple issues with the passenger door opening in flight on a rental plane.

The planned flight was VFR from ZZZ to ZZZ1 via ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 at XA:00 on November [date] 2020 in Aircraft X (Cessna 150) rented from Company. I was PIC; Person Y was the only passenger. We had previously flown Aircraft X on July [date] 2020 from ZZZ; ZZZ4; ZZZ3 and had noted that the passenger door was not closing properly -- a small gap in the upper-left corner of the window frame allowed wind to enter the cabin. The owner of the plane investigated the issue then and found that the upper window frame was bent. I assumed that the issue was fixed by an A&P mechanic after the investigation. The plane has been regularly flown by other pilots since July.On November [date] 2020; I noticed no irregularities during pre-flight. During run-up; I noticed that the gap in the passenger door was still present and was a bit bigger than I remembered it from July. I thought that the slight wind in the cabin would be unpleasant but not otherwise an issue and continued with the flight. During the take-off roll just after rotation; the passenger door swung open. Once we were stabilized on the downwind; I shut the door and reassured my passenger. However the passenger door swung open again -- the wind through the upper-left gap torqued the entire door outward and that overpowered the door latch. So I requested landing clearance from ZZZ Tower and executed a precautionary landing without any incident. I taxied back to parking; shut off the engine and investigated the passenger door. The upper window frame was flexing slightly and could be bent to snap into the correct position. I pushed the frame into the correct position; verified that the frame was now snug against all the door frame inserts and that no wind was leaking into the cabin.I took off from ZZZ around XB:00 and noted no issues this time. As we were transitioning ZZZ3 Class D airspace; my passenger noted that she heard some sound from her door. I verified that the gap in the window frame was not present and that the door was shut properly. Shortly after we flew through the Class D; my passenger also reported that she could feel cold air from near the lower-right part of her door. As we flew past the marina; the door again swung open. This time the door shook violently which caused the window also to be flung open. I requested landing clearance from ZZZ3 was given priority and then I clarified my situation. I noted that reducing the throttle helped remove the violent door shaking. I reached over to shut the door; then pulled the upper window frame back into the door inserts and then closed the window. The ATC alerted me with a low altitude warning; so I decided to ignore the door and climb 300 ft. to intercept the glide slope and fly the plane first. As I increased RPM; the door again flung open. The door was twisting and wobbling around the hinge like a sheet of paper with the hinge as a paper-clip; and either wind or resonant frequency was increasing the severity of the wobbles. My passenger held the door to dampen its shaking. The landing at ZZZ3 was without any incident; and I taxied to a maintenance shop on the field. An A&P mechanic diagnosed that the passenger door needs to be replaced entirely and that the plane was not airworthy. We drove back to ZZZ after ensuring that the owner of Aircraft X knew what had happened and where to find the plane's key.In follow-up communication with the owner; I do not believe that the plane door was inspected and fixed by an A&P mechanic in July. The owner mentioned that he adjusted the door latches and attempted to bend the window frame back into place. This 'fix' ensured that the 'door shut properly 90% of the time'. He mentioned that he drove up to ZZZ3 with a spare C150 door and replaced it -- I do not know that he is qualified to make such repairs. His name does not show up in the airmen registry as holding an A&P license. The owner also mentioned that he was checking the door occasionally and that it had clearly worsened in the lastcouple of weeks and that there is no strength left in the window frame.Based on our conversations; I believe that the owner fixed the discrepancies that pilots reported using methods that are not by the book.(1) Normalization of deviance. I should have canceled the flight after landing at ZZZ after the initial trouble with the door.(2) Normalization of deviance. Owner should have replaced the door in July; rather than waiting for the door condition to get worse and create an [issue].(3) Crew management. I should have briefed my passenger during/after the [event]. She thankfully did all the right things (e.g. dampen the door vibrations) purely on instinct.(4) Aviate & Declare. I did not use 'emergency' or 'mayday' in my communications; despite that; the ATC at ZZZ and ZZZ3 both realized that something was up and gave me priority. Kudos to them. When diverting to ZZZ3; I flew very close to the prohibited airspace near marina to minimize my flight path to the runway.(5) Pre-flight Airworthiness Check. I should have insisted on viewing the maintenance records of the airplane to verify that my previous squawks were satisfactorily addressed.

Air Carrier flight crew reported an uneventful divert due to a fume event during cruise.

During cruise flight at 40;000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously the master caution came on for ELEC and the TRU (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. I as Captain was Pilot Flying and initially transferred control to the First Officer for me to chase down the TRU checklist. I accomplished the checklist; noting that approach mode with the flight directors would be unavailable... At this point the smoke was getting thicker; and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established we notified ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude; and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that the First Officer made me aware that all his flight and NAV displays had failed. He thus transferred control back to me as the Pilot Flying and he took over the smoke/fire/fumes checklist in the QRH.ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1; but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport so that was closest. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach; and used our emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in order to expedite landing. At this point the First Officer discontinued the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20; having noted at step 16 that we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. I asked the First Officer to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch but at that point the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the master caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TRU and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit.With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. I disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS XXL. I quickly realized that electric trim was inoperative and proceeded to trim manually. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so I asked the First Officer to back me up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident where CFR was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR (crash fire rescue) to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our passengers stop breathing fumes.After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. Then we took a breath and asked each other (at the same time) 'well; how'd that go'. Of course sitting on the ground I feel like I can armchair quarterback the situation and nitpick some of the decisions; but overall I feel like we handled the situation well. We had good crew coordination given the circumstances (on O2) and the First Officer did a great job of running the checklists as well as keeping an eye on my flying once we had to transfer controls back to me. It did feel weird turning away from ZZZ2 since it was practically right below us; but I still feel like it was the correct decision given the circumstances and the amount of time it would take to descend; and how much of a distraction an orbiting descent into mountainous terrain would be while trying to deal with smoke.One thing I would do differently has to do with after the situation was over on the ground. I ended up talking with the Chief Pilot; then the firefighters; then the mechanic outside the aircraft on the ramp. By the time I got back inside I couldn't find the flight attendants to debrief and see how they were doing. Upon opening the flight deck door the A had told me that they were all fine; but I would have liked to make sure and check in with them individually. I called scheduling to try and get them to transfer me in order to at least talk with them on the phone; who then transferred me to the scheduling desk where I waited on hold until it disconnected. I still hope to talk with them at some point to learn how things went in the back and find out what we could have done better for them.

It was at this point that I noticed all my flight/nav displays and radios had failed as well as ACARS No Comm" being displayed on the FMS. I came to this decision based on the fact that step 16 states we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. He agreed. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS 17L. I noticed during the approach that the Captain had to trim manually; which led me to believe that we had obviously lost electrical control. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so the Captain asked me to back him up for the manual deployment. After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. A short time later; CFR and a maintenance person were able to find the cause of the TR failure and pulled one of the TR boxes out of the E&E bay (electronics & engineering); which showed significant electrical fire damage. Lesson learned: maintain awareness of the type of emergency and aircraft state; compared to how long QRH steps could take you out of the critical Pilot Monitoring role. This checklist taught me to bring my head back up and get a grasp on the fact that we were in a rapid descent; over mountains; with half of our displays and comms out and I was only half aware of some of the radio calls and aircraft state. This was more concerning to me."

Helicopter pilot reported that after landing; another aircraft was cleared for takeoff from the opposite end of the same runway; resulting in the helicopter taking evasive action. Pilot reported that several other aircraft and confusing ATC radio communications were part of the overall situation.

What happened: Aircraft Y was given a take off clearance for a runway that was occupied by a helicopter that had landed on the opposite end and was awaiting taxi instructions.What led to this: The helicopter was coming in from the east and requested to land on the western side of the airport. The active runways at the time were south to north (XXL and XXR). The Tower cleared the helicopter to land on the numbers of an inactive runway XY; which would keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport; away from the flow of fixed wing traffic. About 5 minutes elapsed between the time the helicopter landed and Aircraft Y flew over the helicopter.During that time I believe the Controller may have been distracted by pattern traffic; Aircraft Z arrival (this was a factor prior to the helicopter landing which resulted in the controller deciding to keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport); a change in Aircraft Y IFR clearance; and by a pilot of an airplane who mistakenly made a final approach to the wrong parallel runway.Starting from the point at which the helicopter lands; the following exchanges were heard.Aircraft A was cleared for touch and go #2 behind Aircraft Z for runway XXL.Aircraft B was cleared to Land runway XXR.A few seconds after Aircraft B acknowledged the landing clearance the tower issue a taxi instruction to the airborne Aircraft B 'hold short of runway XXR I am going to have a departure off runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded 'I am in the air.'The tower replied 'Disregard; Land and hold short of runway XZ; land and hold short of runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded that this was their intention and would be parking in an area that would not put them at risk of crossing into runway XZ.The tower approved a request to taxi back to parking after Aircraft B completed a 180 degree turn on the runway after landing.30 seconds later the tower controller said to Aircraft B; 'Disregard the land and hold short clearance. I won't have that departure. He will be holding in place; though.'The tower instructed Aircraft Y to line up and wait on runway XZ.The 737 had already landed on XXL and the tower cleared a Cessna for takeoff runway XXL.20 seconds later Aircraft B realized he was about to land on top of Aircraft A who had just been cleared for takeoff and asked the tower if he should go around. There was no response. Aircraft B hailed the tower again. I observed Aircraft B descend below 100 ft AGL before deciding to go around. 40 seconds elapsed between the 1st and 3rd time Aircraft B called the tower.The tower gave the departing Aircraft A; a mixed up call starting with 'line up and- cancel take off- cleared for takeoff runway XXL'The tower then gave Aircraft B instructions to remain in the upwind; he would give him a crosswind instruction to follow.Aircraft B apologized for lining up to land on the wrong runway.As soon as the frequency congestion allowed; knowing there was a jet on the opposite side of my runway; I made a call 'Tower; Helicopter (call-sign) holding position on the numbers of [Runway] XY ready to taxi to (name of ramp)'. The call was not acknowledged and 55 seconds later an amended departure clearance; combined with a takeoff clearance; was given to the waiting Aircraft Y. I did not hear the departure clearance and Aircraft Y began racing towards us. Ironically; I may have turned to my student and said to keep an eye on Aircraft Y. As it rushed overhead I made an aggressive maneuver off of the numbers and onto the closest available vacant spot beyond the runway safety area.Previous experiences at this airport have made it clear when a helicopter accepts a landing clearance to a spot; taxiway; intersection; or helipad; they are expected to remain there until given a clearance to taxi. Quite often the controllers will vector an arriving helicopter far around the approach or departure center lines of the active runways and restrict them to altitudes below 600 MSL instead of accommodating a flight path crossing the active runways at a higher safe altitude. Less often are we allowed to land as in the case above in a place safely away from the departing/arriving aircraft; and in a position where we can easily air taxi at a moment's notice. A helicopter is highly maneuverable and this aspect should be used to the utmost advantage when minimizing delays to arriving or departing airplanes. As mentioned earlier the helicopter's arrival was prior to Aircraft Z checking in with the tower. There was Aircraft A on a half-mile final to runway XXL ahead of Aircraft Z. With several miles of spacing between Aircraft Z and Aircraft A; the tower began to ask the helicopter to pass behind the landing Aircraft A. We accepted. The tower immediately reversed their decision due to Aircraft Z scheduled arrival and cleared us to land on the numbers of [Runway] XY with the restriction 'remain north of XX'. We accepted the clearance to land. It is very likely that a helicopter crossing the approach end of XXL shortly after the landing Aircraft A would have had little to no effect on any of the other present arriving or departing aircraft.

UH-60 Pilot reported encountered icing; received accumulation warning; but failed to understand and activate the rotor ice protection system. Pilot reference UH-60 Operator's Manual suggestion.

On [Date]; I was acting as Pilot in Command (PIC) of a UH-60 L Army National Guard Helicopter conducting a round-trip air movement of crew and passengers from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I was sitting left seat; my Co-pilot (PI) sat right seat. I had two crewmembers in the gunner's seats (Row 2); and one passenger in Row 3. Total: 5 souls on board.Earlier in the day; we had flown IFR from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 for a fuel stop before heading to ZZZ. We had received a military weather briefing and were aware of an AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing along the route. We monitored PIREPS and determined as a crew that the risk of anything beyond moderate icing was minimal; as the few PIREPS observed were for light rime ice at flight levels above our planned flight altitude.The conditions observed on the flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ were very stable. There was a stratiform cloud layer; approximately 1;000 to 2;000 ft. thick; that we either flew below or above the cloud layer the entire way to ZZZ. We observed no icing.We were on the ground for approximately two hours after landing at ZZZ. I continued to monitor weather conditions; and it appeared they had not changed from the time we landed. I observed the same AIRMET Zulu and a couple of PIREPS reporting light rime above our planned flight level.Prior to departure; my crew and I conducted de-ice checks in accordance with our aircraft's technical manual; which all passed.After an uneventful climb to our requested flight level of 7;000 ft. MSL; we leveled off. At this time the annunciator panel gave us a warning of 'MR ICE DETECTED'. We had discussed this as an expected possibility; acknowledged the caution; and monitored our ice rate meter; which read 'Light Icing Detected'.At this time; I asked ATC if they knew where the cloud tops were. We were informed that they were at approximately 8;000 ft. MSL. Faced with the decision to climb approximately 1;000 ft. through visible moisture; or descend approximately 4;000 ft. through visible moisture; I requested to climb to 10;000 ft. MSL. ATC gave a clearance to 9;000 ft. MSL. We began our climb.In approximately 1.5 minutes; our icing condition worsened. Our ice rate meter pegged out at its maximum indication of severe icing. The helicopter began to shake; and we lost a dangerous amount of our main rotor RPM (a true [anomaly]). I immediately pressed down on the collective to preserve our rotor RPM; took the controls from my co-pilot; [advised ATC] by announcing 'PAN PAN PAN' on ZZZ Approach frequency. I asked the controller to help me get out of the icing situation and was ultimately cleared down to 2;500 ft. MSL.My crew and I flew the helicopter well; in a level attitude at approximately 2;500 ft. per minute. We maintained 100% rotor RPM during our decent and exited the cloud layer at approximately 3;000 ft. MSL. I tested the controls as we got closer to the surface to ensure I would be able to arrest the helicopter's rate of decent. Upon exiting the clouds; the icing condition improved; and the rest of the flight home was uneventful and under VFR conditions.Chain Of Events:How the problem arose: The problem arose from the unexpected encounter into severe icing.How it was discovered: The severe icing was detected by on the on-board ice detection system; severe vibrations were felt by the crew; and the low rotor warning alarm sounded.Corrective actions: The Good: The crew responded to the [situation] well by manipulating the flight controls to preserve rotor RPM; communicating the [anomaly] to ATC; and flying the aircraft out of the icing conditions.The Bad: The crew did not respond correctly to the initial 'ICE DETECTED' caution. In accordance with the UH-60 Operators Manual; 'The ice rate meter activates the ICE DETECTED caution when the BLADE DE-ICE POWER switch is turned off; informing the pilot of the requirement to turn on the system'. Contributing Factors:Neither the UH-60 Operating Manual or checklist clearly emphasizes the immediatememory item actions required in the event of an icing [situation].An updated -1 weather brief was not obtained from the Air Force Operational Weather Squadron by the Pilot in Command.Human Performance Considerations:The perception of the Pilot in Command that the 'AUTO' function on the ice rate meter meant that the system will 'automatically operate upon detection of ice' was incorrect.The perception of the Pilot in Command that the weather conditions would be the same on the return flight as they were on the first portion was incorrect.The actions of both the Pilot in Command and Co-pilot ultimately saved the lives of the crew; however their inaction to turn the de-ice system on was detrimental to the safe operation of the aircraft.Factors affecting the quality of human performance:Neither the Pilot or Co-pilot complained of fatigue or other exogenous factors prior the flight. Both had a good night's rest and were well within the confines of their duty day at the time of the incident.Recommendations:Ensure aircrew are intimately familiar with the de-ice equipment and capabilities on their aircraft. Recommend that changes be made to the UH-60 Operator's Manual and checklist to emphasize the seriousness of an icing [situation] and the immediate response required. This should be an underlined step. Once the ICE DETECTED caution appears; the immediate action required is for the blade de-ice switch to be turned ON.

Flight Crew reported compressor stalls on the Number 1 Engine and inadvertently shut down the Number 3 Engine.

Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful. We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.

Alerted that Aircraft X might be returning to ZZZ due to problem with #1 Engine. I immediately contacted ZZZ Tower. I was told; right after flight was wheels up controllers in tower saw sparks/flames coming from left engine and also heard 3 to 4 loud booms. Flight returned to airport and landed without issue on Runway XX. I talked to the Captain. He said that right after takeoff; there was compressor stall #1 Engine. They advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. The aircraft was met by the Fire Department. The Captain said he did not know what caused the loss of the #1 Engine. He also said the maintenance told him there was damage to the engine.

Flight Crew reported a GPWS alert while on a visual approach to ROA resulted in corrective action; yet no obvious terrain proximity.

On [Date]; we operated Aircraft X from ZZZ-ROA and I was the CA (Captain) onboard. It was our Day 3 and Leg 4 of the day. I was the Pilot Flying; while my FO (First Officer) was Pilot Monitoring. Both of us were new to this airport; so we reviewed the 10-7 pages and airport diagram to make sure we selected an adequate runway for landing; because they both were relatively short runways in mountainous terrain surrounding area. Once we were in the air and leveled off at our cruising altitude; we started setting up for the approach and briefed it all. As we got closer to the airport and were with Approach; he descended us to 6;000 ft. We both saw the runway and reported it. The ATC asked us to give him at least 6 mile final and we concurred. We looked at the runway and descended down to 4;500 ft. approaching from the southwest to intercept [Runway] 34 localizer. As we got closer to the intercept point for the localizer; the aircraft annunciated 'Caution terrain' 'Pull up' simultaneously; there was no break in between at all. There was also no terrain data that displayed on the MFD on both of our screens. I disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and added power needed to climb immediately. The 'Pull up' annunciation was only said once and went away. We only climbed 500 ft. to 5;000 ft. and continued to intercept the course to land. We also reported the event to the ATC and they didn't say anything. The 'Master Warning' switch light also didn't go on. This event lasted about 2 seconds and we continued to land at the airport.Both of us were new the airport and should've stayed with ATC until intercepted and then call for visual.This event could've easily been avoided by simply just staying with the Approach Control until established on approach; because it is a very mountainous area. Being an unfamiliar crew flying to this area and going visual to land this runway can put you in this situation; even though being in VMC conditions and having runway in sight. I would also like to suggest a guidance in 10-7 to be added regarding landing in this airport and staying with ATC until cleared of mountains and only going visual once cleared and over the valley.

On [Date]; my Captain and I operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to ROA. It was Day 3; Leg 4 of our trip. On this leg; I was the Pilot Monitoring; while my CA (Captain) was flying the aircraft. This was the first time either of us operated to Roanoke; so we reviewed the 10-7 pages; and airport diagram to make sure we selected an adequate runway for landing; since they both were relatively short runways in a mountainous area. Once in cruise flight at our final altitude; we started setting up for the approach and briefed it as necessary. The plan was to set up for the visual backed up by the ILS for Runway 34. As we got closer to the airport and were with Approach; the controller descended us to 6;000 ft. We both saw the runway and reported it. ATC then cleared us for the visual; but asked us to give him at least 6 mile final and we concurred. We looked at the runway; surrounding terrain; and approach plate; and decided to descend down to 4;500 ft. approaching from the southwest to intercept the Runway 34 localizer. We figured this was a correct altitude; as the highest obstacle on the plate was 3;508 ft. As we got closer to the intercept point for the localizer; the aircraft annunciated 'Caution terrain' 'Pull up' simultaneously; there was no break in between at all. There was also no terrain data that displayed on the MFD on both of our screens. My Captain immediately disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and added power as necessary. The 'Pull up' annunciation and all other GPWS alerts were only said once and went away as soon as we started the climb. We only climbed 500 ft. to 5;000 ft. and continued to intercept the course to land. The event was reported to ATC as well; and they acknowledged. This event lasted about 2 seconds and we continued to land at the airport.This was the first time either of us have operated to this particular airport; and should have either stayed above the approach's MSA of 5;700 ft.; or even stayed with the Approach Controller; making him give us headings and altitudes rather than calling the airport in sight and getting cleared for the visual.This event could have easily been avoided by staying with the Approach Controller until established on the approach; rather than calling the airport in sight and getting cleared for the visual. A crew flying to this area that is unfamiliar with the surrounding terrain and conducting a visual approach to this runway can end up in this situation; even with VMC conditions and having the runway in sight. I would also like to suggest some guidance in the 10-7 pages to be added regarding landing at this airport and staying with ATC until cleared of the mountains and only going visual once cleared and over the valley. Something similar to the 10-7 pages for ZZZ regarding the GPWS events would be helpful to other crews in avoiding a similar situation.

GA pilot reported experiencing a NMAC that resulted from ATC sequencing 3 aircraft for landing by using 270- and 360-turns.

I was doing pattern work at ZZZ between XA:00 and XB:00. The airfield had a large amount of arriving traffic during the hours I was flying. After a touch & go on RWY XX; I was asked to extend the upwind before flying a right pattern. About mid-field on the downwind; tower requested a left-360. After my first 360; I was instructed to extend my downwind. A second plane [Aircraft Y] was approaching the airport from the northwest. Aircraft Y was asked to 'make a right 270; keep it tight and get ready to line up behind a [jet]'ATC then asked me to widen out my downwind and look for Aircraft Y making the right 270. At this point it was at my 11 o clock; 3 miles. About 5 seconds later I was able to identify the aircraft; let tower know that I had them in sight and was preparing to line up behind them. About 15 seconds later; tower called me up again; asking 'Aircraft X - extend it out a little bit; actually just follow behind and I'll call your base you will have to follow a jet behind on final'. I read back and confirmed.About 30 seconds later; tower called me up again; 'Aircraft X just so I don't get you too far from the field; make a left 360'. I read back the instruction and began my left 360. At this point; I was already thinking about Aircraft Y as I was planning on how I would get back on the downwind and line up behind them. I believe Aircraft Y was just about to finish its right 270 as I was about 90 degrees into my 360. I was able to spot and track the plane on Foreflight with Sentry; but since I had to make a 360 I lost visual when I initiated my turn. Tower; likely receiving a traffic alert called the other plane to make them aware of me: 'Aircraft X about a mile south making a left 360 - he has you in sight'. I do not think he asked them to confirm that they had me in sight and I can't tell from the live-ATC recording whether they read it back. The added statement 'he has you in sight' was extremely dangerous and could have been fatal. Yes; I had the traffic in sight when I was heading toward it and planning to get behind them; but once I started my left 360 there was no way of maintaining a visual with the other plane since I was now heading the opposite direction. I immediately recognized the potential conflict and started looking both outside the plane and on Foreflight trying to spot and track the other plane's relative position. The other plane did not make a 270 turn; but instead kept turning toward the airport/runway i.e. cutting into my path.As I was about 270 degrees into my 360 turn tower called 'Aircraft X - as you are coming out of that 360 turn do you still have Aircraft Y in sight?'At this point; I was already banking hard left in a steep turn trying to pull away from the converging traffic that I saw coming closer toward me. Turning right was not an option as it would have put me in the middle of final with jets arriving. I do not think the other plane confirmed whether or not they had me in sight. If they did; they flew way too close to me for my comfort and should have initiated an avoidance maneuver. In response to tower's question I responded 'Aircraft X unable' because I had to focus on flying the airplane away from the other traffic. We then passed by each other with much less separation than I feel comfortable. The other plane heading toward the runway; and me pulling hard left to the North-West; initiating a climb up to gain altitude. It is hard to tell exactly but horizontal distance could have been less than 500 feet Vertical distance was virtually the same. It happened very quickly. If I had not realized the potential conflict and mitigated by tracking on foreflight and pulling hard left this could have been a really really bad situation. The biggest mistake here; in my opinion; was ATC communicating to the other plane that I had them in sight AFTER I started my 360. There is no way one can maintain visual during such a maneuver while also flying safely and ATC shouldunder no circumstances make that statement. I also think that having two planes completing maneuvers in a way where their exit paths can conflict (right 270 and left 360) in close proximity should be prohibited.There were multiple safer options here. Aircraft Y could have flown a proper base rather than cutting it short onto final. I could have been asked to fly west; or I could have been asked to fly another 360 right after the first one. The fact that ATC changed its instructions relative to how I should fly behind/around the other traffic 3 times in a minute indicates to me that they were not planning ahead but rather responding to/running behind.In the future; I will call out if ATC tells other people that I have them in sight when I don't (i.e. after starting my left 360). I am also surprised nobody (tower/the other plane) complained about how close this was. I am glad to be back on the ground. I hope this helps keep other people safe in the future!

Center Controller reported an aircraft that was having equipment problems; a VFR pilot in IMC and how the controller helped the aircraft get on the ground safely.

At XA:28Z; Aircraft X checked on the frequency asking for VFR flight following in the vicinity of ZZZ. He was given a beacon code and I displayed a data block on the radar scope; waiting for it to track up. After a minute I told the pilot that I did not have radar contact; and I didn't have a target in the area he stated. I verified his code and location; and had him reset his transponder after another minute went by. At XA:31Z I told him it might be necessary for him to climb before I could establish radar contact. He reported that he was starting a climb to 7;000 feet.One minute after he started his climb; at XA:32Z; I picked up a primary target in the area the pilot reported. I tried to verify the position of the primary target; but the pilot just responded that he was showing zero oil pressure and having electrical issues. As he was saying this; the data block correlated to the code and I radar identified Aircraft X and verified his location. My standard practice; something that I did less than ten minutes prior; is to radar identify; verify location and altitude; and give altimeter. I do it every time; and in that order. When I radar identified Aircraft X; there was no Mode C data; so I asked him to report his altitude. He reported that he was climbing to 7;000 feet and asked for help to get into ZZZ; he was showing zero on his oil pressure. I didn't circle back to the altimeter at this time.I issued Aircraft X a heading to set him up for a pattern into ZZZ. If his engine was about to quit; I wanted him lined up for an airport; not guessing what was below him. I told the CIC I was working a special aircraft; and the OM was quickly in the area. I didn't feel it was in good judgement to add on to the pilot's stress level by pointing out that he was experiencing an urgent situation. It was being handled as such.He asked as he rolled out if he was on the correct heading. I advised that he was 20 degrees off course; and that he should correct. He told me he was using his backup compass; due to electrical failure. That information made a lot of sense at that moment. The backup compass is a magnetic compass. It's one that bounces around as you turn it. The magnetic compass will continue to turn past the heading and then bounce back and correct as the airplane levels off and the compass stabilizes. This is something that an IFR rated pilot would be more knowledgeable about. No gyro turns; or turns with only the backup compass were part of my IFR certificate training. Due to this; I decided to give him small turns that would create an arc to final; and help him maintain better control and orientation.I told him to descend to 5;000 ft. and that I should still have radar contact at that altitude. He responded that believed he'd be able to poke through. I knew it would be minimal conditions; I still believed getting the aircraft set up for a runway was the safest places. As I gave him a turn to the left he stated that he was going to get into the clouds. I asked if he and the aircraft were IFR qualified. He said they were not. I asked if he could maintain VFR conditions. It sounded like he was trying; but didn't seem sure that he would.I told Aircraft X that he could continue down to 4;000 feet and gave him a heading to get him turned more toward the airport. About that time at XA:39Z; just eleven minutes into the situation; an aircraft inbound for ZZZ1 checked on. I issued the ZZZ1 altimeter. This aircraft would end up being held out for the [situation]. I then told Aircraft X he could descend at his discretion to 3;900 feet; but that was the minimum enroute altitude in the area; and the lowest I was comfortable advising him. He said he was starting to poke through at 4;100 feet. I gave him the position and distance of ZZZ1. He responded that he could see some ground.I had him continue his gradual left turn but saw a much more aggressive turn on the radar. I asked if he was circling down to stay in VFR conditions. He said he saw bases at 3;800 feet and it was an unintentional 360. Based on what the radar showed; it was not a controlled maneuver; and probably resulted from an unusual attitude due to spatial disorientation. I asked him to regain level flight; as to maintain control of the aircraft and not get into another unusual attitude. I asked him his altitude; he responded 3;680 [feet]. Up until this uncontrolled maneuver; every report was that he was in marginal conditions; but always seemed to have some visual capabilities. At this point the inability to maintain VFR was imminent.The aircraft showed a northeast heading; I asked him to make a slow turn. Being an IFR rated pilot myself; and seeing how easily he became disoriented already; I wanted to avoid a stall; spin or turning over the aircraft. In the clouds a turn can make your body feel like you are descending; and a climb can make your body think you are turning. A more abrupt climb or turn only magnifies this effect. At XA:43Z as I maintained focus on keeping the pilot's wings level; I offered the option of climbing back up into VFR conditions. He was in favor of the idea. He added that the engine had been running fine; and believed the zero oil pressure reading to be due to electrical issue; not engine issues. With that information I immediately reassessed the IFR conditions to be the most hazardous conditions in the situation.I saw the aircraft again start a west turn that seemed to increase in rate. I gave the aircraft his location and his observed turn. I advised that he level off and focus on flying straight and level. He did not respond. The maneuver seemed unstable and I tried to relay that he needed to get wings level; then start climbing slowly. Anything aggressive would cause greater disorientation. He said the engine was running fine now; no longer a concern. I told him that we believed it to be clear in ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. He said that sounds nice. I wanted to get him into ZZZ3 if it was in fact clear. It was much closer; and based on his workload; fatigue due to stress; and equipment issues; I wanted him in the air the least amount of time possible. The CIC or the OM; I don't remember which; went up to the weather desk to get the most complete weather information available. Other controllers were also pulling weather at surrounding airports. I was focused on getting Aircraft X oriented and into VMC.I told him to fly his present heading and start a climb; advising that there was no traffic ahead. He responded that he was having trouble keeping his wings level. I advised back to straight and level and asked his altitude. The climb was giving him a sensation of turning and he was having trouble overcoming that. I should have advised him to focus on the instruments over his own sensations; but I did not think of it at the time.He said he was at 4;020 feet. I said give me level straight flight and then we'll start a slow climb. I wanted him to remain calm and know that we were going to work through it. He did not answer. Seeing what appeared to be straight flight on the radar scope I advised a shallow climb. He said he was trying to keep the wings level. At that point a VFR aircraft departing ZZZ1 was checking in. I called the traffic to that aircraft; advised the altitude was unknown; and asked Aircraft X to say his altitude. He did not immediately answer. Instead another aircraft keyed up; saying the other aircraft didn't look good on his TCAS and he needed to level his wings. Aircraft X then responded; he pulled into a stall; but was starting back up. I advised him to take it slow. At that point Aircraft Y verified ZZZ2 to be clear. I asked if Aircraft X was staying level. He said yes; 5;000 feet and seeing sunlight. I saw another turn on radar and had him level his wings once again. A minute later he reported on top of clouds and level. I told him maintain level flight; catch his breath; and if there were any airports he wanted to try to get to; we would get the weather for him. In my experience; it was best to remind him that he could exhale. He still needed to have the ability to fly the rest of his flight with electrical issues. I also offered him the opportunity to request an alternate airport. He had equipment that most likely needed to be repaired or replaced. I didn't want to send him somewhere that he'd get stuck. Aircraft X was maintaining a southeast heading and I asked him his altitude. He responded; 5;860 feet. I offered again; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. The pilot was happy with ZZZ2 because it was reported clear. I gave a heading for him to fly that would get him started turning more towards either airport as I waited for the weather information. I recommended going to ZZZ3 because it was the closest. The pilot agreed that ZZZ3 would be his first choice; then ZZZ2. Immediately as he said that; the information was back from the weather desk and I relayed it to the pilot. He said he wanted to shoot for ZZZ2 because it was clear and ZZZ3 was overcast. I gave a few more heading changes and turns to get him direct to ZZZ2. I also lost radar contact on him a minute later as well. I received another report that he should expect to be clear of the west edge of the moving weather some time before ZZZ2; and passed that along. I advised him that he appeared right on course; and I was relieved at XB:08Z.Ten minutes later; while talking to the relieving controller; the pilot thanked us all for the help he received and said he was feeling the love. He even asked to get a forwarding address to send me a bottle of good scotch. Additionally; when calling the facility from the ground; the pilot was very thankful for the services he received. He informed the OM that he had to change pants when he landed; and again wanted to send a thank you bottle for getting him to safety. It was not apparent at the beginning of the situation that the engine oil reading was due to an electrical issue. It was possible that it could have been a number of different factors; but I knew that he could lose his engine at any moment; and it may not sound rough right away. I wanted him to get lined up for a runway as safely and quickly as possible. I gave him the option to get down below the bases; but should have emphasized to maintain VFR; even though it is the pilot's responsibility. During a stressful [situation]; that would be a good reminder to give the pilot. Once the pilot gained confidence that the engine was running properly; I did everything in my power; and with all of my flight experience to keep the pilot focused on not getting into an unrecoverable condition; while maneuvering safely into VMC.During an imminent [hazard]; controllers have to make judgement calls on what is the most prudent and time critical course of action. Access to checklists during these situations would ensure that all services are provided. Controllers could check that they had provided all of the information possible without taking as much attention away from the imminent safety issue. An easier to use weather reporting system would ensure more weather reports are forwarded along from controllers. The current GI method can be tedious and the tie up keyboard use during busier sessions. ERIDS (En Route Information Display System) offers weather reporting by tapping on the information and hitting send. Using this system would increase the efficiency and result in more weather reports being available. Even just having paper weather slips that controllers can hand to a supervisor would improve efficiency.A working knowledge of flight instruments and factors of flight would allow better assistance to pilots in [hazardous] situations. Recurrent training that focuses on best practices during imminent situations would enhance controllers on seldom used skills.

Air carrier First Officer and Captain reported four missed approaches due to weather and then a safe landing at an alternate airport.

I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X from ZZZ2-ZZZ1. I flew the RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach with rain and wind in the vicinity. I attempted to configure early but a strong tailwind made it challenging. I encountered a wind gust which caused me to counter increasing airspeed by pitching up and slightly reduce power to maintain airspeed and continue configuring. This resulted in a position higher than anticipated. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed this also and we articulated that. About that time; ATC directed a go-around. We executed the missed approach and climbed to 3;000 [feet] on vectors for another approach.Noting the conditions; I configured early for the second RNAV RNP XX approach. Rain and wind were still predominant throughout the approach but fewer gust excursions and we remained stable throughout the approach all the way to minimums. At minimums; we both had the approach lights and runway environment in sight and I continued the approach. As I turned final aligning with Runway XX; I lost sight of the runway environment due to the weather. The PM called go around and I initiated go around procedures. We climbed to 3;000 feet on vectors as directed by ATC. We communicated with one another and ensured we were both in the green; we had ample fuel; and agreed to attempt a third approach. On the third RNAV RNP XX approach; I configured early again and remained stable throughout the approach. The wind was still a factor though and required careful monitoring and aircraft correction to maintain a stable approach. Fully configured and in the vicinity of arriving at minimums; ATC advised a wind shift on the field of 330 degrees at 26 knots of wind. ATC asked for our intentions. Due to airline limitations on Maximum Tailwind Component for Landing; the PM told ATC we could not land and we would go-around. ZZZ1 Tower handed us off to ZZZ Departure and they advised us that they 'turned the airfield around' and they would give us vectors for the ILS RWY XY approach and we would be 'number 1' to the field. Again; the Captain and I communicated that we were both in the green; we noted that we had ample fuel; and we prepared for an ILS approach to Runway XY.After intercepting the localizer for the ILS to Runway XY; I configured fully and continued down the glideslope from the final approach fix. It was raining outside and was windy but we remained stable. Shortly prior to 1;000 feet AGL; it grew increasingly difficult to maintain a stable approach. I told the PM that I didn't feel comfortable; the weather was worsening; and it was likely that we would not be stable at 1;000 feet. We agreed and elected to go-around. Just as I began the go around procedure; we encountered a Wind Shear Warning and I proceeded with the Wind Shear escape maneuver. We exited the conditions quickly and transitioned to ATC's directives. We quickly agreed to divert to ZZZ3 and the PM informed ATC of our intention to divert. We climbed to 3;000 feet and flew vectors to ZZZ3.We flew the ILS RWY XYC approach and landed safely at ZZZ3 and taxied to the gate. We shut down the aircraft with approximately 7.4k pounds of fuel remaining. During the deplaning process; the Captain coordinated with the Maintenance and Dispatch and agreed to continue on to ZZZ1 as the weather cleared the area. We added fuel departing with 11.8k pounds of fuel. The Captain flew as the PF and I was the PM for the return flight to ZZZ1. The Captain maintained appropriate communication throughout the event. He communicated with the passengers explaining as best as possible what occurred and what we were doing to ensure their safety while doing our best to land at our intended destination. He kept the flight attendants apprised of the situation after each approach and we discussed each approach; verified we were both in the green; and maintained situational awareness at all times.

Flew RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and was configuring the aircraft early. He was at gear down; flaps 15; and we encountered a wind gust that drove the airspeed indication almost to redline. The FO raised nose slightly and reduced power to slow the airspeed in order to continue configuring the aircraft. As this occurred; aircraft got a little high. As PM; I noticed this and was in process of informing FO when ATC said that we looked a little high and to just go around. We executed the missed approach as directed by ATC and climbed on a heading to 3;000 ft. to vector for another approach.On the second RNAV RNP XX; FO configured the aircraft early and shot approach to minimums. At minimums; approach lights and runway lights were visible; but as we turned to final approach; visibility was lost. I called go-around; and FO initiated go-around. We climbed on a heading to 3;000 feet. We communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for another approach.On the third RNAV RNP XX; the FO had fully configured the aircraft; when ATC advised that the wind had shifted out of the north at 330 degrees and we had 26 knots of wind at our tail. ATC asked our intentions; I told them that we could not land with those winds and that we were going around. At that point; ATC handed us off to departure; and departure immediately advised us that they had turned the airport around and could give us an immediate left downwind to be number 1; shooting ILS Runway XY. FO and I communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for an approach using the new runway.On attempt to Runway XY; we intercepted localizer and G/S. We had continual high winds indicating to me that the aircraft would not be able to remain stable throughout approach and landing. As PIC; I called for a go-around. FO communicated to me his agreement; and I immediately notified Tower of our intention to divert to ZZZ3. FO initiated the miss. As he did; we encountered a brief Wind Shear Warning. FO finished cleaning aircraft up and we diverted to ZZZ3 without incident.We were vectored to ZZZ3 and landed on Runway XYC and taxied to the gate with 7.4 pounds of fuel. I called Dispatch and she said we had plenty of fuel to get to ZZZ1 but as a precaution due to the frontal weather passage; she added more fuel and brought us up to 11.8 pounds. After the front passage; I flew the aircraft as PF uneventfully to ZZZ1. During all of the approaches and the divert I kept the flight attendants up to date and communicated with the passengers at all times. We exercised good situational awareness and followed SOPs during the entire flight.

Flight crew reported a fume event during boarding caused by a 'vape charging device' meltdown in a carry-on bag. An orderly passenger deplaning was executed and necessary emergency responders notified.

During the boarding process of Aircraft X at Gate; a passenger in her assigned seat was holding her carry-on bag on her lap. The carry-on had a vape charger inside the bag and the batteries started to smoke and meltdown. There was smoke and fumes in the cabin. An unknown passenger ran towards the front of the aircraft yelling that there was a fire in the back of the aircraft and for everyone to get off. The flight attendants made an announcement and commenced the Emergency Deplaning at the Gate procedure (which we had discussed in my pre-bridging brief to the FA's (Flight Attendants)). The Purser asked what to do and I told him to continue the process they had started; which was going very well with passengers calmly deplaning up the jet way. The First Officer alerted emergency response and got up from his seat to assist. I was then told by an unknown person; that the smoking bag had been removed from the aircraft by a dead-heading pilot. I ran the Emergency Evacuation checklist to secure the aircraft; grabbed the fire extinguisher (not needed) and stood at the door directing the passengers to continue up the jetway; 'do not take bags or stand in the jetway; and to proceed to the terminal.' I directed the First Officer to go to terminal. There were a few passengers slowing the process trying to grab their carry-on bag; but were directed to stop and continue to the terminal. Once all passengers were off; I directed the FA's to go to the terminal while I swept the aircraft to be sure all crew and passengers were off. I then proceeded to the terminal. At the terminal I found the crew and deadheading crew members at the door; several passengers and agents and the smoking bag lying on the floor next to the ticket counter. I then directed all persons to leave the area; and requested Law enforcement with/dogs and fire and rescue to the bag. Asked the gate agent to call medical assistance and found the affected passenger sitting in the terminal; which I directed Medical to her location. At that point I was alarmed that the threat had followed us to the terminal and was concerned as to its contents. I then briefed fire and rescue; Maintenance as well as corporate security and law enforcement. I directed the deadheading crewmember who had carried the bag to seek medical attention. We coordinated for the FA's to stay nearby to facilitate the eventual allowing of 5 passengers at a time to go back to the secured aircraft to get their belongings. The First Officer was having chest pain and went to the hospital. I declined medical treatment. And met the ZZZ Chief Pilot who assisted me in the process remaining. There were burns on the owner of the smoking bag; and she also went to the hospital. There were no other injuries or incidents associated with the emergency deplaning procedure...but there was some uncertainty among the many constituents affected by the procedure; gate; ground; maintenance. etc. I was relieved from duty with 'p' for the remaining duration of the trip. I received follow up calls from ZZZ Chief Pilot on multiple occasions and was grateful for his support. I also contacted directly Union Safety and spoke with [Representative] who provided assistance and guidance during and after the event. Overall the procedure works; but should be expanded to a joint training scenario. I was most alarmed to learn. That the (brave) deadheading crew member had carried the smoking bag with him during the deplaning and it eventually ended up in the terminal with no oversight. The direction was to deplane away from the threat; not take it with us.The cause was allowing of the charging device and vape apparatus onboard the aircraft as a carry-on. The positive outcome was due to emergency deplaning at the gate procedure and pre-briefing. Well trained and professional back-end crew was outstanding. First Officer reverted to training and promptly called fire and rescue. However once passengers were off; there was confusion and potential danger which needs to be mitigated for future events. Communication and full understanding and procedures associated are necessary.I suggest the need to continue the use of and to training of the 'Emergency Deplaning at the Gate Procedure'. Would recommend suggested briefings for the crew. Also believe joint training would be very beneficial to role play these scenarios...there is a lot going on and many potential pitfalls. This affects all constituents of the normal process; but also many others. Being released from duty by the Chief Pilot was appreciated; however as a reserve pilot; working to get my time for the month; Pay - No Credit does not help in any way. In fact it prevented me from flying another 4 day trip I could have held; and subsequently puts me at zero(0) hours going into the middle of the month.

It was the first leg of the start of the sequence. I had just met the CA (Captain); for the first time; that afternoon. Along with the first time working with the FA's (Flight Attendants). Boarding started as normal; the CA and myself went about our preflight duties. We had finished all our checklists and were just waiting for the Gate Agent to inform us of boarding being complete. As we sat waiting to close up FA-1 shouts up to us 'We have a fire in the cabin'. In the time that it took the CA and I to get over the initial shock factor; the FA's immediately began an 'Emergency Deplaning' of the aircraft. From my advantage point I had no clue how bad the fire was in the cabin. I did not hear any call for an 'Evacuation'; or see any doors and slides deploying; so I assumed that the FA's were just doing the 'Emergency Deplaning'.The CA went to the QRH immediately. I got on the radio to ops and told them of our situation. That we had a fire onboard the aircraft; we were 'Emergency Deplaning' into the terminal; and we needed ARF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting).The CA and I had completed everything we could think of to help the FA's with the situation in the back. Still not knowing how bad things were in the cabin the CA instructed me to exit the airplane. I did so and then followed my 'evacuation' duties when outside the aircraft. As I exited the flight deck I found a clog of passengers not moving out the door. I made my way through them to find a group of passengers have congregated on the jetway. I instructed them to move and get in the terminal building. This helped the flow of passengers off the aircraft. I found one passenger in visible distress on the jetway. I did a quick assessment of the passenger and then asked if they were OK. The passenger complained of burns on their arm. It did not look bad so I asked if they could walk. The passenger said yes. So I got the assistance of another passenger to help them into the terminal. I also instructed them to take the bag that the hurt passenger said was theirs and was standing next to. Later I would find out this was the bag that was smoking. It was not smoking when I was on the jetway and I was unaware this was the threat on the aircraft. I never would have thought that the threat would be off the aircraft in the direction the passengers were going. Or taken off and left unattended.After the passengers were off the aircraft the FA's were coming off and then asked where the bag was. I asked 'What bag? The one on the ground in the jetway?' They responded Yes; that was the one that was smoking. At that point I realized that I sent it inside the terminal. I remembered what passenger had it and told the supervisor; that was on the jetway; that I could identify them to find that bag.The CA completed his final check of the aircraft and we proceeded into the terminal. The bag has been cordoned off at the gate and people were being kept away. The CA remained at the gate until ARF arrived. I took the FA's and proceeded to an unused gate to keep us together and away from the situation.The incident started with a passenger's bag there was no control over the problem. There was some confusion over what procedures were started and what roles the flight deck crew had in an 'Emergency Deplaning'.It was also confusing how and why the fire; smoking bag; was put onto the jetway.
