At that moment we received a GPWS caution that gave us a one time audible alert; and the Pilot Flying began a climb. Shortly afterwards we passed the YARUB fix; and the MEA was now 12;000 so we continued the descent.While monitoring our progress on the approach; I noticed that our altitude was below the charted MEA. I was confused for a minute while I tried to determine if we had made an error and then realized that I had deleted an altitude; and then re-enter it; but had in fact programmed the incorrect altitude. Looking back I can't quite explain my thought process; and after the fact my mistake seems very obvious and amateur. I did reference the chart for the YARUB altitude; and looking at it again '12;000' is written very close to YARUB; and that's my only explanation for how I matched that altitude to that fix; but of course 12;000 is the altitude after YARUB. While I was monitoring our progress I remember thinking that something didn't seem quite right; and it took me a minute to piece together the ATC clearance; our ensuing actions; and to come to the conclusion that I had made a mistake. The ATC clearance to an altitude that was already below a charted MEA caused a moment of confusion and second guessing. I removed an altitude from the FMS that was auto loaded with the approach. A few minutes later; when I realized I had made an error; I attempted to correct it but I put the wrong altitude back in the FMS after incorrectly reading the chart. I asked the Pilot Flying to level off while I cross checked the chart and; FMS; and our position. I then stated that we should climb; which we did.I should not have been so quick to delete an altitude from the FMS which was loaded by selecting the approach. Also; when entering an altitude into the FMS I need to be more careful while referencing the chart and also confirm with the Pilot Flying that I am entering the correct altitude.

While descending into MJT we were cleared by ATC to pass over MEYRS at or above 14;000 feet and cleared the RNAV 35 approach. We had already briefed the approach and checked the altitudes in the FMS. The first segment between MEYRS and the next point on the approach YARUB is 14;800 feet. Just before reaching MEYRS we decided to stop our descent to pass over MEYRS at 14;000 [feet]and hold at 15;000 [feet]. After YARUB the next step down is 12;000 feet. We had been descending in VNAV to make the cross at Myers. My First Officer put 12;000 feet at YARUB and I confirmed it. In VNAV we then started a slow descent to pass over YARUB at 12;000 feet. This was a mistake on my part. We realized at about 12;700 we where wrong and below a published minimum. I stopped the descent and started a climb. We did get a momentary GPWS terrain and responded according. We climbed about 20 feet and it was gone. We had already stopped descending when we got the GPWS. Realizing we where doing the wrong thing by descending in VNAV to cross YARUB at 12;000 [feet].Allowing the Pilot Monitoring to put 12000 feet n the FMS at YARUB. Immediate once we realized our mistake.. Autopilot off. Start a climb. We never did get to 14;800 [feet] because of how we where close to YARUB. I realized that we where low but also safe and never in any danger. I feel like I should have queried ATC about the descent clearance. I should have been more vigilant with the cross at YARUB.

Air carrier flight crew reported a high workload environment on approach into DEN airport; which included several runway changes; confusion over arrival procedures; and an unstable approach resulted in a go-around.

In preparation for our arrival into DEN we briefed for the CLASH 3 RNAV arrival and the ILS to 35R as this was the expected runway from our direction of arrival. We also included in our brief the threat in DEN of runway changes and how we'd handle that especially during the descent phase on the arrival. About 20 NM from the waypoint CLASH on the arrival ATC informed us to expect runway 35L. We then re-set up for that runway and re-briefed. There was still plenty of time for this and there was little time compression. One point of confusion; however; was that the CLASH 3 has a transition for RWY 35R; but doesn't for 35L; which only has a point at which to expect vectors. We spent some time studying the arrival and approach plates to ensure that was the case to make sure we weren't missing something. I asked my F/O to double check as he was the PM and I wanted to concentrate on the descent as the PF. This has always been confusing as some arrivals and approaches have transition points and some don't. There should be some consistency. This was the beginning of some of the time compression which would later result in some workload management issues.Some point after this ATC broke us off of the arrival and instructed us to descend to 9000 feet and gave us a heading. They then assigned us to RWY 35R. We related that we'd just been assigned 35L and they reiterated we were now reassigned to 35R. This resulted in a very rushed set up for 35R as we were now pretty close in to the approach environment. I asked the F/O to set it all up so that I could continue to fly. I quickly dialed in what I thought was the 35R LOC; but it turned out not to be. I could see that he was struggling and tried to help him out. In hindsight; this was a mistake in workload management because I should have let the F/O do all of the set up. I verbalized that we didn't need to re-brief for 35R as we'd already briefed it and so had a plan. Again; in hindsight; I'm not sure this was a correct call; but we literally did not have time to brief at that point.Shortly after this we were cleared the visual approach to 35R. We were roughly 7 miles from FRONZ and discussed not descending too quickly so as not to bust the floor of the Class B airspace. At about the same time ATC asked us to slow to approach speed for traffic ahead of us for 35R. After slowing we ended up just about 2.5 miles in trail. At this point we were apprised of traffic for 35L and received a TCAS TA because of the assigned heading we were given to intercept the LOC for 35R. We both saw the traffic and I decided to hand fly from this point on as we had an overshooting crosswind and given our heading there would have been a good chance of an overshoot of the LOC.At FRONZ I asked for gear down and flaps 15. At about this point I noticed that neither the LOC or GS were engaging but I had the runway and the PAPI and decided to continue as we had been cleared for the visual. The FO asked if I'd like him to try and dial in the correct LOC and I said yes if he had the bandwidth to do so. Soon after we passed through 1;000 feet and we both missed the call out as I think he was still trying to dial in the LOC frequency. Also we never accomplished the Landing Checklist as we never got to final flaps. We got to 500 feet and we made those call outs. At around 400 feet AFL we received a Too Low Flaps GPWS warning and my knee jerk reaction was to call for FLAP 30 once I realized we were still at FLAPS 15. I don't know if the FO ever selected them; however. I quickly realize this was the wrong call and called for us to go around and the FO called for it at about the same time. We executed the missed approach with no issues and were vectored expeditiously for a second approach and landing without further incident.The FO is not submitting a report as far as I'm aware as we had no ATC deviations or non-compliance with FARS.

This is a report regarding Flight X ZZZ-DEN regarding the changes and ATC clearances we received during our descent and approach to land in DEN.When we reviewed the flight plan in ZZZ we loaded the CLASH3 STAR with runway 35R being our selected landing runway. The flight plan had 17R; but DEN was landing North so that was the only change made to the plan on our part versus what dispatch had planned.Prior to TOD the CA fully reviewed and briefed the STAR and approach that we were expecting. We were fully prepared to execute this plan. Upon checking in with a close in DEN center controller we were advised to expect runway 35L with the EBBLR transition. There was some discussion regarding the EBBLR transition by myself and the CA as we were attempting to figure out if the transition and how the transition linked up with the approach. However; we did this again prior to TOD and were able to be prepared for the new arrival transition and approach. As we descended into Denver; we were handed off to DEN APP. This controller changed our runway back to 35R. We were well into the descent at this point and fairly close to the airport. The CA instructed me to load up the new approach and as I was attempting to do so ATC took us off the arrival for vectors and speed changes. At this point we were South of DEN but still fairly close in. I was still working on getting the FMC setup when ATC vectored us due West and then turned us on to final for 35R. The vector was vey poorly planned by the controller and both the CA and I could see that we were going to blow through the localizer if we allowed the A/P to handle the intercept. The CA disengaged the A/P and made a manual turn to join the localizer. At this point we could both see that the vector had us close in behind another airplane in final. ATC requested that we slow to 160 knots. The CA asked for me to deploy the gear and the flaps to down and 15. Shortly after ATC then requested us to slow to the slowest possible speed. Both the CA and I were closely monitoring the separation between us and the preceding aircraft. At this point I noticed there was a message on the FMC scratchpad that I had not seen before and did not recognize. I don't remember exactly what the message was but it did indicate that there was a conflict between the FMC selected approach and what the VHF radios were tuned to. I was rapidly trying to get the correct frequency on the NAV radios but my JEPP app on the iPad was not responding quickly as I was attempting to zoom in to view the frequency box. At this point we were somewhere around 1;000 feet AGL. The CA announced that he had the runway and the PAPIs in sight and was going to land and just disregard the FMC He was busy attempting to slow and again we were both concerned about the separation between us the preceding aircraft. That was what are focus was on at this point. I cannot recall if either the 1;000 ft or the 500 ft call outs were made. We were both totally task saturated at this time. At some altitude below 500 ft we received a warning message 'too low-flaps'. We both looked at the flap position and realized we were still at flaps 15. The CA called for flaps 30 and I monetarily selected flaps 30 before advocating that we needed to go around. The CA also realized we had to go around at almost the same instant I was stating that we needed to go around. So we executed the go around. We did have the 10;000 ft foot missed approach altitude selected in the MCP so we were climbing to that altitude. However; while just climbing through 7;000 the tower told us to maintain 7;000. I advised tower that we were at 7;200. Tower instructed us to maintain 7;100. We descended back to 7;100 feet and flew runway heading and completed the rest of the go around profile. Tower asked us for the reason for the GA and I replied 'configuration'. They handed us off to approach and we were vectored back around for another ILS to runway 35R. We ensured everything was properly setup and landed without further incident.Some comments about this incident. Both the CA and I had discussed the threat of Denver and how they often make changes to arrivals and approaches during cruise. In fact the CA had been reading in the flight ops newsletter on his iPad about the problems we have been having with arrivals into Denver. We were both fully aware that Denver presented a threat and thought that we had planned and were prepared for our arrival. Had we been cleared as planned per our original plan we would have been fine. Even after the first change to runway 35L we had time to plan and brief. It was only after the final switch back to 35R that we both began to become task saturated with the speed changes; the off route vectors; the FMC programming; the NAV radios; the poor vector to join final; and finally the separation between us and the preceding aircraft and the speed changes made while on final in regards to that aircraft. The amount of items needed to be accomplished while this was occurring in the terminal area was long and complex. We both became so overcome that we must have failed to accomplish the landing checklist; which would have had both of us realizing that we were not in the landing configuration.We made errors along the way; failing to get some of the call outs accomplished; FMC programming; and NAV radio frequency selection among some of the errors. However; many of these errors were driven by the nature of the changes being made by ATC in regards to arrival vectors; speed changes; runway and approach changes among other demands being made by ATC in a very time compressed period while flying within (or near) the terminal area.One more note about the runway changes in Denver. I know Denver and am aware of its threat even on departure. So while we were getting ready to depart and head to ZZZ2 I asked the ramp controller which runway was in use for the ZZZZZ SID. He stated XXR. Yet; when we received our push clearance 15-20 minutes later he told us to expect runway XY. I don't know if he was given bad information by the ATC tower or what happened; but yet again here we are in a high workload situation having to make changes to the FMC and request new TO data.Because of our short turn time in Denver the CA decided to debrief the entire arrival event into Denver while in cruise flying back to ZZZ2. We spent a good 30-40 minutes discussing the flight. Threat and errors were discussed; we used the briefing cards and identified what had occurred on the flight. I am not going to make excuses for the errors that we made; even if they occurred during a task saturated situation. However; a couple of my observations from this event were that we had talked about Denver ATC being a threat. We thought that we had addressed this threat by a good solid brief for the originally planned arrival; even after the change to the 35L arrival; we had time to plan and brief. We were ready; but ATC in Denver threw us some many changes and curve balls that we both were task saturated to the point leading to an undesired aircraft state. Fortunately; both the CA and I followed our training and SOP. safely executed a missed approach; and subsequently landed safely and uneventfully on the next approach.

Instructor reported the aircraft became hard to control; causing a return to home base and a precautionary emergency landing.

Finishing up a training flight with a student in Class G Airspace my student advised he was starting to feel nauseous. I took control of the aircraft from my student using the 3 part positive exchange of flight controls. As I took control of the aircraft I noticed the flight controls were extremely stiff on the longitudinal axis (ailerons). When asking the student if he was blocking the yoke from moving he responded with no and I visually confirmed he was nowhere near any of the controls. After maintaining positive control of the aircraft I started looking around both yokes for a reason why there was such an issue with the roll function as well as looking out at both ailerons. I could not find any reason why I was having such an issue maintaining level flight. We had just completed turns around a point and I wondered if a bird or something collided with the underside of the right aileron at just the correct time that prevented me from turning the yoke right or if there was something that caught up the control cables inside the wing that was preventing this. I was about 15 miles and a 180 degree turn from ZZZ1 and about 20 miles straight to ZZZ. I decided that ZZZ was not only straight ahead but 95% could be over water and wetlands versus ZZZ1 which would put me over populations and wooded areas for a majority of the flight as well as the services available at ZZZ (ATC; ARFF; Line services; Maintenance and the aircraft's Home base). The decision was made and I continued straight towards ZZZ and listened to the ATIS while having the student look through the Emergency Checklist for anything that listed flight control issues. I also verified that the elevators and rudder were not experiencing any issues. I attempted to go further to the right but was met with more and more resistance and did not want to risk snapping anything or causing any further issues/damage. I contacted the tower and advised I was approximately 20 miles south of the airport with some sort of flight control issue and requested a straight in priority landing on Runway 1. Flying straight I would have intercepted the extended centerline on a very shallow 10-15 degrees. Tower advised me to continue and expect the request as well as asked if I needed anything. I advised I did not and was trying to work the issue while maintaining in control. About 10 miles out I realized that while I was maintaining control at 107 KIAS I had no idea what the aircraft would do as I slowed to approach speed of 66 KIAS. I also noticed that I was applying a considerable amount of right rudder to maintain straight flight. At point I made the decision with the unknowns there and having to be uncoordinated as I would be approaching the ground I would prefer Fire Services standing by as well as identify as an emergency to open up any further options that could be available as I may only have 1 shot at the approach once I get down towards that 66 KIAS. I advised my student to tighten his seat belt and that my arms were starting to get tired holding the airplane level that I would need him to use CRM with me and help with Power settings and flaps. At about 1;000MSL I told my student that at 800AGL I wanted him to release the top latch of my door and by 500AGL I wanted him to release the side latch so the door could be unlocked and we can focus on landing in the last 500ft. As I crossed the threshold at about 80KIAS with 2 notches (25 degree) of flaps and about 5 degrees of intercept of the centerline I had my student reduce the power to idle and maintained control through landing but did end up left of centerline.After the aircraft was fully on the ground rolling out I released the yoke which went full deflection to the left. I taxied the aircraft back to the FBO apron and shut down the aircraft. I had my Senior CFI meet us to have him look for a possible issue. After the aircraft was completely shut down I had him go and try to move the yoke which he did with no issues. Further investigation it was noticed that the autopilot (AP); Single Axis; roll knob was turned to the left. The autopilot was never a thought as upon hiring over a year ago I was advised by the then-Assistant Chief Flight Instructor that the Auto pilot did not work; was disconnected from power but not able to be removed from the bottom of the panel. I never thought anything of it because during night flights the AP never had any backlighting to show it had power. My senior instructor and I started up the aircraft and initiated the Autopilot which produced the same effect that I experienced in flight. We conducted a full check of all systems and found nothing else that could have caused the issue. We determined that the location of the AP the student could have inadvertently brushed the switch activating it with no knowledge as there are no lights to indicate it is powered or active. We also came to the conclusion that this incident was not a flight control malfunction as much as an unintentional activation of the AP as the AP did what it was told. Speaking with my Senior CFI we decided that I would personally verify any statements of inoperability from another pilot even if they are a superior with Maintenance and make sure the correct items are done for such items. I am also working on a full lesson for all of my students on the AP; how it works; issues experienced and multiple ways on how to shut it off until a decision could be made to keep the AP with it known active or make the AP inoperative and remove it from the aircraft.

Pilot reported electrical failure in flight; which resulted in a return to departure airport.

The mission of the flight was intended to be a discovery flight. The pilot observed the METAR and TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) at ZZZ before the flight and determined the weather was sufficient for the mission of the flight. The pilot completed weight and balance data along with performance calculations before the flight for the aircraft along with full fuel and two people. The pilot then conducted the pre-flight on the aircraft; which had been hangered the night before. The specific aircraft had been flown once before by the pilot in a checkout flight. During the pre-flight inspection the pilot noted that the landing lights were squawked inoperative on the dispatch sheet and the parking brake of the aircraft was placarded as inoperative. During the pre-flight the pilot noted no other irregularity with the aircraft. Additionally the pilot noted that the alternator belt was taut and in place; all the aircraft lights operated correctly; the Pitot tube was properly heated when tested; and the flaps extended at a normal rate to its full extension. The PIC requested the fuel tanks to be filled to its fullest extent; which was done by a ramp worker; and the PIC noted that there were about 6 quarts of oil in the engine. Upon inspection of the electrical system; it appeared to operate normally. The PIC then entered the cockpit on the right seat; with the sole passenger sitting in the left seat. The PIC then gave the pre-flight briefing to the passenger and also demonstrated how to operate the flight controls and engine controls to the passenger. At this point the PIC then started the engine with the assistance of the passenger and then the PIC taxied to the run-up area. At the run-up area the pilot received the current ATIS and then performed the run-up as described by the checklist. The run-up proceeded without any irregularities discovered- notably the amperage gauge indicated that there was neither a charge nor discharge on the battery. The PIC then completed the run-up checklist and received the departure clearance. Shortly after; the PIC then received the taxi clearance and began to taxi to runway 8 via taxiway E1. The pilot then held short of runway 8 and proceeded with the before takeoff checklist and briefed the takeoff checklist and procedure. After contacting ZZZ tower; the pilot then took off from runway 8 and was given instructions to climb on heading 190. The pilot climbed out at Vy (74 KIAS) up to 8500 feet MSL. The climb proceeded as normal; the aircraft was handed over to ZZZ departure who instructed the PIC that they could fly at their desired heading and altitude. The PIC performed the climb checklist while simultaneously describing the function and purpose of the primary aircraft instruments to the passenger. Upon reaching the top of climb; the PIC began to set cruise power and pitch. The PIC also began performing the cruise checklist. Notably; the PIC saw a layer of a few clouds at the aircraft's 12 O'clock; and therefore turned left to navigate east of the clouds. At this point the PIC also turned on the pitot heat as the aircraft was navigating relatively close to the cloud layer and the surface temperatures were reported to be below freezing. (At this point this is where I believe the failure occurred. After review of the flight; I believe that this is a case of alternator over-voltage. At this time all the lights [NAV/STROBE/BEACON] were on; as was the pitot heat and the avionics system which may have been too much load for the system to handle.) In this middle of conducting the cruise checklist and navigating around the cloud layer; PIC received a call from ZZZ departure saying that they lost our transponder code and altitude on radar. They requested that the PIC reset the transponder; which the PIC did while also responding to departure. During the response transmission the PIC noticed that they could not hear their transmission through the headset and that they heard no reply from ZZZ departure.Shortly after; the PIC noticed the lights on the radio stack were flickering; which caused the PIC to suspect an electrical failure was imminent. At this point the PIC turned the aircraft to a circle pattern and reduced the power setting to economy cruise then began troubleshooting the problem. The PIC first checked the amp gauge and saw that it indicated there was discharge on the battery; then the PIC looked at the circuit breakers and saw that none of them were out of their regular position. After this; the PIC then turned off both the master switch and the alternator switch; waited 10 seconds; and turned it back on. At this point all the electrical systems on board the aircraft had failed. After failing to fix the problem the PIC then began to perform VFR lost-communication procedures. The PIC used their cellular device to call the FSS number and talk to the briefer; who then gave the pilot a weather briefing in the area along with valid SIGMETS; AIRMETS; and the local METAR at ZZZ. Shortly after that the call failed to FSS; but the PIC noticed that they had received a missed call from ZZZ TRACON on their cell phone. The PIC called the number back immediately and requested vectors back to ZZZ. The TRACON controller then provided a heading which the PIC flew while periodically giving altitude updates. When the field was in-sight; the TRACON controller gave clearance to land runway 3. The PIC then configured the aircraft for landing and performed a no-flap landing without incident. Upon landing the controller gave clearance to taxi to the FBO ramp via C; G taxiways. The taxi to the ramp proceeded without incident and the PIC then shut-down the aircraft and performed a post-flight inspection. It was noted that with the post flight there could be no clear cause of the electrical failure; and the alternator belt was still taut in place similarly to the pre-flight inspection.

Air Carrier Pilot crew reported too many frequency changes; EFB taxi chart confusion and taxiway sign confusion during taxi to runway.

After being cleared out of the parking alley we were instructed to taxi RB to the RB bridge. As the Pilot Monitoring I read back the clearance correctly to company ramp and the Captain correctly repeated it to me; but due to our focus on an aircraft that had just pushed back from the adjacent pier between us and the RB bridge; the Captain taxied over to RA instead. Shortly afterward we were asked to call a phone number; at which point were informed of the taxi error. I did not catch this error due to my relative inexperience at the airport (when I look at the respective bridges I don't immediately identify which is which) and the fact that I was obsessed with being on the correct frequency and listening for radio calls due to prior communications and taxi difficulties at this airport. This increased my workload inside of the cockpit and served as a distraction from my monitoring duties outside the cockpit.At the time of this incident I had obtained what I consider sufficient experience with this airport's operational complexities; yet I continue to personally experience and witness countless communications and taxi difficulties among our crews. This has led to near paranoia with my handling of communications and taxi operations at this airport. I now clearly brief the Captain on each frequency in each radio (active / standby) and obsessively announce the communications radio number I'm using at that time; i.e. 'now monitoring metering on 119.95; com 2'. The unfortunate consequence of this is increased workload and chatter in what should be a quiet cockpit with both sets of eyes up and outside. I am now convinced there are too many frequency changes between the gate and the runway at this airport. Metering needs to be done at the gate; much as it is at other airports so we exit the ramp and contact ground and then tower as we approach the runway -- just as we do at literally every other airport in the nation. All double-character taxiways need to be changed to single character names so they don't sound the same (or similar). This would also reduce the frequency time required to issue and read-back clearances. 'RA' should be 'A'. RB should be 'B'. 'WB' should be 'W'. The taxi to 15L is (and I did you not) 'Whiskey Golf; Whiskey Bravo; Whiskey Victor' which pilots (incorrectly) abbreviate as 'Whiskey Golf; Bravo; Victor' because they too realize the needless verbosity in the taxiway names. This is ridiculous. There are 26 letters in the English language and no where near 26 parallel taxiways at IAH airport. Therefore; all parallel taxiways should be given single letter names ('A'; 'B'; 'C'; etc.) and crossing taxiways given an associated single letter/number name such as 'A1; A5; A10'; etc. as is the case at many if not most of the airports in the US. I have also noticed that the taxi diagrams for the IAH airport is extremely poorly documented; with taxiway names adjacent to the physical representation of the associated taxiway; which leads to confusion in identifying the taxiways on the chart. Perhaps if the taxiway names were single character in most cases the diagram would be able to fit the single character name directly over the taxiway. Incidentally; just for reference; the vector charts built into the competitions product allow near infinite zooming and very clearly identify each taxiway because the text fits directly over the taxiway representation. Perhaps it's time to spend some money on the competitions product for our crews and dump our current supplier which is always crashing at inopportune times (yes; including during taxi). Additionally; ATC and ramp must be more consistent and explicit when they tell us to change to a new frequency as to whether they want us to 'monitor' or 'contact' the controller on that new frequency. I receive 'Aircraft X; taxi spot 1; metering on 119.95' all too often; and I am then forced to waste more frequency time asking whether I should monitor or contact them. I am at my witsend with the IAH airport and its operations. Someone needs to do something about this airport before more of our pilots are unfairly targeted for enforcement.

While taxiing on RC after departing alleyway; crew given instruction to taxi around an aircraft in front then taxi via RB bridge. Crew taxied around the aircraft as instructed but since the other aircraft was abeam Gate X and very close to the RB bridge; both thought we heard to taxi to via the RA bridge. We also changed frequencies to East Ramp and missed any calls from Company Ramp. We never heard any more calls from either ramp controllers until East Ramp called and continued our taxi. Unbeknownst to us; the ramp controllers had to stop a Aircraft X to prevent a nose-to-nose situation. We were asked to contact ramp via telephone and that's when we were informed of our error.This was a case of confirmation bias as we both thought we heard to taxi via RA bridge since the other aircraft was so near RB. I am familiar with the normal flow of ramp traffic and that RA is usually for westbound aircraft; though this is not always the case.

Corporate flight crew reported communication issues with ATC resulting in a minimum fuel situation due to a Center going ATC Zero.

The events described here are recalled to the best of our ability. The situation was very dynamic; and communication was often difficult. On date; on a flight initially planned from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we were flying in a type X aircraft between FL360 and FL400. Everything was proceeding normally until a reroute that would have taken us to toward the west side of State Y and State X; then to ZZZ2 on the east side of State X; then back to ZZZ1 in central State X. This is unusual; but we assumed it was due to weather in central State X. We also thought there was a good chance the route would be changed; so we were not overly concerned. As we were approaching the southern limit of ZZZ Center's airspace; we received another relatively complex re-route taking us to ZZZ3 then northeast back to ZZZ1. At approximately that time we started hearing reports about airports in north and central State X being closed. While we could see some weather on NEXRAD radar; it did not seem to be severe enough to close so many airports. However we had received no other explanation for the situation. After evaluating the new routing and analyzing the situation with the closed airports we determined it would be unwise to continue on that route to ZZZ1. We initially requested and received clearance to change the destination to ZZZ4. Also; at about that time we received instructions to contact ZZZ1 Center at a point some distance ahead (however the exact location is now forgotten).As we programed in the new destination and continued to hear reports of all or most airports in central and north State X now closed; (most likely not actually closed but unavailable in a non-radar environment already overloaded with traffic) we determined we were approaching minimum fuel and continuing on into an unknown situation would be unwise. We then requested a diversion to ZZZ5 and declared minimum fuel. We were told ZZZ5 was also closed. Our minimum fuel status was never acknowledged; even though we stated 'minimum fuel' twice. At about this time we were told to hold at ZZZZZ waypoint. We were not given an EFC time and as we started the hold; we lost contact with ZZZ Center. At this point we were on the verge of declaring an emergency; but an airline flight began relaying messages between us and ZZZ Center. We stated we wished to divert to ZZZ6 and were told that was approved but we needed to do so VFR; even though we were at FL270. Shortly thereafter we were told to contact ZZZ Approach even though we were still in the flight levels. Since we were basically over ZZZ6 we did a rapid descent and contacted approach while doing so. Eventually we were vectored for an approach and landed at ZZZ6.It should be noted that we were never informed that we were no longer in radar coverage; or that we would lose communication with ZZZ center before establishing contact with ZZZ1 Center. We were also never informed that ZZZ2 Center had gone to ATC Zero. We had also been cleared to lower altitudes; significantly increasing our fuel burn. We later learned during a phone call with ZZZ Center that ATC kept the ZZZ2 Center airspace open even though the center had gone ATC Zero. The methodology FAA Air Traffic Control Centers are using to deal with COVID related ATC Zero situations is extremely confusing and dangerous; especially when attempting to route traffic through a non-radar environment. It requires the use of complex routes that include waypoint names that are difficult and time consuming to say and spell. Had we been informed that ZZZ2 Center was ATC Zero we would have diverted before ever reaching ZZZ2 Center airspace; added fuel and waited for the center to re-open. Had we been informed of the lower altitudes we would be required to fly or of the extended routes required we would also have made other plans.As it was; we remained in a reactionary mode for much of the flight. We were unaware of the situation with ZZZ2 Center until after landing. While we never failed to comply with an ATC clearance; we were apparently still expected by ZZZ1 Center in spite of being cleared by ZZZ (as best we can tell) to divert to ZZZ6.We have the highest respect for air traffic controllers. But on date the ATC system itself severely failed. In addition to the primary events of this particular report; at various times during today's flights numerous other ATC irregularities (to be generous) occurred. For example; after receiving an IFR clearance on the ground at ZZZ6 we were cleared for a VFR takeoff and told to contact Approach in the air; that they were expecting us. Upon contacting approach; who did not seem to be expecting us; they instructed us to climb to 3;000 feet. We were then just left there; in some strange limbo state; not knowing if we were VFR or IFR; at night; at 3;000 feet; in a jet at 250 knots. After prodding approach; we eventually received our IFR clearance; the same one we were given before takeoff. We have no explanation for this.Furthermore; when arriving at ZZZ4 we; and several other aircraft; were instructed to hold as published at ZZZZZ1 Intersection while we were stacked up for the RNAV Runway X approach. However; there is no published hold on the RNAV Runway X approach at ZZZZZ1. There is a hold in the same physical location on the ILS X approach; but the name of the fix is ZZZZZ2; not ZZZZZ1.It was not a good day for us or ATC.

Our flight began and proceeded normally. Clearance was issued without any indication of flow problems in route. However; approximately halfway into the flight; reroutes were issued encompassing routing to ZZZ7 and ZZZ3. Multiple changes ensued and it is difficult to recall them all at this point. We surmised that we were operating as in a non-radar environment. However; we were never told that was the case. We complied with instructions. In the process of calculating and verifying routing and ETA's; additional instructions were given. Bear in mind some of this rerouting required headings; in some cases; 120 degrees off course. Additionally; we also had 120 plus knot headwind. Both of these factors combined were a bit unusual and prompted me to apply additional focus on to verify ETA's. We were ultimately informed that we would not be able to land at our destination; ZZZ1. Other requested nearby alternates were denied. We requested reroute to our next filed destination; ZZZ4. However; upon quickly re-calculating our fuel we determined we could not safely make that destination.At one point we were instructed to hold at ZZZZZ waypoint. We complied with instructions and held at ZZZZZ. In the hold we requested landing at ZZZ5 and were informed it was closed as well. At this point I remember discussing the possibility of declaring an emergency and landing before getting into a fuel critical situation. We were very close to ZZZ6 and requested landing there. Near this time; we realized that ATC did not hear us. Another airline flight crew relayed a VFR clearance from ATC to descend from FL270 to ZZZ6. In close proximity to ZZZ6; I initiated a relatively rapid descent approximately 4;000 FPM. Upon establishing communication with the local controllers at ZZZ6; the flight proceeded more or less normally until landing.On the ground at ZZZ6 we were informed that ATC would be back to normal at XAX0Z. We took on extra fuel as a precaution; filed and took off for ZZZ4. Upon receiving clearance to ZZZ4; ZZZZ6 Tower gave us the unusual clearance of proceeding VFR with the assurance that ATC was 'expecting' us. We took off VFR originally cleared to 2;100 feet. We continued to prompt for higher altitude and were cleared to 3;000 feet. For the initial part of the flight we were in limbo regarding when we would receive an IFR clearance. We were also relayed a phone number for ZZZ Center and instructed to call them when we landed in ZZZ4.Due to all the confusion and delays we arrived at ZZZ4 later than normal for us. We arrived at the time the tower was closing with multiple airplanes landing ZZZ4. We received; what seemed to me; a rather nebulous holding instruction for a fix a bit hard to identify given approach outages at ZZZ4. However; it was manageable and after descending in sequence through the holding pattern we landed safely at ZZZ4. I do not know if this situation is normal at the time of cessation of Tower operation at ZZZ4; however; it was very cumbersome. Upon landing at ZZZ4; we contacted ZZZ Center as instructed. It was a cordial conversation on both sides attempting to fully understand what had occurred. I realize COVID-19 has been a challenge to us all; however I would strongly suggest a different approach to the ATC Zero situation we have now. Such a distraction of multiple clearances with little time to verify and stabilize orientation before another one is issued; coupled with calculations for diverting; and lack of communication is a challenge and potentially dangerous for one aircraft. When that is multiplied by tens of aircraft; it seems to me that has to be detrimental to safety. I was as close to declaring an emergency as I have ever been. Again; I realize COVID has been a challenge to us all. I also realize yesterday was an equally frustrating challenge for ATC personnel; and it is certainly not my intention to impugn them in any way. If I can further help or facilitate a better solution for pilots and ATC; I would be more than happy to help. I hope this account from a pilot perspective is useful.

Center Controller reported safety concerns with another Center facility going to ATC Zero during peak traffic times and the confusion/stress this causes the controllers.

I am an Air Traffic Controller. It is my job to keep people safe while maintaining an orderly and efficient flow of Traffic. All of that was thrown out the window this night. I was instructed by management who were following orders received from the Command Center to ship numerous aircraft into a black hole (ZZZ1 ATC Zero). These pilots and passengers left the safety of a radar environment with no radio communication; no approved separation; and no one watching over them.The first ZZZ1 went ATC zero for COVID cleaning in the middle of the day and it completely overwhelmed the ZZZ2 [Center] controllers. The sectors became completely unmanageable. Aircraft from ZZZ1 Center entering ZZZ2 [Center] checked in responding to an RA.Training was insufficient and we were not prepared for what was about to happen. The last time I received training on non-radar separation was in 20XX in a classroom in Oklahoma City. I had no real-life experience with it until this week.I arrived at work I received a verbal briefing from my Supervisor. I was handed a sheet covered with tons of airports; routes; altitudes requirement; and minimal phraseology. Not only was this an insufficient amount of time to absorb the information; the instructions on the sheet were incorrect. We were told to get estimates over a fix and make sure he had 10 minutes between aircraft. In actuality we were supposed to assign a time for them to cross the fix. Also; the phraseology we were given when switching the aircraft did not include 'radar service terminated.' It was only after I got off position I realized that I had not given that critical piece of information to the pilots.I was so busy trying to sort out who needed what route and what was the appropriate altitude that I was unable to print strips and pass estimates. Knowing I was overwhelmed I called for help on 2 occasions. However; management and the tracker were so busy helping other people that they could not hear my calls for help. The information sheets we were given had so much information on them it was very difficult to know who needed what. At one point my information sheet was being used by another Controller. This made it very difficult to know what I needed to do with the aircraft. It was a very chaotic situation for everyone.As soon as I was relieved from my position I immediately notified my Supervisor that I had not passed any strips or estimates. I left with a sinking feeling in my stomach not knowing if the planes I shipped were actually separated. Concern over whether they made it through the black hole and arrived safely to ZZZ3 [Center] weighed heavily on my mind.Below are a few examples of Aircraft that were placed in dangerous situations as a direct result of the decision to misapply non radar rules and by allowing ZZZ1 [Center] to go ATC zero in the middle of the day during peak traffic times.Aircraft X- Took the clearance and left ZZZ2 [Center] airspace entering ZZZ1 [Center] ATC zero airspace. At some point the pilots realized that they were not allowed to fly non radar. Since they were no longer in communication; they turned their plane around and flew back into ZZZ1 [Center] airspace without a clearance. This jeopardized the flight because they were at FLXXX. This was an altitude we were using to clear aircraft through ZZZ1 [Center] airspace on non-radar routes. No separation was provided for this flight and they may or may not have had a loss. I have no idea if he was head on with another aircraft at the same altitude. This was an extremely dangerous situation.Aircraft Z - Level at XX;000 feet in ZZZ1 [Center] airspace. ZZZ1 [Center] updated his data block to VFR and put him on my frequency. ZZZ1 [Center] did not call and coordinate anything on his flight. The pilot checked in stating he was on an IFR flight plan in IFR conditions and wanted to climb to get out of the clouds. I told him I did not have authorization to change his altitude and if he could climb VFR to get out of clouds it would be OK. In hindsight this actually may have been an emergency. If he was in fact VFR like his data block indicated; he may have been VFR in the clouds. He later reported that he was VFR on top at XY;000 feet. Additionally; ZZZ1 [Center] put this aircraft on my frequency and he never even entered my airspace. At XX;000 he would have entered ZZZ [TRACON Airspace]. At XY;000 he entered the sector adjacent to me.Aircraft Y - Checked in about 15 miles inside ZZZ [TRACON] airspace level at X;000. The pilot said he was on an IFR flight plan; in the clouds and ZZZ1 told him to contact me. This Aircraft also never entered my airspace. I am almost positive that ZZZ1 [Center] violated ZZZ [TRACON's] airspace with this aircraft.Another aircraft had some confusion on his clearance limit. While in ZZZ1 ATC Zero [Center] airspace he entered into holding and was calling for help. After holding for an unknown period of time he became low on fuel. Eventually he was able to get a hold of someone and land at a nearby airport. This incident is deeply concerning. This aircraft was holding and eventually descended to land while we launched numerous aircraft through this area. How many losses of separation might we have had with just this one plane? He was also in distress and had difficulty reaching an Air Traffic Controller for help. This is a prime example of why it is important to maintain communication with aircraft while they are in a non-radar environment.We had two Aircraft at FLXXX with less than 2 miles separation when they reached ZZZ4 Center's airspace. Apparently; there was a major speed overtake and the trailing aircraft caught up to the lead aircraft.I had an aircraft checked in from ZZZ4 Center who informed me that their estimate over the fix was way off.What we did this day was in violation of the 7110.65 non radar rules and Federal Aviation Regulation for pilots. During non-radar; pilots are required to stay in communication with air traffic controllers and report time checks to make sure separation is maintained. These pilots had no radio communication and were never assigned a time to cross the fix. Also; controllers working the aircraft had no way to keep track of who had what time. We were asked to pass the time to the Supervisor; an impossibly task given the circumstances. We also flooded the route with significantly more aircraft than were intended to be on them. The volume was too high and unmanageable.Everyone working that day knew this was a bad idea. Union; Controllers; supervisors; upper management and our facility chief all knew this was unsafe. We expressed our concerns but were ignored and forced to proceed. I cannot express how deeply concerning and unconscionable this scenario was. We are lucky that we did not have a mid-air or an aircraft in distress that resulted in an accident because they could not receive assistance from ATC. These pilots and passengers were on their own. On this day we were most definitely NOT the safest airspace in the NAS. Without the proper tools and training in place this is an extremely unsafe situation. Interference with Air Traffic Control facility services can lead to loss of life.We need proper training and practice before we are ever asked to do this again.Rules and regulations must be adhered to.Radio communication should be kept between ATC and pilots at all times.We should not overwhelm the controllers. Traffic reduction is a must in situations like these.A tracking sheet should be kept at the scopes to know who was assigned what routes and times over the fix.Extra staffing should be called in to work these extreme situations.After major events there should be study groups put together to come up with better procedures. Air Traffic Controllers and supervisors that worked the traffic should be included in these study groups.When controllers; management and union say this isn't safe or we shouldn't do this then extra precautions should be taken. We are here to work traffic. We know better than anyone what [the] limitations are. Our voices should be heard and when we say something isn't a good idea we are probably right.

Air Carrier flight crew reported a heading deviation caused by not following SOP's and a change to the crew's normal procedures due to the pandemic.

While operating our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I was the Pilot Monitoring. At the time of the event; I was eating my catering and the Pilot Flying and I both found it easier for the PF to respond to ATC and manipulate the FMS. At some point at cruise altitude; ATC cleared us to fly direct from present position to 'ZZZZZ.' The PF responded to ATC and erroneously typed 'ZZZZZ1' into the FMS scratchpad and entered the waypoint as the direct-to navigation fix after both pilots checked the resulting dashed 'proposed course line' on the PF's ND screen. After several minutes; ATC inquired if we were proceeding direct to 'ZZZZZ' as he showed us drifting right of the intended course. This alerted us to double-check our navigation and to discover that we were navigating to the wrong fix; the misspelled 'ZZZZZ1.' The PF corrected the spelling of the assigned waypoint in the FMS; proceeded direct to 'ZZZZZ' and explained our error to ATC.I can identify three things that might have prevented this event: 1) The normal procedure and best course of action would have been for the Pilot Monitoring to stop eating; respond to ATC and manipulate the FMS. I do not; however; think this was much of a contributing factor. The PF is a 'strong' and extremely competent pilot highly experienced on the aircraft. I don't think the PF's assumption of those duties was particularly taxing/burdensome to the PF as we were in cruise at a very quiet and low-threat portion of the flight. It is not unusual for a PF to respond to ATC and manipulate the radios and FMS while a PM is eating. I have always personally tried to not touch anything other than my food while eating in the aircraft and think this is an especially important practice during the current health pandemic. While I could have sanitized my hands once I completed the radio calls and navigation tasks; it was more convenient to allow the PF to perform those duties for me. 2) The best course of action would have been for the PF to scroll the flight plan and chosen the assigned Direct-To waypoint 'ZZZZZ' from the flight plan. However; the aircraft's FMS is slow to respond; making scrolling through a long flight plan somewhat laborious; tempting one to effect the change via the scratch pad method. The PF alternatively could have checked the paper copy of the flight plan for the correct spelling of the waypoint before typing it into the scratch pad. 3) I had the 'PROG' page selected on my FMC and did notice that the course to the incorrect 'ZZZZZ' was almost 25 degrees to the right of the bearing of ZZZ1 and thought it odd to be navigating that far off the bearing to destination. This matched my curiosity about the dashed 'proposed course line' displayed on the PF's ND when the erroneous fix was entered into the scratch pad. However; knowing that the destination was more than 1200 miles away at the time; I assumed there was a significant 'bend' in the original flight plan. Had I mentioned my observation to the PF; it might have cued the PF to check the spelling of the waypoint as the PF made the entry from an assumed spelling. When checking off frequency with the controller who made the direct-to assignment; the PF apologized for the error and asked if we should contact anyone for further discussion/explanation. The Controller indicated that he did not believe that would be necessary.My time-in-type; time-in-position and total-time are not readily available and I don't want to delay submission of this report in order to track down those numbers. I therefore entered a generic '1' in each of those blocks in the report. Each of the numbers actually totals in the thousands. Fatigue was somewhat of a factor in the event. It was the last duty day of a pairing that had us flying a mix of long and short legs; including international legs to and from an international country; and crossing the country and multiple time zones. We shifted between flying and non-flying duty periods several times and scheduled rest varied from long to short periods. Obtaining 'quality' rest was a challenge and I most definitely accumulated a sleep deficit by the day/time of the event. I estimate that I slept a total of 5.5 hours during the rest period prior to the duty period of the event; one sleep period of 4 hours and another nap of 1.5 hours; waking approximately 3 hours prior to reporting for the event duty period.

First; I can't confirm all the information requested above. I don't remember exactly which Center we were talking to or pinpoint where we were relative to a fix. I think we were with ZZZ but it might have been ZZZ1; and we were south of ZZZ1 and west of ZZZ2 at the time; going direct to ZZZ2. I was the FO and the Pilot Flying. We were cleared direct to ZZZZZ. The Captain/PM was eating his catering so I was also answering the radio. When we received the clearance to ZZZZZ it was easier for me to enter the fix in the FMC than it would have been for him; so I typed that in. About 10-15 minutes later the Controller said that he showed us about 45 degrees off course and asked whether we were going direct to ZZZZZ as cleared. We double-checked for NAV selected to the fix; looked at the course deviation; and checked the FMC; and they all confirmed direct ZZZZZ. On closer examination; though; we realized that we were actually going to a fix called ZZZZZ1; and that I had misspelled the correct fix when I typed it in. I didn't select it from the fixes listed on the flight plan; and should have done that instead of typing it in. That would have obviated the error. The aircraft made a fairly significant turn to the right when I executed the direct-to command and I thought at the time that if I'd known it was such a big difference in the track I'd have requested direct sooner. The Captain later said that he'd thought it was strange that the bearing/distance on the FMC didn't match what the airplane had turned to when we made the turn; and wished that he had said something at the time so that we could resolve the discrepancy. I should have caught the misspelling at the time; but I also should have selected the fix from the list instead of typing it in. I indicated that fatigue was a factor with this event because I think I would have caught the error or not made it in the first place. We overfly ZZZZZ often and I've noticed the variant spelling before. It was the last night of the trip; though; and I'd not had more than 4 consecutive hours of sleep (or more than 5.5 total) on any of the previous days.

Air Carrier Flight Crew taxiing 747-8 aircraft reported taxiway incursion on closed taxiway.

Descent and approach were briefed with expectation of [Runway] XXL at ZZZ. ATC advised during descent to expect Runway XYR. ATC was advised that we were a 747-8 and a request for [Runway] XXL was made. ATC advised that Runway XXL was not available unless operationally required. Runway change checklist was performed and performance obtained for [Runway] XYR. Captain briefed that a right turn [off] [Runway] XYR was not allowed except for Taxiway E. However we did not expect to make this exit so he briefed a left turn at [Taxiway] K or roll to the end. Arrival and landing were normal; after slowing through 60 kts. we were past [Taxiway] E and the Captain stated that he would be exiting left on [Taxiway] K. As we began our left turn toward the high speed taxiway I noticed a line of lights on the ground marking the taxiway closed. These were very dim and low to the ground. Very hard to see. I said very affirmatively; STOP; STOP Barrier. The Captain [stopped] the aircraft and then corrected taxi course. The aircraft did encroach on the first few feet of Taxiway K but not far enough that he couldn't correct back onto the runway. On our rollout ATC did issue an invalid taxi clearance that was a distraction. The taxi clearance was corrected after our [query] and the remainder of the taxi was uneventful. Post flight review of NOTAMS (Notice to Airman) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service) revealed that the taxiway was NOTAM closed and was missed on our part. The poor lighting of the taxiway closure barrier was a large factor in us not seeing it sooner.

Prior to top of descent we briefed and prepared to fly the ILS (Instrument Landing System) approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. Our airport briefing page does say that arrivals between XA:00 and XB:00 should expect Runway XYR for landing; but goes on to state that 747-8 aircraft should expect XXL. Upon check in with ZZZ Approach; we were told to expect [Runway] XYR. I reminded the controller of our aircraft type and queried whether [Runway] XXL was available. We were told that due to noise abatement procedures at that time of day that we could only use [Runway] XXL if it was due to operational necessity. After a quick discussion with the Captain; we decided that due to our light gross weight; we could accept [Runway] XYR. We quickly reprogrammed the FMS (Flight Management System) and briefed the new approach; to include the many 747-8 taxi restrictions and the fact that taxi to parking was likely to be somewhat complex. We decided that a left turn off the runway on Taxiway Kilo was the most likely scenario. While we did these things quickly; I felt that we had covered all of our bases and did not feel rushed or that the workload was too high. What both the Captain and I missed however; was the fact that [Taxiway] Kilo was closed. We had both reviewed the NOTAMs (Notice To Airmen) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service); but since we were planning on landing on [Runway] 8L; I believe we both simply failed to register the Taxiway Kilo closure; as it did not apply to our original taxi plan. The approach and landing were uneventful and both the Captain and I were focused on identifying Taxiway Kilo in order to vacate the runway. At no point during our approach or rollout did Tower relay any instructions on how we could expect to vacate the runway. As we began to make the turn for [Runway] Kilo; the IRO (International Relief Officer) forcefully stated 'Stop! Stop'. He had managed to pick up the extremely dimly lit barricades that marked the closure. The Captain managed to get the airplane stopped before we were committed to Taxiway Kilo. Around the time we stopped; Tower transmitted that [Taxiway] Kilo was; in fact closed; and that we could expect to make a right turn off the runway at Taxiway Charlie. This was an invalid clearance; as the -8 is restricted from using that portion of [Taxiway] Charlie. As we were about to query Tower; I believe he realized our aircraft type and issued a clearance to taxi clear of the runway at the end. The rest of the taxi was uneventful. I think there are several take-aways from this incident. First; the IRO was worth his weight in gold this morning. Had he not spoken out in a timely and forceful manner; I think there was a very good chance we would have impacted the barriers or at the very least been unable to continue our taxi. The IRO was the last link in the error chain and that link held strong. Second; I think both ZZZ Approach and the Tower Controller were both unaccustomed to a 747-8 arriving at that time of morning. Landing on [Runway] 4R presents a number of taxi challenges to a -8; and perhaps the best practice may be for -8 crews to declare 'operational necessity' and request [Runways] 8L or 8R unless there are other extenuating circumstances. In the event we must land on [Runway] 4R; a simple 'plan to vacate the runway at X' from Tower would be extremely helpful. Finally; while I do believe the way our situation evolved created somewhat of a setup regarding the closure of Taxiway Kilo; the information was in fact available in the NOTAMs and via ATIS. I overlooked that information largely due to an incorrect expectation bias. I am aware of my ultimate responsibility to digest that information and will make an effort in the future to pay more attention to the 'Plan B' options in addition to the expected one.

A321 Captain reported recurring fume events which have resulted in flight crew experiencing physiological symptoms. Reporter questioned whether maintenance corrective actions are in need of review.

Fumes on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. This report is to highlight the procedures used to resolve fume events. It isn't to report the fume event. In summary; after the flight and cabin crew smelled fumes during flight and after landing; Maintenance worked to resolve the problem. After performing various procedures; Maintenance said the problem was fixed three separate times. Each time; the flight and cabin crew pointed out that the fumes were still present. Even so; a manager from another department was brought in to see if she smelled any fumes-she did not. So; as the maintenance policy allows; the aircraft was returned to service; overruling six professional and very experienced flight and cabin crewmembers' specific and detailed descriptions of the characteristics of the still present fumes' smell; the locations in the flight deck and cabin where the fumes were detected and the air supply vent locations from which the fumes were emanating. Approximately an hour later; a flight crew reassigned to ferry the aircraft to ZZZ2 started the #1 Engine; smelled the fumes and refused the aircraft. The fume event began during descent below at 5;000 ft.; at 15 miles from ZZZ1 airport when I noticed musty smelling fumes on the flight deck coming from the eyeball vents on both the overhead and instrument panels. I recognized the smell from previous experience (along with information supplied by both Air Carrier and the Pilots Association); as being from petroleum based fluid being heated and entering the air conditioning system. Being close to the ground and landing; I wanted to find a solution quickly so I closed the flight deck vents to see if there was any change. There was not; so I reopened them thinking that if the fumes were transient that air flow might move the fumes through and off of the flight deck. I also started to feel slightly nauseated so I donned my O2 mask. After donning my O2 mask the nauseated feeling subsided somewhat. Landing was made without incident. At taxi speed I opened my window; turned off the air conditioning packs and taxied to the gate. I then spoke with the flight attendants to see if any of them had smelled the fumes. The flight attendant at Door 3L said that shortly before landing some passengers asked him about a smell in the area. Once they had pointed it out; he said he had then smelled the fumes. No other flight attendants reported smelling the fumes at their jumpseat locations during flight. I wrote up the fumes in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logs); then completed and submitted a smoke; odor; fume form. When Maintenance arrived I described the smell of the fumes to them. None of the mechanics with whom I spoke (four I believe); smelled the fumes. From then until when the flight was cancelled at XA:00; one mechanic (of the four); acknowledged that he smelled the fumes 'slightly' and only one time. During this time; Maintenance completed procedure(s) three separate times and after each time said that they didn't smell the fumes and wanted to sign off the AML. Each time; my flight and cabin crew pointed out the smell of the fumes in the cabin and flight deck; so Maintenance continued their procedures. At some point after those three attempts to resolve the problem; one mechanic told me that the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that day. Soon after that; a manager from another department was asked to walk through the cabin and see if she smelled the fumes. After a bit I checked my schedule and saw that we were reassigned to take that same aircraft back to ZZZ at XC:00 on [Date]. That was consistent with the last I heard from the mechanic who said the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that night. Around XD:00; I saw that another crew had been reassigned to fly our aircraft to ZZZ2 at XE:00. I texted the Captain on that flight to be sure he was aware of the seriousness of the problem. He replied; stating that after they had started the #1 Engine; the fumes returned. He did not accept the aircraft. I then called [Pilots Association] Safety for some guidance. I am concerned because; despite all the procedures in place to determine whether the source of the fumes is eliminated; the methods to determine whether the fumes are present or remain:1. Expose maintenance personnel and possibly other people to the fumes and their potential harmful effects (isn't that what we're trying to avoid?).2. Allow using the olfactory senses of random individuals that; (a) may not be able to detect the smell of the fumes; (b) have never smelled the fumes and/or; (c) have no knowledge of the seriousness of the smoke; odor and fume events and their potential and documented health threats.3. Allow the complaints and input of those that do smell the fumes to be ignored or overruled by any randomly chosen person that does not smell them. It seems that the goal should be that if just one person still smells the fumes; the problem isn't solved and the aircraft won't be released to flight status.

Air carrier flight crew reported executing a go-around due to ATC spacing with another aircraft on final. The flight crew overshot their altitude during the go-around and cited the aircraft light weight as a contributing factor.

Coming to ZZZ on the ILS [Runway] XXR; we were continually slowed by ATC for spacing of traffic ahead and behind. At about 1;200 MSL on glide path still IMC Tower told us to go-around. I was PF and hit GA button and advanced power levers. We went through missed approach procedure; but as flight guidance was attempting to be set the aircraft was also capturing the level off of 2;000 MSL so took a little longer to complete. Meanwhile we were a little late on turning to 195 heading. ATC queried us as we were in the turn. We had also climbed to 2;180 feet before stopping and returning back to 2;000 immediately. After we got settled ATC vectored us back to ILS with no further issues. ATC told us they had to send us around because aircraft on final for parallel Runway XXL behind us had gotten .99 miles from us. Spacing needed to stay a min of 1 mile.I should have paid more attention to altitude and started turn to 195 even if flight guidance wasn't quite set yet. Also pulled back power sooner or not add as much to avoid going through altitude.

During our arrival into ZZZ; when told to run base (heading approximately toward ZZZZZ [Intersection]); we were slowed to 170 KIAS. We were maintaining 4;000 feet throughout base turn and intercept turn onto final. Once established on final (approximately 20 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]) we were slowed further to 160 KIAS; with traffic approximately 4 NM in front of us. Once we intercepted the glideslope; we maintained approximately 1;000 feet above the preceding traffic; but gained to within 3 NM distance. Meanwhile; ATC vectored a airline flight onto final for [Runway] XXL close behind us.I told the First Officer (PF) to potentially fly a half-dot high on the glide slope to avoid any potential wake from the preceding aircraft. Once we reached approximately 10 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] we were slowed further to 150 KIAS.As we continued down the approach; the TCAS showed us to be approximately 2.5 NM from the preceding traffic; with the traffic behind us close in trail (unable to tell the specific distance). At approximately 600 AGL; ZZZ Tower issued a Go-Around; with nonstandard missed approach instructions (Right turn heading 195; climb and maintain 2;000). The First Officer initiated the Go-Around and the Captain (PM) proceeded to re-program the Flight Guidance.Due to the light passenger load; the subsequent climb rate caused the Flight Guidance to immediately switch from a Climb indication to an Altitude Capturing indication; which caught the Captain off-guard; and he tried to re-configure the Flight Guidance back to a Climb indication. The Flight Guidance again sequenced to an Altitude Capture indication. At this point; the Captain (PM) noticed the aircraft was off course to the left approximately 35 degrees and was rapidly approaching 2;000 feet. The Captain brought this to the attention of the First Officer while also simultaneously acknowledging ATC stating 'Turn right heading 195.' The Captain also prompted the First Officer to reduce the power setting; as the airspeed was approaching maximum flap speeds. The missed approach up to leveling off at 2;000 feet was all hand-flown (i.e. not with the autopilot).Once the aircraft was established on the appropriate heading; altitude; and configuration; ZZZ Approach vectored the flight around for a second attempt at the ILS 16R; which occurred without further incident. In researching the First Officer's seniority; he has been here less than X years (Date). After debriefing the flight; he stated that that was his first Missed Approach / Go-Around in the actual aircraft EVER.Since we had been slowed down significantly early during the approach; we knew we could expect to be sandwiched in between other aircraft. However; we did not know that ATC needed only 1 mile separation between aircraft on parallel ILS approaches (told to us by ATC during our second attempt). There was no mention of spacing requirements on our first approach.Due to 'COVID loads;' the aircraft type climb rates are very good; requiring steeper than normal attitudes so as to not exceed flap speeds. This factor; combined with the First Officer's relative inexperience with missed approaches; caused a momentary loss of situational awareness by the First Officer.This required the CA to not only re-configure the flight guidance for a missed approach; but also ensure the First Officer did not over speed the flaps; communicate with ATC; and ensure the aircraft was following appropriate flight guidance (which was a non-standard missed approach).Also contributing to the loss in situational awareness was the altitude at which ATC issued the Go-Around: 600 AGL. This caused a significant startle factor in both the Captain and First Officer. Had ATC mentioned anything about a potential missed approach; we would have been much more prepared.Last-minute ATC-issued Go Around instructions (below 1;000 AFE); caused by inadequate spacing with simultaneous parallel approach aircraft.RECOMMENDATIONS:1. ATC NEEDS to let crews know 'be ready for a missed approach' if there is potential for a spacing issue. We were given our Go-Around instructions at 600 AGL. This is a very high-risk area to issue a Go-Around; when spacing throughout the entire approach was tight. Some sort of notification to us would have primed for a potential Missed Approach and therefore could have avoided any loss of situational awareness and subsequent heading / altitude deviation.2. STOP ISSUING NON-STANDARD MISSED APPROACH INSTRUCTIONS. The ILS [Runway] XXR's Standard Missed Approach instructions are to fly runway heading to 900 feet; then climb on heading 195 to intercept the ZZZ 210 degree radial; maintain 2;000 feet. This is VERY similar to what we were assigned (heading 195; climb to 2;000 feet). However; when we're given nonstandard missed approach instructions; not only do we have to interpret what it is ATC actually told us; but also program that into the Flight Guidance. This programming is CONTRADICTORY to what our normal Flight Guidance programming procedures are. Had ATC simply said 'fly the published missed approach;' that could've aided in our appropriate handling of the aircraft.LESSONS LEARNED:Don't trust ZZZ ATC to not screw up. If spacing looks tight; brief a missed approach; even if it's done on the Final Approach Course. Also; do not trust your fellow crew member to fly a perfect Missed Approach. Watch them like a hawk for course; airspeed; and altitude management; and IMMEDIATELY speak up if there is even a minor deviation.

BE-36 pilots reported a fire of unknown origin at engine start requiring evacuation and the airport ARFF to respond.

We had completed the pre-flight check of the aircraft and pulled it from the hangar at ZZZ Airport to the alley way between hangars.We had completed the pre-start checklist items; picked up the ATIS and our clearance to transit out of the SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area).The aircraft started normally. There was a single backfire after or as the engine started but not too uncommon. The throttle was retarded following normal procedures.Shortly after engine start the cockpit began to fill with an acrid smelling smoke from under the left side of the panel. The engine was immediately shutdown and we exited the plane. All electrical (master/alternator/ignition) was shut off.Co-pilot grabbed the fire extinguisher as we exited. After exiting the Tower was called. The Tower called the on-field fire company. Response time was about <5 min as the on-field company was sent to the wrong side of the field.We opened the engine cowling to see if we could identify a source and possible extinguish. No fire was evident in the engine compartment. The fire departments had not yet arrived.The prop began a very slow rotation as if the engine was trying to crank.We went to check to verify that the Master Switch was off. It was.Smoke from the panel was much heavier. Appeared to mostly originate from the pilot side.Close evaluation showed flames from top of the left side-wall upholstery.We used the fire extinguisher to extinguish the flames along the sidewall. The amount of extinguishing agent or time for a full discharge seemed less than expected (perhaps 30 seconds).Fuel valve was moved to Off.A person called indicating that the Emergency Locator Transmitter had activated. We began a search for the beacon to deactivate. Determined that it is behind the panel in the back of the passenger area behind the stretcher. Requires panel removal.Fire department from ZZZ arrives.They verify that there is no excess heat in area where the flames were extinguished or other locations.The mechanic we used at [Company] arrived and began assisting with assessment and possible causes and removal of the ELT.Fire departments determined that no action on their part was needed and departed. On the scene perhaps 30 minutes.No immediate cause was noted the A&P from [Company].We returned the plane to the hangar. We called [Company1] to see if they could determine any immediate cause. We were trying to decide if we needed to use [Company1] vs [Company2].The technician from [Company1] saw no immediate issues.We disconnected the ground side of the battery; wrapped and secured to make certain no contact could occur that might provide a power source.We left the airplane doors open or ajar to allow for ventilation and secured the hangar.The plan at this point was to have the aircraft moved to [Company2].

We pulled the aircraft out of the hangar; shut the hangar doors and climbed into the cockpit for the start. We completed the normal procedures checklist setting the parking brake; received our SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area) clearance and shut down the avionics for start and noted the time as XA:X0 pm. The engine was primed with the auxiliary fuel pump; mixture was set to full rich and throttle to full open. The ignition was turned to start and as the engine began to turn over it ignited; and the throttle was retarded to slow the RPM to approximately 1000 RPM. As the RPM was beginning to stabilize; there was a backfire explosion and almost simultaneously smoke began pouring out from the defroster duct? at the left side of the wind screen and from underneath the dash panel by the PIC (Pilot-in-Command)'s rudder pedals. The smoke intensified filling the cockpit and the door was opened to relieve the smoke. Since the smoke was continuing; the mixture was pulled; the ignition was turned off removing the key and the battery and alternator switches turned off. Co-pilot exited the aircraft to determine a cause of the smoke and as he was investigating; I pulled the fire extinguisher from behind the co-pilots seat. I then exited the aircraft while he continued to walk around the nose of the aircraft looking for any source of fire. None was noted and the smoke was ventilating and dissipating. I called the tower on my cell phone to notify them of our situation and asked for fire assistance. I told Tower we were [at] the hangars on the east side just south of the terminal building at hangar. Tower took immediate action to alert the airport firetruck and ZZZ City Fire Dept. We did not see any evidence of a fuel fire or flames exiting the engine compartment although we did notice that the propeller began to rotate slowly for a few terms before stopping completely. The engine compartment was opened and there was no evidence of any fuel or oil leaks or any fire or smoke damage to the engine compartment. We went back behind the right wing and looking through the cockpit door; co-pilot noticed flames between the sidewall and left rudder pedal. He activated the fire extinguisher and sprayed the area of the flame; extinguishing it.While waiting for the fire equipment to arrive; I called Maintenance to ask them to have a mechanic come over and evaluate the situation. Fortunately; their lead was on the way to the east side and he arrived to look at the aircraft. Shortly thereafter the Airport Operations Director was first to arrive on scene and supervised the arrival of the fire equipment. The airport team was first ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) unit on the scene and were very professional in evaluating the situation so that no unnecessary action was taken. The smoke gradually dissipated and the aircraft was checked for residual hot spots; none of which were found. The fire equipment returned to their stations and the aircraft was hangared until it could be moved to the local maintenance facility.

Pilot reported application of the wrong MEL complicated the flights unnecessarily.

In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly; and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag.
