However after becoming distracted (which I will explain later); I noticed my altitude got down to that approximately 9;600 MSL for which I knew was not right; and immediately began corrective action while simultaneously ATC queried my altitude and I made mention of correcting. I saw I was just passed HLMET and quickly climbed back up to the crossing altitude of 10;000 MSL. Shortly later the controller mentioned the possible pilot deviation may have led to a loss of separation; although no TA/RA's were issued by either aircraft. Here is where I want to bring to attention the possible safety issue as related to the situation and what resulted in me becoming distracted and task saturated. Starting at an ATC controller back before TRACON; which was Salt Lake Center and while on the QWENN 5 RNAV Arrival off the MLF VORTAC transition; I was left extremely high by the center controller; for which I was expecting to receive the 'Expect' crossing restriction at FRNZY intersection at 15;000 MSL on the chart. I could hear multiple aircraft in front of me getting the FRNZY at 15;000 MSL restriction; but also complaining of being left very high and possibly not being able to make it. As I started to see the FMS computer show a required 3;500 FPM decent to make that restriction; I thought I better ask the controller for a descent; however the frequency was congested and it took many more minutes until finally the controller just issued me to now cross FRNZY at 16;000 MSL and 250 KTS. I replied that I would do by best; but it would be tight to make. Mind you that this new altitude required my attention to reprogram the altitude into the FMS as I anticipated and setup for 15;000; and still it showed a required 3;800+FPM decent to make it. I immediately initiated the decent for which I used the VNAV mode in the FMS/autopilot to make the crossing; which also required idle power and the activation of the aircraft's speed brake system to induce drag to not over-speed in the decent. During the decent on the arrival there was also light to bordering on moderate rime icing in IMC and snow showers. When the engines are at idle power they do not produce enough bleed air to keep the Anti-Ice/De-Ice systems operating; for which I got warning that they were not being kept hot enough; so I was trying to introduce small amounts of power to try and get more bleed air flowing to those systems; all the while trying not to over-speed and setup for the instrument approach. Being single-pilot this induced a very high work load; which caused me to become task saturated and behind on preparing for the approach. After finally passing FRNZY at the 16;000 MSL altitude and still in icing conditions and IMC I was simultaneously passed to TRACON approach control which issued me the direct HLMET; cross at 11;000 MSL; cleared approach restriction. I continued the decent down out of 16;000 MSL to 11;000 MSL still using VNAV on the autopilot (more on that later). I noticed I was still nearing around idle power and adding what I could but was still having trouble keeping the speed under control and still behind on setting up the approach. Somewhere around 12;000 MSL I got an indication that the speed brake panels went down; even though I didn't select it. Wondering what happened I looked out the pilot side window at the wing and noticed they were in fact still up; just no longer indicating it in the cockpit. This distracted me; as I knew I needed them extended to maintain my speed and help to try and keep power up and bleed air flowing. It took mybrain a few moments to try and figure out what was going on as there is no abnormal procedure for that in the checklist. I decided to recycle the speed brake switch; for which they then operated normally (retracted and extended); and then gave all normal indications. Throughout that situation is when the altitude deviation occurred; as after I was confident there was not a problem with the speed brakes and they just needed a reset; I accidentally went through the 11;000 MSL attitude down to the approximately 9;600 MSL altitude. Upon speaking with Maintenance later on the ground they feel that the system was activated for so long throughout the decent continuously; they work trapping hydraulic pressure to hold it up; that logically that pressure must have bleed down some; causing them to blow in-trial/down just enough to give an indication in the cockpit that they were sent fully down; and that this was not a malfunction or cause for investigation for repair; especially since they functioned normally after the reset. The indication only looks for full up or full down deflection; so if they blew down a little due to reduction in trapped pressure; it made sense to them. Again they continued to function and indicated correctly the rest of the flight. Back to the VNAV function I used on the autopilot to meet the crossing restriction; as that is the recommended function to meet crossing restrictions; and the function I always use to reduce pilot workload. Somewhere during the sequence of the approximate 3;800-4;000FPM required descent the VNAV system apparently kicked off and defaulted back to just a raw pitch autopilot decent; in which with everything else going on I failed to notice. I can only attribute this to it not liking or taking issue with that rapid of a required decent; and thus defaulted out of it. With 1500+ hours in type; I cannot recall ever descending so rapidly; to were I would have seen or noticed its inability to function through that rapid of a decent. Had VNAV stayed activated; it would have saved the deviation from happening as the approach was loaded with all crossing restriction altitudes and it would have followed them; for which I was also expecting it to do. Although this 'event' happened in Tracon airspace; I feel the safety issue started back in Salt Lake Centers airspace by being left very high on the arrival. ATC needs to be cognizant especially when icing conditions are possible/present some or most aircraft cannot descend that rapidly and keep critical anti-ice/de-ice systems operating properly with idle power descent. Additionally; giving instruction to meet a crossing restriction that requires 3;500+FPM descents is unsafe and not conducive to being able to setup and properly execute a stabilized approach; and leads pilots to get behind. After giving this event thought I am recommending to our flight department to not use the VNAV function of the FMS/autopilot for required descents over 3;000 FPM; but rather use vertical speed mode and monitor carefully. In addition; we will no longer accept any crossing restrictions from ATC that would require over 3;000 FPM; and rather state unable and require a re-sequence back on the arrival via a course reversal to help lose altitude and keep from the pilot getting behind the aircraft and task saturated. Us pilot use the term 'slam dunk' when ATC tries to do this; where they keep you very high and then plop you right on the arrival/approach. This condition does present safety issues due to the above mentioned items.

EMB-175 flight crew reported a cabin fumes event during approach descent.

Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the Flight Attendants that there was an odor in the vicinity of row X. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning or acrid smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row X; to whom it was very noticeable; which was also confirmed by FA 'B'; but only when they walked up to row X. There was no visible plume anywhere in the airplane. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.The FO was flying the airplane (PF) so they took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. The comment about a fuel smell drove the pilots to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; while we requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated; clearing other aircraft from our path. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit [Runway] XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of runway. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down (left-hand-side) engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down (right-hand-side) engine #2. Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I 'Deice' and Type IV 'Anti-Ice' fluid; with engines running; at the X Pad.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. FO also said that after landing they briefly noticed an odor.We could have [advised ATC] earlier on in the event. This would have allowed us traffic priority earlier in the descent (and speeds above 250 KIAS once below 10;000); getting us on the ground sooner and reducing the overall time of pax/FA exposure to fumes.We flew the same airplane the following day; and the airplane was cleared by Maintenance with no defects found. Nothing was wrong with the airplane itself. Fumes remaining localized in a certain area of the cabin suggests internal point source emission rather than external ingestion or airplane system malfunction. However; at time of writing; we still do not know; definitively; what caused the fumes.The FAs are commended for their prompt notification and accurate description of the nature and extent of the fumes. FO is commended for flying the aircraft while coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF; while the CA ran checklists and coordinated with the FAs; then flying the approach almost to minimums. Working together seamlessly is key in these situations; and the CA commends the crew for a job well done.

Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I and Type IV fluid; with engines running; at the South De-Ice Pad.Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the FA's. I (the FO) assumed it was the FA's notification that they were seated. Instead; they communicated to the CA that there was an odor in the vicinity of row x. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row x; to whom it was very noticeable. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.I (the FO) was flying the airplane (PF) so I took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. Since the CA was communicating with the FA's; I trusted his lead on necessary checklists to run; as he had the first hand information on the situation in the cabin. During this time; we had entered IMC conditions; and I was flying the airplane and working the radios; receiving several heading; altitude and speed changes during this time.The comment about a fuel smell drove us to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; during which I requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon landing; I cracked the Thrust Reversers (TRs); and briefly noticed a smell in the flight deck. I then decided that the use of TRs may not be the safest procedure; as it was still unclear what was causing this smell. Thus; I immediately stowed the TRs and decelerated using only the brakes (long runway; good braking action).Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of XXL. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down engine #2.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. This was my 2nd precautionary ARFF event on 2 consecutive workdays (though separated by a period of leave). Having had the time to reflect upon the first event; I felt calmer and more prepared this time. I focused on making a successful approach (almost down to minimums).One error I made was to start configuring and thus slowing down too early. Due to several heading changes and an ATC request for us to slow down while the aircraft in front of us on the approach sped up to best forward speed; I had felt momentarily disoriented regarding our distance to the ZZZ1. Luckily; my brain was about 5 miles ahead of the airplane. Once I realized my error; I paused further configuration (which was gear down flaps 3 at that time) until closer to the ZZZ1.Considerations that were made were items for fire and emergency evacuation; should a fire develop after landing. Luckily; this was not the case.To my knowledge; it is still unclear what caused the smell. If it would have been more severe (filling the entire cabin and flight deck); then the checklist for smoke/fumes would have been appropriate.Overall; I feel that this event was handled well by everyone involved.

B-747 First Officer reported a CFIT event that was resolved and completed an uneventful landing.

I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on this ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight; XXX on [aircraft]; arriving into ZZZ1 from the south east; at night; in VFR conditions. Due to the winds out of the north at ZZZ1 (310 at 12 gusting 21); RWY XX was the only landing runway on the ATIS. Upon loading RWY XX; the ZZZZZ [arrival] would not show as an available arrival in the FMC. ATC did not assign the ZZZZZ arrival but instead gave us direct ZZZZZ1 (a waypoint on the ZZZZZ); and then direct to the airport. These ATC instructions were given near ZZZZZ2 [fix] on our flight plan. With the Captains concurrence I executed direct ZZZZZ3. Additionally; the Captain had me select ZZZZZ3/12;000 as a hard altitude in the FMC to help with descent planning (12;000 was a crossing altitude restriction on the ZZZZZ1). I then placed ZZZZZ5 as the waypoint that would follow. As we got closer to ZZZZZ3; Approach directed us to maintain present heading with a further descent to 10;000. This heading did not keep us in a direction tracking the ZZZZZ arrival over the water along [geographic fix 1] ; but instead brought us on a more westerly heading over terrain on the southwest side of [geographic fix 1].Approach then directed a descent to 8;000. Then directed a right turn to 250. Then directed a further right turn to 260. And finally; a descent to 7;000. Approach then asked: 'Do you have the field in sight? 2oclock 21 miles' The Captain and the Observer both spoke up to speaking that they could see the airport. I as well saw the lights of the airport and felt comfortable concurring. The Captain said he could accept the visual and so I then relayed this to Approach. Approach than cleared us the visual approach RWY XX. At this point the Captain looking at his descent planning showed us slightly high on the VNAV descent path and started a descent below 7;000. Shortly after this and around 6;200 ft; a GPWS alert 'CAUTION TERRAIN' enunciated. Looking at my Terrain display; the AMBER terrain mapping showed terrain off to our right. The Captain immediately arrested his descent and the Observer and the Captain and I visually confirmed the terrain off to the right of our flight path. Shortly after this ATC further directed us to begin our right turn towards the field. The Captain and I continued to maintain visual separation with the terrain and delayed further descent until comfortable the terrain clearance was no longer a concern. We then conducted an LVSA on the MCP and an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. [Reporter added concerns] accepting a visual approach at night. Although we could see the lighted airport environment ahead; what was not so apparent was the dark terrain just below the city lights that was still ahead and to the right of our flight path. At night; the city lights in the distance can cause night vision to be affected and spotting unlit terrain between your flight path can be potentially more difficult to see. Accepting a visual approach is not something that should be done lightly. The better course of action was to recommend to the Captain we delay accepting a visual until we were closer to the field and the terrain well behind us. ATC did not help matters by asking us to an accept a visual approach as early as they did. A mistaken assumption could be made that the terrain protections of 7;000 was past us and a descent to establish an already slightly high VNAV path to RWY XX could be initiated. Clearly the terrain ahead was much closer to our altitude; we had several miles to go before a descent below 7000 should have been initiated. The GPWS 'CAUTION TERRAIN' was a very clear on this point. The importance of GPWS Terrain monitoring [is that] GPWS is an essential situational awareness tool and one the pilot monitoring only had displayed initially. Had the Captain also had TERR selected this may have mitigated the early descent; but as pilot monitoring I should have done a better job monitoring the TerrainMapping display. Clearly after the 'CAUTION TERRAIN' annunciation appeared; the Yellow Terrain mapping became very clear on both our displays. Additionally; when descending in mountainous terrain it's also important to remember that the GPWS system will only display terrain data that is 2;000 feet below or closer to the aircraft. Depending on your range ring and your location and rate of descent; you can quickly go from no terrain colors to quite colorful ones in short order. Vigilance in monitoring Terrain Mapping along your flight path is key. Lastly; had this situation happened in [different type aircraft]; the terrain profile view function would have provided significant situational awareness to the crew on the terrain that was still ahead. [Regarding] RNAV approach to XX; the [company] aircraft behind us had received approval to fly to a point on an RNAV approach to XX; an approach that is currently not available on our aircraft. Had this been available; this would have been a valuable tool providing altitude protections and a significant aid to situational awareness. Even if not an RNAV approach; a visual approach page like the ZZZZZ3 VISUAL Rwy XY that is available in JEPPS would have also aided in better descent planning for the RWY XX visual approach.

Air Carrier flight crew reported a track heading deviation during approach due to communication issues with ATC. The First Officer cited the Captain wearing a face mask on the flight deck may have contributed to the communication problems with ATC and between them.

We conducted the ZZZZZ4 arrival and joined the ILS XX approach from ZZZZZ [Intersection] as briefed. When the Captain contacted the Tower; the Controller cleared us to land XX Right. The Captain read back the clearance. I said; 'Can you confirm Controller wants us to land on the right? We're on the ILS XX Left.' The Captain confirmed with the Controller cleared to land on the right. The Controller responded 'Affirmative. XX Right; Cleared to land.' At the time; we were well above 1;000 feet in visual conditions with the runway in sight and; so I had no objection. I clicked off the autopilot and side-stepped to XX Right and we landed. No issues arose with ATC or any other traffic. The next day; the Captain reached out to me and we spoke over the phone. Captain learned that we had actually been cleared for the ILS XX Right approach and Captain intended to file a report. A couple of days later I was finally able to confirm that this was correct. We aren't able to determine if it was being read back correctly or incorrectly; but there was never a clarification type of response from ZZZ Approach. It's also important to bring up that the Captain was wearing a face mask throughout the flight operations which did contribute to difficulties in communication with myself and with ATC at various times during the trip. This likely was a contributing factor to our deviation. Another contributing factor was the violation of sterile cockpit below 18;000 feet by the Captain and myself. Personally; I was distracted by our conversation as well as the fact that Captain was wearing a mask during the flight.Complacency is also a factor as the ZZZZZ4 Arrival usually results in the ILS or visual to XX Left.I think our company needs to take a harder stance on mask-wearing during flight operations in the flight deck. I recommend that the company forbids the use of masks by pilots during flight operations to ensure that communications are clear and effective. In this case; it can be assumed that the Captain was repeating the clearance saying 'XX Left' but the Controller did not hear it clearly and assumed Captain was saying XX Right. Therefore; Captain was never corrected and we continued with what we had expected in our heads. There were multiple points throughout our trip that ATC did not understand the Captain and asked who was calling or needed clarification on what Captain was saying because it was difficult to understand with the mask. I thought on several occasions throughout our trip that it was the Captain's choice to wear it but if we have an emergency situation that I really hope Captain would take it off so that effective communication could be established and maintained. An emergency situation did not occur; but clearly an issue did arise with our approach to our destination.

ZZZ had a broken layer at 1;700 feet and we were expecting to do an approach. Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ4 arrival we had set up for the ILS [Runway] XXL. We were assigned to join the ILS [Runway] XXR at ZZZZZ [Intersection] and then later cleared for the ILS XXR approach. We did not fly the ILS XXR. We flew the XXL approach and when we were on with Tower; we told them we were inbound on the ILS XXL. Tower cleared us to land XXR. By the time we contacted Tower we were out of the clouds and could see the runway. We verified two times that we were cleared to land XXR and not XXL. And Tower confirmed that we were to land XXR. Since we had visual on the runway; we side stepped and landed on XXR. We were probably at 1;500-1;600 feet AFE when we side stepped. We were confused as to why they had changed runways on us; but we knew that XXR was longer than XXL and that the landing speeds were the same and we were familiar with the airport. As we side stepped; I programmed in the ILS XXR so that we had a backup source even though we visually had the airport in sight. Later in the evening it still didn't sit right with me that we had a runway change that late; especially since we had been on an IFR approach. I realized we had in fact been assigned ILS XXR all the way back on with Approach. They never corrected me. So; I either read it back correctly but we were really hearing what we wanted to hear (ILS XXL) or they never corrected me and we all missed it. The approach was stable all the way through for XXL and the sidestep was done in a safe manner.I attribute not being sterile in the descent as a factor even though we were assigned to join ILS XXR at ZZZZZ prior to FL180. I would say complacency and expectancy were the primary factors. XXL wasn't closed and we were set that we would be doing the ILS XXL. It was also the last leg on the last day of our trip and we had had a long day. I had been up since 8 or 9am and we had flown 4 legs. This flight landed around XApm.I can say that I once again am reminded how serious our jobs are and that miss hearing a simple 'L' vs 'R' can be life changing. I can only say that I am thankful that this took place during a low traffic period and that we were able to maintain a safe condition. I'm honestly not too sure how to avoid this situation. I believe that writing down my clearances would assist in allowing me to verify and that maybe I need to make sure to turn my headset up so that I won't miss ATC.

B757 flight crew reported loss of B hydraulic system caused a go around and a precautionary landing.

Uneventful flight to ZZZ. On final ILS XXR at ZZZ; below 2;500 feet; inside ZZZZZ but prior to ZZZZZ1; LOC and GS Captainured; flaps 20 set; Captain called for leg gear down and disconnected AP and A/T. At this moment; the L HYD SYS PRESS Master Caution Lt illuminated. At first I thought the light was associated with the AP and A/T being disconnected. It took a couple seconds to recognize that it was the HYD pressure light. At this time also we were checking in with XX_1 r outside ZZZZZ1 and were cleared to land. Very shortly after I accepted the leg clearance; the Captain alerted to Go Around and made the Go Around call to Tower. We accomplished the normal go around procedure and shortly received a LDG GEAR DISAGREE caution as the gear did not retract due to the initial emergency. We repositioned the gear handle to the down position and that caution extinguished. After reaching 3;000 feet and completing the GA procedures; the Captain continued to fly the AC and I accessed the Non Normal procedure through the FM on my EFB. The HYD section has a large index and initially I inadvertently selected the HYD SYS PRESS L and C non-normal and after the first two steps realized we were in the wrong checklist and switched to the HYD SYS PRESS L (only) Checklist. I ran the checklist aloud as the Captain continued to fly. Step 7 instructed not to use auto brakes. When completing the deferred items; the flaps and gear were already in the proper configuration and due to the post Go Around altitude and box pattern vectors; though not unduly rushed; I inadvertently failed to re-run the descent checklist as part of the deferred items; missing the last reminder to not use autobrakes. We did run the deferred landing checklist; and the Captain flew the approach to landing. After touchdown the auto brakes engaged firmly and the Captain immediately moved the speed brake lever slightly fwd to disengage the autobrakes and proceeded to manually brake the AC along with use of the RT engine reverser. We slowed to a gentle stop with approximately 1;500 feet remaining on Runway XXR. Due to the lack of runway steering we remained on the runway; coordinating with ground personnel; and monitored brake temps. After an initial external check by ground personnel; we secured the engines; remaining on APU power for the remainder of the ground ops evolution and tug to our gate.

Communicating with ZZZ approach on the ILS XXR to ZZZ between ZZZZZ and ZZZZ1; with the flaps at 20 and after lowering the landing gear; we received an EICAS message L HYD SYS PRESS. I was Pilot Flying; hand flying with the A/P and A/T off. The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. At ZZZZZ1 we switched to ZZZ Tower and informed them we would abandon the approach. We were given a northerly heading and a climb to 3;000 [feet]. I decided to abandon the approach using V/S mode as we were at approximately 1;600 feet; and to reduce my workload; engaged the right autopilot. I inadvertently called for 'Gear Up' which did not occur due to the loss of the left system. We realized this error when a 'GEAR DISAGREE' EICAS message appeared and returned the gear handle to the down position. The gear remained down from the prior approach through the eventual landing.I stated the I had the airplane and the radios and directed the First Officer to run the L HYD SYS PRESS non-normal checklist.We also pulled up the status page and noted the loss of quantity from the left system; less than .2 with RF showing.We initially started the L and C HYD SYS PRESS checklist but caught the error when the checklist called for an action regarding the center system.We then proceeded to run the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist; but made an error; missing the 'do not use autobrakes' step. I would eventually select Autobrakes 4 for landing.ATC asked me at this point if I needed the equipment standing by and I declined.Upon completion of the checklist up to deferred items; I [advised] with ATC.ATC asked us which runway we would like; and I inquired about [Runway] XYL. ATC said it would be available as a visual approach. I decided to re-use the ILS to XXR as we were set up for it already; would benefit from the precision guidance at night; and it had an approach light system that [Runway] XYL did not. The length of [Runway] XXR provided our required landing distance; with margin; plus around another 4;000 feet.I sent a brief ACARS message to Dispatch stating I had [advised with ATC] and would be landing in ZZZ. I should have included the nature of the [event] and our need of a tow in the body of the message. Despite being somewhat concerned about the time available as I was stuck in a high drag configuration; I still had enough time to send a more complete message and should have done so- it would have been a few more keystrokes. I also had enough time to re-run the non-normal checklist. Doing so would have caught the autobrake restriction. The First Officer and I discussed this in our debrief.I then briefed the purser using the TEST acronym; advising that we would NOT need to prep the cabin for evac.I do not recall asking for the equipment to be standing by; other than stating we would need to be towed off the runway. The equipment was in fact standing by for us at landing and detected hydraulic fluid that contaminated the runway.ATC had provided a modified box vector for us; and as we were approaching base I exchanged roles with the First Officer and assumed aircraft control as Pilot Flying. I called for the deferred items. Another opportunity exists in the deferred items with a descent checklist step stating the autobrakes should be off. In our debrief; we discussed that the were a number of items in the deferred items checklist that were not applicable to our situation such as alternate gear and flap extension. This may have led to the error and missing the descent checklist step. We committed to running future checklists step-by-step.The flaps 20 approach was uneventful; and I used the autopilot and autothrottle until short final. Approach had given us a discrete frequency for ZZZ Tower and the rescue equipment. At landing; I felt a sensation similar to anti-skid activation and immediately disengaged the autobrakes by slightly advancing the speed brake lever; and came to a stop using the operable reverser and manual braking.ZZZ Fire and Rescue assessed our aircraft and we set up for a tow-in. ZZZ Fire and Rescue noted hydraulic fluid contaminated the runway.We proceeded under tow to gate. At the gate; I discussed the event with Dispatch and the [Chief Pilot].In my debrief with the First Officer; we went through the debrief card. The items that seemed to go well included workload management; automation management; and our planning and decision making. The humbling items that could have gone better would include my monitoring and cross check of the items on the non-normal checklist. In a future event; with time available; one of us will independently re-run the non-normal checklist before committing to the approach. Calling for the gear up as we abandoned the approach was a rote response. With a hydraulic issue on arrival in the terminal area; next time we will maintain the existing configuration unless performance reasons dictate otherwise.Communication with Dispatch should have been more thorough; next time I will spend an extra two minutes to send a more informative message to Dispatch.

EMB-145 flight crew reported low engine oil pressure on final approach and continued the approach to a precautionary landing.

After being cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL in ZZZ we received an EICAS 'E2 OIL LOW PRESS' red master warning message on the EICAS display. I cancelled the red warning and advised my First Officer (FO) to reduce the thrust lever to idle on engine number two. I observed the oil pressure for engine two indicating in the red at about 34 PSI; but fluctuating around the top of the red level; and with occasional fluctuations into the bottom on the green range; and which caused the EICAS warning to extinguish; but then reappear once again triggering another master warning for the same condition about 30 seconds to a minute later. Engine number one was still operating within normal engine parameters (green indications); however. The FO was the pilot flying the aircraft; with the autopilot coupled to the [Runway] XXL ILS. As engine number two was still operating at idle thrust; and as I deemed that there was insufficient time to safely compete the required QRH checklist items during the approach prior to landing; I advised the FO to continue the approach. Therefore; rather than perform a go around so as to provide an adequate amount of time to complete the QRH inflight engine shutdown checklist; I made a call to ZZZ Approach and advised the Controller of the situation - that the aircraft had low oil pressure on engine two and that engine failure was imminent. The Controller queried me if I [needed priority handling]? I replied in the affirmative; and subsequently advised the Controller that the we did not require immediate assistance [for the time being]. The ZZZ Approach controller requested the number of souls on board and approximate fuel. I advised the controller that we had XX passengers and X crew for a total of XX souls on board and that we had XXXX lbs of fuel; and approximately 2 hours fuel (endurance - at single engine burn). ZZZ Approach gave instructions to contact ZZZ Tower; who issued a landing clearance for Runway XXL. I advised the FO to disconnect the autopilot and continue to hand fly the approach to landing with the engine number two at idle thrust. The low oil pressure master warning occurred shortly after the glideslope intercept and normal thrust reduction at an altitude of approximately 10;000 MSL; at around the ZZZZZ fix; on approach to runway XXL. The aircraft configuration at the time of the first EICAS warning was flaps 9; gear up; with a speed of 200 KIAS. As we had already planned to make a normal flaps 22 approach and landing; I elected to continue the approach configure the aircraft for a flaps 22 landing as originally intended. I advised for the aircraft to be slowed to 190 KIAS and the approach to be continued. Landing gear down and flaps 22 was selected at ZZZZZ1 FAP and at which time the before landing items were completed. I then communicated with the flight attendant an abbreviated brief on the CABIN EMER intercom - that we had a low oil pressure indication on engine two; and that we had about 1 minute to go before landing; and to make sure to be seated. A normal landing was successfully carried out; and upon rollout I advised the FO to activate just the engine number one thrust reverser to aid slowing of the aircraft. I took control of the aircraft at the 80 knots and continued to slow the aircraft using moderate braking to a safe exit speed off the runway at the high speed taxiway exit 1. I taxied to a stop just after turning onto Taxiway M. I instructed the FO to advise the tower the we momentarily stopping on Taxiway M to perform checklist items. The tower advised us to contact ZZZ Ground. I then instructed the FO to shutdown engine two and back this up with the QRH and to then perform the after-landing checklist. A number of ZZZ rescue fire service trucks were approaching the aircraft. Cognizant that the close proximity of emergency service vehicles would cause some concern for the passengers; I made a PA announcement to the explaining the situation and that once the personnel hadperformed a visual check for any smoke emanating from the rear of aircraft fuselage; we would continue the taxi to the gate as normal. Once personnel confirmed that there was no visible fire or smoke present we requested to continue the taxi to the gate as normal. We then taxied to the gate as normal with the exception that I elected to not set the parking braking - due to a possible risk of smoke or fire developing; as the brake temperature on the left inboard brake was indicating in the amber caution range - but requested for the ground personnel to chock the wheels instead to give time for the brake temps to cool down. A normal shutdown check was performed and with normal passenger disembarkation. I immediately wrote up the discrepancy in the aircraft logbook and contacted the company dispatch to explain what had occurred and requested to speak with maintenance to discuss the write and the event. I advised Maintenance Control of the discrepancy details and what occurred. Maintenance Control then advised that they would need to place the call on hold while they checked if I needed to be transferred to the Maintenance Duty Manager or to receive a callback from a Maintenance Supervisor. I then performed the aircraft terminating checklist and went outside to inspect the aircraft exterior. I then received a call from a company Maintenance Supervisor to needed some additional information about the event. While on the phone call with maintenance I received a call from someone else in Maintenance (possibly the Duty Manager). As no voicemail or text was left by on my phone; I expected another callback from Maintenance Control; but which did not occur; however.In my view; appropriate decisions and actions were made by all crew members. And given the dynamics of the situation; that these decisions and actions were necessary to mitigate the safety risks; to the passengers; to the aircraft; and in the interests of other relevant aviation stakeholders; and which contributed to a safe resolution and satisfactory outcome.

We were cleared for the visual approach to [Runway] XXL; when we received a master warning and EICAS message E2 OIL LOW PRESS. The Captain identified and cancelled the warning and we verified the oil pressure in the red on EICAS as well as checking the oil quantity on the to data page; where we saw only 4 quarts in the number two engine. I was instructed to bring the number two thrust lever to idle to prevent further damage. At this point we were between the IAF and FAF on the XXL around 190 knots with flaps 9. The Captain and I agreed due to the time available before touchdown and severity of the situation to leave the number two engine at idle thrust. The Captain called ATC and advised ATC of our situation; ultimately [requesting priority handling]. The Captain advised ATC of souls on board and remaining fuel onboard; stating we did not need immediate assistance. ATC handed us off to Tower where we got our landing clearance for XXL. The Captain then called the Flight Attendant and gave her a report to prepare for normal landing; advised the situation; gave her time till touchdown; the flight attendant stated cabin was secured. As we neared the FAF I called for gear down and flaps 22 for the final configuration with a landing checklist. We had already briefed to do a flaps 22 landing due to forecasted wind. The Captain had me disconnect the autopilot and hand fly the approach to maintain best control of the aircraft. We performed a normal landing with number two engine at idle thrust; which was successful. At 80 knots; we transferred controls and captain advised me to tell Tower we would need to stop once clear of the taxiway; which I promptly did. ZZZ Tower instructed us to contact Ground and cleared us to stop on the taxiway. The Captain instructed me to shutdown the number two engine; and promptly back it up with the QRH to verify all necessary steps were taken for the E2 OIL LOW PRESS master warning. We completed the QRH items and after landing checklist at this time. Operations vehicles contacted us and the Captain asked them to verify no smoke; fumes; flames etc.; coming from the number two engine; which happened to have no indications. We then contacted ground control to taxi into the ramp area. Prior to movement we noticed the left hand inboard brake was in the yellow arc; in which the Captain elected to leave the parking brake released and have the wheels chocked at the gate. After parking; we accomplished the shutdown checklist; deplaned all passengers and cargo. I stepped outside to do the post flight walk around and found the bottom navel covered in oil; therefore verifying the oil leak. After returning to flight deck the captain was on the phone with Maintenance control; writing up the discrepancy; the Maintenance Duty Manager explaining the situation. We completed the terminating checklists to finish. I believe the decisions by the crew and actions performed; were the best course of action for the dynamics of the situation and time frame we worked with.

Air carrier light crew reported a Cabin Press Warning EICAS message while crossing a mountain range on a one pack deferred flight. Flight crew completed an uneventful landing after developing a successful workaround.

We were assigned an aircraft to take from ZZZ to ZZZ1 that had the BLEED 1 system on MEL. The FO and I discussed before departure in our threat based briefing about how the BLEED 2 system would have a hard time pressurizing the entire aircraft all the way up to our cruise altitude of FL XX0 and how we should make the climb as shallow as we could without exceeding VMO or any airspeed restrictions in order to help the BLEED 2 system pressurize the aircraft.After takeoff the aircraft was pressurizing normally but then somewhere around approximately 7;000 feet on the climb we noticed that the cabin altitude was increasing at about the same rate as our actual altitude and there was only about a 2;500 foot difference between the two. Knowing that only one bleed system was trying to pressurize the aircraft we continued with the hopes that it would catch up and pressurize normally.At 12;500 we got the Cabin Press warning so we leveled off and asked ATC for the lowest altitude they could give us; we were over the [name] Mountains at this time so the lowest altitude they could give us was 12;000 feet. At 12;000 feet the cabin pressure was holding steady at about 9;500 feet but wasn't increasing or decreasing any further.The FO and I discussed running and looked at the pressurization fail checklist but both agreed that the checklist was designed for a 2 bleed operating system and that this was a unique situation.At this point I called Dispatch and Maintenance to discuss the best plan of action; after some discussion Dispatch told us that we needed to return to ZZZ because we didn't have drift down performance for our route of flight at 12;000 feet. By the time this was decided we were almost on the other side of the mountains and I could see the town of [name] about 30 miles to the southeast of our position. My decision was to not turn around and cross the mountain range again at 12;000 feet without drift down performance. When Dispatch became aware of our position we both decided that the best plan of action was to continue to ZZZ1.We landed in ZZZ1 without any further incidents.In hindsight there are two things I wish I would have done differently. The first thing I should have done was to not continue over the [name] mountains with the pressurization not adequately pressurizing the aircraft. I think my continuation was due to the fact that I was unfamiliar with how the pressurization of the aircraft performed with only one bleed system operative and it was my first time operating the aircraft with that particular MEL. If I had it to do over again I would have asked for delay vectors while we waited to see if the pressurization would catch up with our altitude and that way I could have avoided crossing the mountains at an altitude without drift down performance and just returned to ZZZ.The second thing I would have done was to at least run the unpressurized flight checklist; it was a short flight with a very high workload and even though we were still partially pressurized it would have been a good checklist to run just to see if there was anything else we were missing.

Bleed 1 was consistently giving a #1 bleed hot caution on previous flights. Therefore; the bleed 1 source was placed on MEL. The only guidance from the MEL was that we shall not turn on the affected bleed valve. Climbing out of ZZZ; we were filed too FLXX0. Bleed 2 was on bleed 1 was off. Upon reaching 12;000 feet the cabin press master warning light appeared. We leveled off and descended to 10;000 feet. We contacted Maintenance Control and Dispatch. I took the radios and was already PF. Due to not having drift down performance and already being pass the mountains Dispatch and the pilots agreed that it was best to continue to ZZZ1 as we had a lot of fuel. We noticed the aircraft was very slow at pressurizing during the climb we attempted to help the system by reducing the rate of climb. This seemed to have little affect. It was almost expected by us that the master warning would go off. Once it went off we noticed the aircraft was at 12;000 feet. But the cabin pressure was at 10;000 feet. So there was a small pressure differential. We therefore decided that we would not put the masks on as this would make commutation more difficult with each other and there was no need for an emergency descent. We descend to 10;000 feet as soon as possible this allowed the cabin to descent to 8;000 feet which was much more normal. We contacted Maintenance Control first as we knew what caused the problem. They advised us to call Dispatch. Drift down performance was not available for our altitude so by the time we contacted Dispatch we had passed the mountains and we agreed with Dispatch that it was safest to continue to ZZZ1. Due to the aircraft not pressuring and knowing the issue causing the problem we did not run the cabin press checklist as this would have advised us to turn on bleed 1 which is specifically what we were told not to do in the MEL. By descending down to 10;000 the master warning went away. We continued to ZZZ1 with no further issues.1) It's important to continually monitor the pressurization panel. 2) Maybe contact [Dispatch during preflight for other options]. 3) Knowing that if the bleed source is on MEL; we should expect the aircraft to not pressurize.4) I would not feel comfortable flying an aircraft with this MEL again unless we were filed below 10;000 feet know the system would not pressurize.5) The MEL was not clear on what to expect with this system inop.

Flight Crew reported miscommunication lead to a departure with a fuel leak that required a diversion and a precautionary emergency landing.

Preflight and pushback were uneventful. We started the left engine and taxied out on one [engine] with an ATC designated takeoff time of XA:44L. We started the second engine during taxi; all uneventful. While holding #1 for takeoff; Tower informed us that a [other] airline crew had noticed what they thought might be a fuel leak. We immediately thought of returning to the gate; but then Tower came back and told us to disregard the previous concern and that it was a different aircraft with the possible leak. We were then cleared for takeoff. Just before switching us to Departure; Tower said that there appeared to be some vapor coming from around our left engine. We scanned the instruments to see if there were any parameters that would be cause for concern; but everything looked normal. It was also humid air; and sometimes contrails can be seen in those conditions coming from the flaps during takeoff. Once above 10;000 feet; the Captain called Flight Attendant 1 and asked him to look at the left wing/engine to see if he could see any leaks or causes for concern. Once his visual inspection was complete; he called back and said that he did see what appeared to be vapor coming from under the left engine. We then had him come up to the cockpit; and the Captain sent me back to confirm the Flight Attendant's concerns. I did see what appeared to be vapor coming from under the left engine; although it was difficult to tell exactly where the vapor was coming from. I went back up to the cockpit; told the Captain what I had seen; and we immediately began considering divert options. During this entire time; we were still climbing out and monitoring our fuel; including the fuel burn; engine fuel flow; and balance between wing tanks. During climb out; all of the indications seemed to be normal; but once we leveled off; the fuel burn began to diverge slightly from the planned fuel at each waypoint; and the imbalance between wing tanks began to grow; but it was all still within limits. Engine fuel flow was normal with no difference between the two engines. While continuing to monitor our fuel; ATC said that they had received a call from ZZZ Operations telling them that a runway inspection after our departure had revealed that we had leaked fuel on takeoff. At that point; we made the decision to divert. The weather was clear everywhere; and we had multiple good divert options. The Captain coordinated with Dispatch and we made the decision to divert to ZZZ2. The Captain spoke to the flight attendants and the passengers while I coordinated with ATC for the diversion. While enroute to ZZZ2; the fuel imbalance really became apparent. Just as were handed off to ZZZ2 Approach; we got the ECAM for FUEL IMBALANCE - FUEL LEAK PROCEDURES APPLY. We focused on the approach and landing; and planned to shut down the left engine once clear of the runway. We coordinated with ZZZ2 approach to have ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting) meet us in the echo pad to confirm we weren't leaking fuel; and then follow us to our gate. We executed that plan without incident; parked the aircraft at the gate and deplaned the passengers. Obviously we would have preferred to not take this airplane into the air. Maybe not a causal factor; but I would like to know if our ground crew noticed anything during or after engine start. We started the left engine first while still pushing back; and then made a right turn out that would have given them a good look at the problem engine. [The other] airline obviously noticed something; although once the Tower said that it was a different aircraft; we no longer considered a return to the gate. Once we had taken off; I felt that we handled the issue appropriately. Although I can't be sure if there were indications during engine start; I would hope that our ground crews are alert to any possible abnormalities that could arise during/after engine starting; including leaks.

After pushback; Ground informed us we had a wheels up time to ZZZ of XA:44. We started the left engine and decided to single engine taxi until we got closer to departure time. I made about 130 degree right turn from the ramp to the taxiway. When we got over to the other side of the terminal; we started the right engine; about 6 minutes prior to our wheels up time. As we were running the final checklist items the Tower called and said [another] airline had reported a plane with what looked like a fuel leak. as we were talking about it; the Tower called us back and said disregard it was a different aircraft. The Tower then cleared us for takeoff. After we were airborne the Tower told us it look like there was vapor coming off the left engine. All the engine parameters we normal so we continued our climb. After we got above 10;000 feet I called Flight Attendant 1 and asked him to go look at the left engine to see if there was any fluid he could see. He called back and said he saw something so I sent the First Officer back to see if he could tell what it was and where it was coming from. He said it was hard to tell but it did look like vapor coming from under the engine. The fuel was not out of balance more than normal and we checked the fuel against the flight plan and it was not significantly off so we continued the climb. We were looking at our options in case we had to divert when Center called and said ZZZ had inspected the runway after we took off and found fuel on the runway. At that point we tried to call Company OPS to get a phone patch to Dispatch but no answer. I got on the crew phone app on the iPad and got in touch with our Dispatcher and we decided to go to ZZZ2. As we went further towards ZZZ2 the fuel imbalance started to appear. It was very slow but it was noticeable. As we approached ZZZ2 at 12;000 just before talking to Approach; we got an ECAM [Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor] fuel imbalance; fuel leak procedure apply. We already knew we had a fuel leak. Landed in ZZZ2 without incident. Had the ARFF make sure the fuel leak had stopped after we shutdown the engine on the echo pad away from the gate. Taxied to the gate and deplaned the passengers. I think when ATC called us back and said disregard then cleared us for takeoff; it took away any thought about returning to the gate. I was very surprised our ground personnel did not notice the leak after we started the engine.

Air carrier flight crew reported an altitude and track heading deviation during approach to an international airport. The crew stated this sequence of flights; since the COVID-19 pandemic started; are very long and fatiguing which may have been a factor in the event.

Intercepting the unstable Localizer on a 225 vector; approximately 16 nm final; the aircraft started to join the Localizer. The Localizer shifted to the right and the aircraft began a hard right turn to intercept passing of approximately 240 degrees. I instructed the FO to stop the turn and come back to the left toward final approach heading. He did not reply to my direction and did not act. As the aircraft passed approximately 255 degrees; I took command of the aircraft; disconnected the auto-pilot and started a turn back to the Localizer. I was concerned about the numerous aircraft on final for Runway XX. In my turn back to the Localizer I overshot the Localizer and deviated from the assigned 900 meter altitude by approximately 100 meters. I intercepted the Localizer; got back on altitude; and flew an uneventful ILS and normal landing. This all happened unexpectedly. The hard right-hand turn to intercept is unprecedented in my XX years of flying [this type aircraft].Unstable Localizer and Autopilot aggressive turn to intercept. Fatigue affected my flying after taking the aircraftThe current schedules to service this country during Covid leave no extra margin of safety when things like this go wrong. Multi-leg days; with long turns between flights; after crossing X time zones leave little margin of safety. Also; the very long trip extensions for crew members leads to fatigue.

I was the PF for the 2nd leg of the night which was a night recovery. At altitude I had briefed the STAR and approach; and once the descent started; we received numerous altitude; heading; and airspeed clearances as the controller was trying to work what appeared to be a fairly large recovery into ZZZZ [Airport]. ATIS reported that simultaneous ILS approaches were being flown to [Runway] XXL as well as [Runway] YY. Approaching ZZZZ; we were being vectored for the ILS Y; Runway XXL and at about 20 miles were cleared 'heading 215; maintain 180 knots to 8 miles; maintain 900 meters until intercepting the Localizer; report established.' We were already configured at flaps 15 with the ILS tuned and the approach checklist complete. The assigned heading provided a comfortable 15 degree cut; but with winds of about 120 at 25 knots at our altitude (overshooting crosswind); and parallel approaches being conducted; with the autopilot still engaged; I was diligently watching the automation. I pressed the APP/LAND tile and initially the aircraft maintained heading; but after a few seconds; it started making some gentle (level) turns left and right. Initially these turns were mild and we even chuckled at what a poor job the AP was doing to maintain heading to intercept. Suddenly; the magnitude of one of the turns to the right increased markedly and the aircraft was in a level turn to the right of approximately 25 degrees angle of bank with the heading coming through approximately 230 degrees. As I spent just a few seconds (no more than 4 or 5 I would say) trying to determine what the autopilot was doing; the CA called out; 'turn left; turn LEFT; I have the airplane' and executed a maneuver that I would describe as similar to a PRM breakout maneuver. He disconnected the AP; added power; and reversed our turn; climbing and accelerating in the process. The maneuver was aggressive enough that I thought it possible the CA had SA to something that I was missing since I had already started to reach for the heading selector in order to get the plane to level its wings and come back to the left (note: things were happening very quickly now and I did not verbalize this FMC input since I would have just been trying to talk over the CA telling me to turn left even though the airplane did start to shallow its turn to the right once I pulled the selector). I verbalized 'you have the controls' and monitored his inputs. As former fighter pilots; the CA and I both have fairly wide comfort zones and although the maneuver was fairly aggressive; I was still comfortable with the aircraft's attitude and remained quiet as I monitored the aircraft's flight path. I did not want to add to the confusion of the moment by asking questions or saying anything unnecessary since the CA was very purposeful in his maneuver. Now things became quite busy because in addition to receiving a 'bank angle' audible warning due to our steep turn to the left; the approach Controller began talking to us rapidly. He made several transmissions and told us repeatedly that he had us on a heading that was not going to intercept the Localizer and that we were above our assigned altitude and asked what we were doing. I replied that we were still below the glidepath at approximately 930 meters; and maneuvering to intercept the Localizer. After a few more moments the CA stabilized the aircraft's attitude; I selected FMS speeds (since we had accelerated to approximately 210 knots and needed to slow back to 180 knots); and he began a turn back to the right to intercept the Localizer. The CA re-armed the approach (but never re-engaged the AP); slowed to the assigned speed; returned to the assigned altitude; and leveled the wings on an appropriate intercept heading. The FD provided what appeared to be valid guidance to shoot the rest of the approach. The aircraft was configured and stable before glide-slope intercept and the remainder of the approach proceeded normally with me remaining in my role as PM.We went from conducting a routine controlled approach; to one where I think we had widely differing perceptions of what was actually occurring in the space of literally about 4 or 5 seconds. This rapid breakdown of CRM resulted in actions that were perhaps more aggressive than they needed to be; and a deviation from the ATC clearance. I would actually say there were two separate events. The first being the aircraft's unexpected and overly aggressive turn to the right to capture the Localizer for ILS Runway XXL; and the second being our response to it. The first I would potentially attribute to a software issue; a problem with the ILS tune; or some sort of RF interference. As far as the second I would suggest the following; 1) Even though I did not feel fatigued during the approach; it was at the end of a long day and it's possible I underestimated my level of fatigue. That said; I did have some coffee prior to Beginning of Daylight (BOD) for this reason and; I felt like the CA and I were both alert and engaged and don't feel like my response to the aircraft was unacceptably slow or inappropriate. 2)The CA believed that the intercept angle was excessive (he referenced 45 degrees during our debrief) and that based on his prior experiences; there was no way the airplane was going to be able to capture the Localizer. Since I had not experienced the automation act in the manner it did during our approach; I was perhaps more comfortable than I should have been with the AP's ability to capture the Localizer; even with the admittedly substantial intercept angle that we had before the CA took the controls. 3) The CA stated during the debrief that he thought we had already flown through the Localizer; and that he was therefore worried about a lack of separation from the traffic that was flying the ILS to Runway XX; to our right. I did not perceive that we had flown through the Localizer for the following reasons: a) We were in a phase of flight where we both (certainly I was) monitoring the raw Localizer data in anticipation of Localizer capture; and neither of us ever called 'Localizer alive'. I felt like I was hawking this for the reasons listed above (overshooting crosswind and proximity to other landing traffic). b) The AP commanded a turn to the right; which in my mind it would have only done if it were trying to intercept the Localizer from the left. c) When ATC contacted us; it was to say that we were not on an intercept heading. He did not indicate that we had flown through the Localizer or were encroaching on the protected airspace between the approach corridors for the active runways. He never issued a vector to East which is likely what he would have done had he perceived there to be a risk of loss of separation. d) When we finally got the situation under control; the aircraft intercepted the Localizer from the left.Again; this entire narrative took place in what I suspect was less than a minute. Between the uncommanded turn to the right and the CA taking the controls; maybe 5 seconds passed. That said; I could have acted sooner and certainly should have verbalized when I reached for the heading selector to stabilize the heading; since that may have precluded the CA from taking the controls and executing the 'escape' maneuver. I think in the CA's mind; we were probably already past the point where that was going to mitigate our situation since he perceived that we had already crossed the Localizer; but it might have helped. I wish the CA would have verbalized why he was maneuvering as aggressively as he was. I thought that perhaps he saw an impending collision that I did not have SA of; and so I stayed quiet for longer than I should have before I started to rebuild the picture and work to develop a CRM. Ultimately; he was well within his authority to act in the manner he did and fully adhered to the company's three step intervention process. This was a tough one for me to analyze and I welcome any feedback you might have.

Flight crew reported having a stick shaker activation during a go around; which was attributed to a hydraulic system failure.

I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) for the flight and first approach. It started with a C HYD QTY (Center Hydraulic Quantity) EICAS in the terminal area of ZZZ. The QRH was completed. A RNAV GPS approach was conducted with the autopilot and autothrottles off. Weather was day/VMC. Immediately after gear and flaps were extended there was a complete failure of the C hydraulic system with the associated EICAS messages. I announced to the PF (Pilot Flying) that we would have to abandon the approach and complete the QRH. I coordinated a go around with Tower. I explained our problem and our need to perform the QRH before another attempt to land. While talking to Tower; I failed to monitor our airspeed after the First Officer (FO) arrested the rate of descent. I had not given him any guidance as to maintaining a particular speed or altitude. The stick shaker got my attention. I called 'Speed' just as the PF added power and recovered quickly.Tower handed us over to Approach. I explained the need to perform the QRH; the time needed to complete the QRH; and that we would only have 2 of three hydraulic systems. A few minutes into working on the QRH procedure ATC advised us that they were [giving priority to] us. ATC asked for souls on board and fuel state. The QRH was completed. I elected to become the PF for the landing. The landing and rollout were successful. Emergency vehicles escorted us to parking.Of course I wish I could do it over. I'm not happy with my initial performance with the problem. The system failure happened at the most inconvenient time. Nonetheless the decision to not land and fix the problem was easy enough. However; my initial execution was poor. After announcing the problem to the PF; I should have simply called Go Around. That would've put us back into the 'Aviate' phase and eliminated the stick shaker activation. Then I would've told Tower of the Go Around. Everything else would have sequenced properly for the remainder of the flight.

The Captain was PM and I; the First Officer was PF for our flight. Takeoff; climb and cruise were uneventful and no issues or indications were observed until descent into ZZZ. After obtaining the latest weather at ZZZ we decided Runway XX would be the most suitable based on the winds (270/3) and we would plan on and request the RNAV XX into ZZZ. We loaded the approach; requested landing performance via ACARS and briefed it as a normal flight.Descending into the area required the use of the speed brakes in order to keep the aircraft on the established VNAV path as well as slow down to 240 kts when passing 10;000 ft. Once reaching 9000 ft on a downwind position we first saw the C HYD QTY EICAS message appear. The PM checked the status page and noticed a magenta 'RF' and an indication of 0.45 for the center hydraulic quantity. The PM ran the C HYD QTY QRH and the only information listed was 'the hydraulic quantity is low'. We completed the checklist; called for recall review; cancelled it and discussed that we would write it up once on the ground in ZZZ and advise maintenance of the issue. We continued our descent for the RNAV XX approach; reducing speed and configuring for the landing. We were issued a heading and to maintain 3000 till established and we were cleared for the approach. I had setup for an approach as briefed; set 1200 in the altitude window and the aircraft began a shallow descent in VNAV PATH down to the minimums. After calling for 'gear down; flaps 20'; I set 160 kts in the speed window and the C HYD SYS PRESS EICAS message appeared. I called for 'flaps 25; landing checklist' when the PM alerted me of the EICAS message. After this a series of additional EICAS messages appeared and discrete lights illuminated. I noticed LEADING EDGE; TRAILING EDGE; and TE FLAP ASYM as the associated discrete lights had illuminated as well and got my attention. As the list of messages and indications appeared; the PM stated 'We can't land like this; we're going to need to find a place to go figure out what's happened'.As the PF; I had set 146 as the target speed for the approach and had just disengaged the autopilot and authrottle as briefed on the arrival briefing for automation intent. After the PM made that statement I hesitated to continue descending as I knew we could not land in this condition. The PM advised tower that we had an issue and would need to stay in the traffic pattern in order to troubleshoot the problem and would not be able to land at this time. At this moment I noticed the low speed awareness tape had not continued trending downward and minimum operating speed (red and black tape) was now very close to our current speed. Shortly after the stick shaker came on for roughly one second as the airspeed trended into the minimum operating airspeed range. I immediately added thrust and added forward pressure on the control column to increase airspeed and stop the stick shaker. The PM called out 'Airspeed' as I was taking corrective action. ZZZ tower informed us we could climb to 3000 ft. to abandon our approach and to run the necessary QRH. The PM set 3000 in the altitude window; we both verified it and I pressed the GA (Go Around) switch on the thrust levers. We conducted the GA profile; when bringing the flaps to 20 I could feel the asymmetric condition as the aircraft pitched up and the thrust increased. Continuing with the GA the PM raised the landing gear up; we maintained runway heading and set a speed of roughly 185 kts in the climb out. During the climb out the master caution light was intermittent as the gear doors and landing gear indications were intermittent as well. I remained PF with the autopilot disengaged and the auto throttle engaged. The PM attempted to engage Right Autopilot Command but we noticed this did not initially work so I continued flying manually with no autopilot. ZZZ approach advised us to proceed direct to the ZZZ1 VOR and stay within 10 DME while we ran the QRH and advised them of our intentions. At this time ATC asked for souls on board and fuel remaining and we advised them we had 2 souls on board and roughly 2 hours of fuel. The PM ran through the C HYD SYS PRESS QRH; noticing the center hydraulic quantity was down to 0.15 at one point. With no success completing the QRH; we completed the descent and approach checklist from the deferred items followed by the alternate flap extension and alternate gear extension checklists. The leading and trailing edge flaps successfully extended to 20 and the landing gear was down and 3 green lights were illuminated. At this time the PF and PM switched roles as the captain stated he felt more comfortable conducting the approach to landing. The captain stated the briefing remained the same and talked about the different Vref as a result of the new flap setting. After a positive transfer of controls; I advised ZZZ approach we would like to return to ZZZ and conduct the RNAV XX approach. We were vectored on a left downwind for the approach at which time the PF reduced speed to the target speed of 156 based on a flaps 20 Vref of 151; while I completed the landing checklist from the deferred items. We advised ATC we would be able to land the aircraft normally; they informed us that ARFF (Aircraft Rescue & Fire Fighting) would be standing by the runway just in case. We landed Runway XX and exited at taxiway 1 and told tower we could taxi to the international cargo ramp without any additional assistance. We left the flaps down at 20 after landing in order to prevent any further issued with the flight control movement. After blocking in on the ramp; maintenance came up and informed us that a substantial amount of hydraulic fluid had leaked onto the right main gear. We completed the necessary post flight paperwork; placed it in the trip envelope and then conducted a post flight inspection speaking to ARFF and maintenance about the exterior of the aircraft. At this time the captain and I grabbed our flight bags and headed to the Company transport to leave the airport.Looking back on the event I think there were a few things that could've been done differently. The initial indication of the C HYD QTY should have been a sign that something may have gone wrong; and after running the associated QRH we could've perhaps asked to slow and configure early to identify if there was an issue while at a higher altitude rather than on final approach. My role of PF on final approach. Despite the indications; discrete lights and overall confusion that was occurring at the time I should've had focused solely on flying the airplane and not getting distracted by the other things going on. This may have prevented the stick shaker event from occurring. There was no clear command to go around once we encountered the C HYD SYS PRESS EICAS message. Rather than wait for instructions or what the Captain was trying to diagnose; I should've called go around instead of remaining at 2500 ft with the airspeed trending downward in that configuration. As the other crew member I could have voiced my opinions in a more assertive way; stating what I believe may have happened as well as consulting the Captain if he felt we should identify as an emergency at the time.

Flight Crew reported a flap half speed and spoiler/stab fault status message resulted in a diversion and a precautionary emergency landing.

On takeoff roll for Runway XX in ZZZ; the Pilot Monitoring (PM) noted the status message of Flap Half Speed and SPLR/STAB fault. Being a non-time-sensitive situation; the Captain indicated that we would wait until 10;000 ft. to run the QRC/QRH. As we accelerated to 250kts; the over speed clacker activated. We confirmed that the flaps and gear had retracted; we continued and leveled off at our initial assigned altitude. We informed air traffic control (ATC) of our status; we asked to be kept at current altitude and to provide us with vectors in order for us to run the appropriate checklist.We ran the QRC/QRH for the associated messages; and given that the over-speed clacker was activating while the slats and flaps were indicating zero; we asked the Flight Attendant to visually check the flaps and also inquired if we had any flight crew member on board. We cross-checked our primary flight instruments against our standby and confirmed that our true airspeed (TAS) and ground speed (GS) matched. We proceeded to ask ATC what they indicated for our GS; and it all confirmed with each other. The Captain and I agreed that we had finished running the appropriate checklist; and although our flaps were indicating '0;' we concluded that there was a possibility of structural issues with the wings/slat/flap system and decided we wanted to divert to an airport with a long runway in the vicinity in case the flaps would not extend for landing. The Captain advised the flight attendant; passengers; Dispatch; and ATC of our current situation and that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. The Captain and I agreed on a plan. We decided to take a long final into ZZZ1 Runway XXR; this would permit us to burn fuel; assuring a landing that did not have an overweight or above maximum landing weight situation. The plan also consisted of deploying flaps and landing gear early; emphasizing airspeed; aircraft controllability; and flap extension speeds. We advised ATC that the nature of our [situation] may require a high-speed landing. Since we indicated flaps/slats '0' with the Overspeed clacker activated; we decided to error on the side of caution/safety that the position indications of the flaps/slats might be incorrect. We considered that there may be structural damage out of view and that the flaps/slats could be bound or bind upon extension due to the abnormal situation that we were experiencing. The Captain and I also briefed that if the flap extension resulted in a flap failure or asymmetrical extension/control; we would abort the approach and landing to run the appropriate checklist. The Captain and I configured the aircraft for landing at ZZZ1 and concluded the landing without any further incidents. Upon landing; we cleared the runway and came to a complete stop on the first available exit. The Captain advised the passengers to remain seated with their seatbelts on while the emergency crew inspected the aircraft for any visible damage. We were released by the emergency crew and continued our taxi to the gate. The Captain requested the flaps/slats to stay deployed so that we would not cause any damage and that this would also allow maintenance to determine if it was safe not to retract them.Maintenance could not determine what could have cause this to happen and determined to to keep the aircraft grounded until further evaluation.

On takeoff roll RWY (Runway) XX in ZZZ; the PM (Pilot Monitoring) noted status messages of SPLR/STAB FAULT and FLAPS HALFSPEED. Being a non-time sensitive situation; I noted that we would wait until above 10;000 ft. to run the QRC/QRH. As we accelerated to 250kts the overspeed clacker activated. We confirmed that the flaps and gear had retracted so leveled off at initial assigned altitude; informed ATC of our status and desire to remain at altitude and requested vectoring to run the appropriate checklists. We ran the QRC/QRH for the associated messages and given that the overspeed clacker was activating and the flaps and slats were indicating zero; we asked the FAs (Flight Attendants) to visually check the flaps and also inquired if we had any flight crew members on board. We cross checked our primary flight instruments against our standby and also confirmed that the TAS and GS (Groundspeed) matched. I asked ATC what they were indicating for our GS and it all confirmed with one another. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) and I agreed that we had finished running the appropriate checklists and although our flaps were showing '0' we concluded there was a possibility of structural issues with the wing/slat/flap system and decided we wanted a long runway in case the flaps would not extend for landing. I advised the flight attendants; passengers; ATC and Dispatch of our situation and that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. PM and I agreed on a plan that we would take a long final into ZZZ1; ensure a landing weight below maximum landing and configure for landing early with an emphasis on airspeed; aircraft controllability and flap extension. We advised ATC that the nature of our [situation] may require a highspeed landing. Due to the fact that although we indicated flaps/slats zero with the over speed activated; we errored on the side of caution/safety that the position indications might be incorrect; there may be structural damage out of view and the flap/slat system could be bound or bind upon extension due to the abnormal situation. We also briefed that if the flap extension during approach resulted in a flap failure or asymmetrical extension/control we would abort the approach and landing to run the appropriate checklists. We configured the aircraft and landed in ZZZ1 without further incident.
