My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me; considering time zones; but again; I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously; having made this error for the first time; I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward. As far as the possible fatigueaspect; our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible. I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued. There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed; but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day. So; I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it. Therefore; I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan. I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level.

Climbing out we were assigned to maintain 16;000 ft. First Officer (FO) was pilot flying. Altitude was verified at '1;000 to go' call. As we went through 15;000 feet; I said 15;000 climbing 16;000. FO was hand flying; as we near 16;000 (about 100ft to go) I noticed he wasn't slowing down the climb rate. I looked over and his altimeter was set to 29.92 instead of the altimeter we've gotten when I checked in of 30.16. As I looked over ATC asked if we had the 16;000 ft altitude assigned which I replied affirmatively. As I was done talking to ATC I told the FO he had the wrong altimeter setting; and that our Altimeter was 30.16. FO did level off at 16;000 ft but he had a wrong altimeter setting. FO may have pushed the standard 29.92 altimeter inadvertently at some point after initial departure. As the altimeter were set and cross checked for departure on the ground. We had checked our level off altitude on the 1;000 to go call. But I didn't notice at that time he had a wrong altimeter setting. I think on the 1;000 feet to go call we should have notice this discrepancy; but I was looking at my PFD and not his. FO should have mentioned that his altitude did not match with mine at the 1;000 to go call.

B737 flight crew reported an air turn back after 3 knob throttle split developed in climb with a lack of power on an engine following a 2.5 hour maintenance delay for a fuel leak issue.

All events through pushback were accomplished without note. During pushback; a puddle on the ramp aft of the normal oil spot was noticed behind the #2 engine. Puddle was not present on the walkaround. A stream of drops along the ramp was also noticed while the #2 engine was run. After five minutes the fuel leak had not stopped and we towed back to a gate. Maintenance was called; ran several tests; and two engine runs. The leak dissipated as the tests were completed. No fuel appeared to be leaking while engines were running; except for one within limits from the heat exchanger. Forms were completed to indicate it. Aircraft pushed and started again. No leaks were noted.Shortly after takeoff/cleanup; Captain announced a split in the thrust levers. Autothrottles were used for takeoff with VNAV (climb page 2L adjusted for 202 knots at 1;000 feet AGL). Looking at the engine instruments; I noticed the #2 thrust lever about three knob widths ahead of the #1. #1 N1 was at commanded power with the #2 N1 showing the white commanded power bar of about 95%; but the engine only producing about 88-89%. Further advancement of the throttle lever produced no increase in power. Vertical Speed was selected and we reduced our climb rate to bring the power back. As the power came back; the throttle synced and power matched. VNAV was reselected and as the power returned to full climb; the split reappeared with the #2 indicating a commanded increase without the engine delivering the power.As this was being discussed; the center tank fuel pumps were turned on (750 pounds in the center tank). Immediately after the pumps were turned on; the power matched and all indication were normal. As soon as the center tank fuel was exhausted; the split returned. Crew leveled at FL 270 and elected to return to ZZZ. As power was less than full climb at cruise/descent; and no abnormal indication were present during these flight conditions; no QRH Checklists were run. The rest of the return to ZZZ was completed without note. Engine performed as expected from level off to shutdown.Contract Maintenance expressed an increased level of calls from aircraft coming from the paint shop; fuel leaks were common with these aircraft. Would recommend a Maintenance individual check and run engines prior to returning the aircraft to the line.

Origination flight on an aircraft that had just come out of the paint shop. Preflight was uneventful with no fuel drips or puddles noted. We pushed five minutes early. On push back #2 was dripping fuel and did not stop after a short time and engine was shutdown. After consultation with Maintenance Control; we returned to the gate and called Contract Maintenance. Contract Maintenance did four motoring tests as directed by [company's] Maintenance. With each test; the dripping became improved. Then an engine run was completed with decreased dripping; but not to a small enough level to allow Dispatch. Contract Maintenance then opened the cowl and did an engine run to determine location of drip. After that run; the component dripping was identified and the dripping had decreased to an amount that allowed MEL. MEL was completed. This was about a 2.5 hour process. Ground Ops and Operations were very helpful with accommodating the Passengers as well as they could. I had given periodic in-person updates to the passengers. Finally; we pushed-back and the engine starts were uneventful without any drips. Uneventful taxi. We took off on Runway XX with a headwind 20G30. On push up of thrust; #2 lagged a bit and I pushed the thrust lever up to get closer to match and continued my crosscheck. As we approached V1/VR I noticed #2 still lagging by a few percent and pushed up the throttle some more. Normal on centerline liftoff and climbout. After liftoff; I informed the F/O (First Officer) that we had a split throttle situation. We cleaned up on schedule and began to evaluate the situation (again the aircraft had no adverse flight characteristics). With the aircraft cleaned up and climb power set; we observed that although the #2 demand pointer was correct; the #2 N1 lagged approximately 2-5% N1. Once our climb rate was reduced in Vertical Speed and at a slightly lower climb thrust setting; the engine was normal and tracked normally with the demand pointers and thrust lever position. To this point we had continued to follow ATC instructions to keep it simple. We found that the engine reacted the same with the autothrottle On or Off. Also we had 750 pounds of fuel in the center tank; so once established in the climb we turned the pumps on and immediately #2 N1 returned to normal operation at full climb power. When center tank was empty and pumps turned off; the malfunction returned. With this information we leveled off and informed ATC that we would probably need to return to the airport. While level we reconfirmed no other abnormal conditions or switches out of place. Also at level flight in this situation there were no conditions that warranted a QRH Checklist although it was discussed. F/O and I discussed the situation and decided that without the aircraft able to achieve full climb thrust on Main Fuel pumps only; the safest choice was to return to the airport. F/O flew and talked to ATC; while I informed flight attendants and passengers of need to return to the airport for safety reasons and gave them our ETA. I called Station Ops on VHF and informed them of our need to return; get a gate; and asked them to contact Dispatch. We also confirmed via ACARS with Dispatch the need to return due to engine unable to achieve full climb power (or something like that). The F/O did a very good job and stayed ahead of the aircraft preparing for the briefings; descent; and Approach Checklist. We referenced the Diversion Checklist to ensure we had covered the suggested items. We accomplished a normal descent and asked for a long visual approach to increase probability of a stable approach and landing without the need for a thrust needful go-around. F/O flew stable approach and landing with normal braking. No emergency was declared; no special handling requested; and a normal weight landing occurred. Uneventful taxi-in and shutdown. Flight was canceled and the passengers accommodated as best as Ops could. Debrief with the flight attendants yielded that although disappointed in their flight being cancelled; they were appreciative of the Safety of turning back. Immediate notification with XXXXXX was done after engine shutdown with Dispatch; Supervisor; Maintenance; and Chief Pilot.The Location X crews both above the wing and below the wing were very familiar with the Maintenance trouble shooting of engine drips on starts because they have seen it more the once from aircraft coming out of the paint shop. An engine run after paint shop would have found this problem before a revenue flight was disrupted. Maybe this may be a prudent practice--an ounce or prevention may have saved a pound of Customer frustration. Perhaps a faster crosscheck by myself might have allowed a reject option in the 70-90 knot range; but even then there was no decrease in power and I perceived the N2 engine thrust close-enough to N1 engine thrust to ensure a safer option than a medium speed reject.

C172 pilot reported an airspace incursion occurred when the engine began running rough and the pilot was troubleshooting. The roughness eventually dissipated and pilot exited the airspace.

On Date at ZZZ airport; I fueled the airplane; conducted a preflight (includes checking oil quantity and taking a sample of all three fuel sumps); reviewed my direct course back home and updated my weather (VMC) for the short flight to ZZZ1. During the pre-takeoff checklist (engine run up); I notice a slight roughness in the engine. I leaned out the mixture control which cleared out the roughness. I set the mixture control for my takeoff; but not to full rich. I left it leaned out a little for the departure and climb. During my climbout; I always look for off airport landing spots (should I need one). I did not see any good locations and I told myself that I want 4;500 feet once clear of the Class B airspace altitudes. It was shortly after my desire to get to 4;500 feet MSL ASAP that the engine was not performing as it should in cruise climb. I applied full power and checked the engine instruments (all green; but RPM was towards the low end). I was getting a shallow climb at an airspeed of about 90. I then immediately performed the initial emergency procedure; carb heat on; mixture full (then adjust if needed) and check fuel selector on both. That seemed to bring the performance back; but not immediately. Shortly after that the engine then started to run rough. My thought was spark plug fouling or magneto (I know it was not a cylinder failure; because I have experienced that in a twin engine airplane). I adjusted the mixture control first. This is logical; because if you check the mags before the mixture control you could increase spark plug fowling. At some point through all this my mind went into altitude; altitude; altitude. Unfortunately; I had that 4;500 feet MSL in my mind. While dealing with the engine situation; I continued my climb to that altitude. I got the rough running engine cleared out. Once I was done keeping the airplane in the air (dealing with low performance and then the rough running engine during the cruise climb phase); I checked my position and noticed that I was in ZZZ3 Class B airspace (west end of and close to the 6;000 feet MSL corridor; but I was in the 4;000 feet MSL corridor). I immediately descended below 4;000 feet MSL (3;800 feet MSL). Once clear of the Class B airspace/Mode C veil; I climbed back to 4;500 feet MSL. No airplane conflicts were noted. Once on the ground at the ZZZ1; I performed an engine runup and checked the mags full and leaned mixture settings. Both checked out okay. My plan is to check the oil; fuel and talk with a mechanic. I am confident that the fuel is okay since I checked it after fueling at the ZZZ (but I will check it again). I have cancelled my planned flying for the next week and no flying the Skyhawk until the items are checked out. Once I got home; I chair flew the scenario that I just experienced and realized that all my training and personal home chair flying has been geared to multi-engine; on an IFR flight plan and in radio communications. My scenario was single engine; VFR and not in communication. Do not get me wrong; I always review the emergency procedures before a flight for the airplane that I am flying. Also; the poor engine performance that I experienced did not seem to be carb icing. Since the air filter and bracket were replaced at the annual inspection; the carb air intake system will be looked at. What I learned and what I will do going forward so that this does not happen again:I learned that in my continued personal chair flying training that I need to go over single engine emergency; VFR and not in communications scenarios. This situation reinforced with me that single engine performance (VFR; non-communications) incidents come with a high workload especially when dealing with keeping the airplane in the air. It showed me that I became focused on keeping the plane in the air (altitude and rectifying the engine situation) and that navigating and communicating was lacking with this incident. Going forward; in addition to reading theemergency procedures that I currently do for every plane that I fly and chair flying multi-engine scenarios; I will chair fly single engine (SE) scenarios. I need to emphasize aviate; navigate; and communicate in any SE situation. When flying under Class B airspace and within a Mode C veil do the following:1. Obtain flight following when flying VFR; especially when flying in a Mode C veil. I would already be in communications should I need to report a problem. 2. Mark along the course line a line with an arrow from the departure airport to the point when the plane will be cleared of the Mode C veil. Also; put a B next to this manually drawn line.3. Apply a post-it-note on the instrument panel that I am in a Mode C veil airspace.I will talk to my Flight Instructor and review this flight to obtain feedback and discuss my ideas and additional ways to prevent this from happening again.

Air Carrier flight crew reported a track deviation caused by an automation error while on final approach to DEN. Both pilots and ATC intervened to correct the deviation.

As this report is not timely; it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF; for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified. I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much; the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN; RW 16R; as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But; the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE; but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal; still pissed that I allowed this to happen; I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue; no loss of separation; and no need to file a report.Looking back; how this could have been avoided... first of all; I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night; briefing and installing one arrival and approach then; at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes; and programming; was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist; procedure; or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last; but I know what I will and won't do next time.

During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase; we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF; the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival; we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain; as Pilot Monitoring (PM); selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF; I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV; VNAV; opened the speed window for the appropriate speed; requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did); and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint; the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green; engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds; and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn; ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft; a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required; there was no loss of separation; there was no safety issue; and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up; preparing; and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints; altitudes; and sequencing verified in the FMC.

Air carrier flight crew reported departure procedures require clarification by ATC and departure charts regarding direction of turn for southwest departures.

We were taking off from ELP on Runway 22 and had an initial clearance for the TDOWN3 RNAV Departure. Tower cleared us for takeoff with revised clearance to turn left to 200 and climb to 17;000 [feet]. I was the flying pilot manually flying. As we were accelerating and getting the aircraft to a clean configuration we were issued a frequency change to Departure. Upon checking in we were immediately given further instructions which included a right turn after reaching 6;200 feet to 060. Both of us misunderstood the turn right part of the clearance. The FO (First Officer) read back 'passing 6;200 heading 060' and had no response from the controller. We climbed through 6;200 and turned left. We were about half way through the left turn when the controller saw the mistake and told us it was a right turn; but then told us to continue the left turn. He later asked us to call them for possible pilot certificate action. There are several causal factors [due to direction of turn by flight crew]. First; having a clearance for an RNAV departure that has a left turn from Runway 22 sets you up to expect a left turn out for protected airspace even after receiving a last minute change to the departure plan using radar vectors. Because the radar vectors are given last minute the old departure stays in the FMC showing the original route on our map displaying that left turn; so even though we were not following the route displayed it probably influenced our thought pattern. There is no published departures turning out to the right from Runway 22 due to mountainous terrain if you are departing east. Secondly; we also had prebriefed the engine failure procedures that have you turn out to the left for the same reason. Third; from a 200 heading to turn right to 060 is counter intuitive because it is more than 180 degree turn. All of these factors I think caused expectation bias to turn left and not hear the right turn instruction. Fourth; the controllers failure to emphasize the right turn part when it is more than 180 from current heading and his not ensuring the read back was correct. Controllers need to emphasize the direction of turn especially if it's more than 180 degrees and ensure they get a correct read back. On the phone the controller said this was normal to avoid traffic from Mexico. If this is a common procedure to use radar vectors to turn us out an opposite direction of our assigned clearance then there needs to be some notes somewhere in our charts so we can prepare for that ahead of time. This non published procedure could cause conflicts with terrain in the event of an engine failure.

The missed approach and takeoff engine failure profiles for Runway 22 tell you to turn left. The TDOWN 3 SID; we were assigned; tells you to turn left off of Runway 22. The reason all of the departures turn left on Runway 22 at El Paso is because there is high terrain if you turn right. On takeoff; we were told to climb to 17;000 feet and turn left to heading 200. When we contacted Departure; the controller quickly blurted out a long; involved clearance. I responded; 'Passing 6.2; turn to 060.' He did not respond back to my radio call. On a heading of 200; the heading of 060 is to the left. As we entered the left turn to 060; the controller informed us that he had told us to turn right to 060; he also told us to expedite our left turn and continue to a heading of 010. When we rolled out on the heading; he told us to call a phone number because of a potential violation. I read the phone number back to him and asked him to verify. He did not respond because he was working two frequencies; and was talking to another aircraft on the other frequency. When we called the phone number for El Paso Departure Control; they told us that left turns off Runway 22 often conflict with traffic at a Mexican airport. So; they often vector you to the right. The Captain and I have both been in and out of El Paso numerous times; and have never gotten a right turn off Runway 22. None of our guidance for El Paso says to expect a right hand turn. Expectation bias caused us to hear 'turn to 060' instead of 'turn right to 060.' Also; the Departure Controller was working two frequencies and did not catch that we said 'turn to 060.' Here is what he blurted at us at 1;000 feet AGL while we were retracting the flaps; '[company name]; radar contact; turn right to 060 and climb to 17;000.' He also had a thick; Hispanic accent. If the keyword was 'right'; it didn't help that he placed it in the middle of a sentence with no emphasis or follow up. If left departures off Runway 22 conflict with Mexican air traffic; perhaps they need an updated departure procedure. The ATKNN 5 Departure off Runway 22 turns right; but it continues west bound. There are no departure procedures for Runway 22 that turn right initially; and then continue to the east. Also; none of our guidance tells us to expect a right turn off of Runway 22.

E145 flight crew reported an engine failure in flight caused an air turn back and precautionary landing.

Departed gate dual engine power out onto taxiway. Captain was Pilot Flying. Took off [Runway] XXL heading 220 to 5;000 [feet]. It was a normal ALT-TO1 take off. Prepare for level off at 5;000; reduce power for a 24;000 1000 fpm climb. Prior to 5;000 cleared to 15;000 apply climb power. Stable climb at 24;000. At approximately 5;000 [feet] there was a loud bang and the aircraft shook; moments later the ENG 1 OUT EICAS message is presented. Captain ensured AC control; while the First Officer [advised with ATC] and asked for level off at 8;000 [feet]. Cleared as requested. Captain set a 500 fpm climb and turned on the auto pilot and the First Officer began the engine failure checklist. During the checklist; the Flight Attendant called us to inquire about the bang; told him about the failure and our imminent return to ZZZ and that we would call him back shortly. Completed the engine failure checklist. Engine restart was discussed but we decided not to attempt it because of the bang; there was likely damage. After completion of the engine failure checklist the First Officer began the single engine landing checklist. During this time we leveled off at 8;000 [feet] and received some vectors from ZZZ Departure. While the First Officer prepared the landing data The Captain called the Flight Attendant back and made an announcement to the passengers. Departure reached out shortly after that and the Captain requested an approach to [Runway] XXC and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue equipment) standing by. Transferred to approach continued vectors on course Captain and First Officer quickly reviewed the approach setup and confirmed below landing weight. ACARS message sent to dispatch to inform them of the engine failure and return to ZZZ. Around 500 ft AGL the auto pilot was drifting left of course. Turned the auto pilot off corrected and made a normal touchdown on [Runway] XXC. Exited the runway [and] directed to taxi beyond intersection and CFR was on a separate ground freq. parking break set; after landing complete. CFR confirmed there were no indications of a fire; they followed us to the alley. We parked and deplaned normally. No injuries were reported and no one requested medical attention.

We departed gate with both engines running onto taxiway. Captain was the pilot flying. We executed a normal ALT-TO-1 takeoff from 10L turning to heading 220 and climbing to 5;000 feet. After Takeoff Checklist was complete and we were established in climb power. Captain prepared for level off at 5;000 feet by reducing power for a 240kt 1;000 fpm climb. Prior to 5;000 feet we were cleared to 15;000 feet and additional power was applied reestablishing a stable climb to our new clearance altitude.While climbing through approximately 5;000 feet a loud bang occurred and the aircraft shook. Moments later the ENG 1 OUT EICAS message was presented. Captain ensured aircraft control and we determined that we would climb to 8;000 feet to ensure we would be above weather build-ups in the immediate area while we continued to work through the emergency. I [advised] ATC and asked for level off at 8;000 feet which we were cleared for. Captain set a 500 fpm climb and turned on the autopilot and I began the Engine Failure Checklist. During the checklist the Flight Attendant called us to inquire about the bang. He was told about the failure; our imminent return to ZZZ; and that we would call him back shortly. During completion of the Engine Failure Checklist; a potential restart of engine 1 was discussed. Fuel; Oil; and N1 Rotation were present; however; it was determined that due to the loud bang that occurred; it was likely that substantial damage may have occurred to engine 1 and as such; a potential restart attempt would not be prudent. The Engine Failure Checklist was completed. During this time we leveled off at 8;000 feet and received additional vectors from ZZZ departure. After completing the Engine Failure Checklist; I began the Single Engine Landing Checklist. While I prepared the landing data; Captain called the Flight Attendant back and made an announcement to the passengers. Departure reached out shortly after that and Captain requested an approach to [Runway] XXC and to have Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) standing by. We transferred to approach control and continued vectors to the ILS [Runway] XXC localizer. It was confirmed that both the Engine Failure Checklist and Single Engine Landing Checklist were complete. Captain and I reviewed the approach setup and confirmed the aircraft was below landing weight. I sent an ACARS message to dispatch to inform them of the engine failure and subsequent return to ZZZ and requested a gate be assigned. We continued with the approach. Around 500 ft AGLl the autopilot began drifting left of course. Captain turned the autopilot off; corrected; and made a normal touchdown on [Runway] XXC. We exited [Runway] XXC at exit and were directed to taxi past the intersection and stop on taxiway where CFR was standing by on a separate ground frequency. The parking brake was set and after landing checklist completed. CFR confirmed there were no indications of a fire. Taxi was initiated to gate and CFR followed us to the alley as a precaution. We parked and deplaned normally. No injuries were reported and no one requested medical attention.

Air carrier flight crew reported numerous overlapping problems caused them to depart for destination airport with reduced IMC capability and minimum fuel; resulting in minimum fuel before landing.

Upon taking the aircraft; the number 3 MFD was inoperative which; per the MEL; required the Captain to complete all flying duties. While at ZZZ the Captain noticed that the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terrain Inop; and Terrain fail message were indicated in the EICAS. The Captain called maintenance who immediately deferred the issue and the Captain completed the logbook entries. Prior to push I entered the appropriate information into ACARS which did not match the PERF INIT which the Captain entered. We verified the numbers multiple times and determined that the ACARS had to be inaccurate. We also verified our numbers with the updated AOM. After calling Dispatch it appeared that their was a fleet wide issue with ACARS. It appeared to me that some information that is generally manually input may have already been calculated in the zero fuel weight of ACARS (85lbs for crew bags). Prior to the ACARS issue we notified Ground Control to receive an off time into ZZZ1 which we were given a departure time. At that point the Captain decided to complete the paper form X. We notified the ground crew of the delay who informed us they had to leave for another aircraft and would not be back for about 30-40 minutes. The Captain decided to have them push us from the gate in the event our issue was solved prior to their return. We completed the appropriate checklists and pushed but did not start any engines. Then notified ATC of the delay to void Off Time. The Captain then called the company for approval to open the cabin window to hand the form paper copy to the ground crew. Once the form was completed we called ops; handed the W&B out the window; and re completed the before start checklist all the way through. We also discussed not utilizing ACARS W&B throughout the flight (added workload). We then notified Ground that we were ready to verify off time prior to starting engines (fuel management). They gave us an immediate wheels up time so we started the engines and taxied to [Runway] XX. I used my IPAD to verify weather at ZZZ1 prior to push which was reporting calm winds ; few 050 TCU and 10 miles vis and again I checked prior to taxi which they were reporting calm winds; 046 CB; 10 miles. On departure from [Runway] XX we were given a turn to the west and eventually a heading to the north with a climb to 8;000 [feet]. When given direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ4 Arrival we had to vector around a few storms. We also had to vector around storm clouds on the arrival and were given vectors off the arrival by approach due to flow into ZZZ1. Within this period we both discussed the weather; verified the TAF; and discussed needing an alternate and potential fuel issues. After updating the D-ATIS we verified that the field visibility had dropped below 3 miles so we messaged Dispatch asking for/if we needed an alternate due to visibility. Dispatch responded that the TAF was good and we didn't need an alternate. The Captain started to become concerned because he was showing extreme areas of precipitation along the arrival and approach. Other aircraft ahead reported heavy rain. There were multiple discussion with ATC about getting in to ZZZ1 but I don't remember if they advised aircraft were going missed. We received normal vectors into the approach to Runway XYL and my first awareness of wind shear is when the aircraft in front of us called wind shear and missed. With our Windshear capabilities inoperative we were both paying very close attention to the aircraft's instruments. After intercepting the localizer and passing the Runway XYL FAF the precipitation was worsening. Somewhere between 1;700 and 1;200 feet the aircraft instruments were showing increased gains and losses and began to vibrate significantly. The Captain called wind shear and we completed the wind shear procedure up to the missed approach altitude of 3;000ft. Tower gave us runway heading and eventually turned us to the west with a hand off to approach. Prior to the handoff we began discussing fuel and alternates. The Captain suggested ZZZ2 which we messaged to Dispatch. Dispatch recommended ZZZ3. I recommend that we not go to ZZZ3 because of all the weather that was building between ZZZ1 and ZZZ3 and it also appeared weather was building at ZZZ3 per my IPAD. We asked ATC about ZZZ3 and they indicated that ZZZ3 had similar weather to ZZZ1 so we determined based on fuel and ATCs information that ZZZ3 was not an option. It seemed to me that Dispatch was adamant about diverting to ZZZ3. We also discussed other airport near ZZZ1 (off field) that could be potential alternates. After the check in with Approach they asked us our intentions which we replied stand by and began rough fuel calculations to ZZZ2. The Captain quickly determined that fuel to ZZZ2 was inadequate due to a 15-20 minute flight and approximately 2200lbs of fuel on board. (Increased fuel burn at lower altitude; storms in the area; and potential unknown issues on arrival at ZZZ2). We then asked ATC about aircraft success in to ZZZ1 which they replied that some aircraft were making it in and some were not. We then requested Runway XYR because it was the closer runway and informed ATC of our minimum fuel situation. The Captain notified the Flight Attendant; we ran the appropriate checklist (ATIS; build it; bug; brief it) and continued vectors to Runway XYR. There were two aircraft in front of us which one was able to land and another missed (aircraft in front of us) due to wind shear. After recalculating fuel requirements the Captain determined that a missed would put us in an emergency fuel situation therefore we [advised ATC]. I believe that upon intercepting the localizer we were somewhere around 1700-1800lbs. During the approach the gains and losses of altitude did not seem significant but it appeared to be difficult to maintain the localizer although I did not see anything greater than one dot. There was also added pressure to continue the approach due to the fuel situation. During the approach tower asked the aircraft that made it in where they broke out and they replied 'right at mins'. At around 800 feet I called out that I could see the ground which was not visible as we got to 500 ft. At 300 feet I called approach lights in sight 12 o'clock and continued to call out the approach lights. The aircraft began to drift right and I called the runway environment insight at 11 o'clock. Throughout this period it was apparent that the Captain was having difficulty seeing the runway. When he finally looked up and determined that he did not have adequate references; and the aircraft was not in a safe position to land; he called the missed. Immediately on the missed it was apparent the at least 90 percent of the airfield was VFR. We could see all of Runway XZ/XA; including approach paths; so we made a decision request XZ and due a VFR pattern into XZ. Tower provided we could use whatever runway we needed so we continued with XZ; entered the left crosswind; base; and landed. During the miss we did not climb to the missed approach altitude; left the gear down; and kept the flaps at nine because of the immediate landing after the missed to Runway XYR. We updated the FMS with Runway XZ and extended a line for reference because there are no approaches in our pubs for XZ. We did not rerun the performance information again because the field length was 10;500 [feet] which was longer than Runway XYR and it was an immediate landing. We also received fuel EICAS alerts during the missed and a fuel critical prior to landing XZ. All approaches were conducted with flaps 22. Emergency vehicles were on scene which we did not require. Upon taxiing into the gate the field went in to a ground stop due to lightning. In all the entire flight segment from door closed to door open was 3.4 hours. I would say that this flight provided the crew with several threats. To name a few; my PFD was inop so only the CPT could fly; windshear; GPWS; and TCAS were inop; pop-up weather wasoccurring throughout the flight route; fuel considerations; ACARS not accurate due to new AOM changes; delays prior to departure; delays in route; other aircraft encountering wind shear; and potentially an inexperienced dispatcher. There was also a significant pressure to land the second approach. I felt that we handled the situation very well as a crew and discussed and analyzed any and all potential alternatives but were cornered due to the fuel situation. I do wish I had analyzed the winds better throughout the duration and been more aware of the weather at the field during the Runway XYL wind shear event. With most of the airfield being VFR it was absolutely possible to successfully complete approaches to the XB runways and XZ/XA [runways]. The only area impacted by the weather was the XY runways approach segments. Therefore; if winds were within landing limits we could have immediately requested an alternate runway from ATC.

While conducting the setup check in ZZZ; the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terr Inop; and Terr Fail messages appeared on the EICAS. Maintenance was called and the affected system was deferred per MEL. The aircraft also had an MEL for the First Officer MFD; and an NEF item in the cockpit. ACARS would not produce accurate weight and performance numbers; and Dispatch informed us that this was a known issue. We elected to perform a manual weight and balance with the Form X. The TAF for ZZZ1 was forecasting VFR and radar looked fairly benign. The First Officer obtained the D-ATIS for ZZZ1 which showed Winds Calm; visibility 10SM; Few at 5000; Scattered at 8000; with no other weather (information M). Due to this; extra fuel for weather was not considered by us or Dispatch. While in our initial descent the First Officer and myself noticed the weather in ZZZ1 was deteriorating and sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking if we should get an alternate. Dispatch replied that no alternate was needed; and we assumed that they had more up to date information than available to us in the air. Our radar was depicting areas of extreme return (red and purple) blanketing the approach and airport with other aircraft saying it was a smooth ride; but heavy precipitation. While outside of the final approach fix on the ILS Runway XYL; other aircraft were heard going missed due to windshear. ATC informed us that some aircraft were landing and some were going around. We elected to continue the approach as we were not experiencing any abnormal flight conditions. Inside of the final approach fix; I was unable to maintain positive aircraft control on the approach path due to airspeed; altitude; and course fluctuations. I made the determination to execute a windshear escape/go around. The Flight Attendant was notified of our situation. We contacted Dispatch to request a diversion and suggested ZZZ2. Dispatch replied that ZZZ3 was a better option; but ATC informed us that ZZZ3 was having similar weather to ZZZ1. I used the FMS to determine a rough fuel burn to ZZZ2 as 1400 lbs not including any deviations or approaches. We were also low on fuel; approximately 2;200 lbs after the missed approach. We discussed and agreed that we did not want to end up in ZZZ3 with such low fuel and similar weather issues. We decided to attempt a second approach at ZZZ1 after ATC stated that some aircraft were landing successfully. It was apparent that we would be below divert and possibly final divert on the second approach so we declared Minimum Fuel. We requested ILS Runway XYR due to perceived improved conditions and the closer approach for that runway. During the approach; the Flight Attendant called and said that a passenger was in the bathroom and asked if we could delay the landing. I advised her that due to our fuel situation; it would not be possible. She was able to get the passenger back to his seat before final approach. While on the approach; we overheard the aircraft in front of us go around for windshear. Our fuel level was low and a go around would put us in a fuel critical situation. We [advised ATC] and continued the approach. We experienced difficulty in maintaining the approach course and I used my PIC authority to continue the approach since a missed approach would leave us with inadequate fuel for much option. The First Officer called approach lights in sight; and we continued to 100 feet above the field. The First Officer called Runway in sight; and when I looked up; I did not see a runway and was disoriented due to the extreme precipitation and reduced visibility and immediately executed a go around. We were now showing a very low fuel level; and it was unlikely we would have enough fuel to get to another airport or reattempt an approach. I used PIC emergency authority to request a circle to land Runway XZ. We were able to maintain visual contact with Runway XZ during the maneuver. We had no time to get any type of performance numbers; and reasoned that since itwas longer than Runway XYR we could land. The landing was conducted without incident. As we engaged E/TO Reserve on the windshear escape; I entered this in the logbook and contacted maintenance. See attachments for reference if needed.Many threats existed in this incident including: pop up weather; weight restrictions; the need for paper performance calculations; an inoperative MFD; an inoperative Windshear system; and lack of an alternate. The weather and TAF looked ok during the planning portion of the flight; it was not until enroute; that everything deteriorated. I believe we acted in the best manner possible given the stressful situation and lack of backup options (fuel and/or alternate). It was a unique scenario that required a unique response. I believe we made safe decisions based on the current parameters. In hindsight; I would have been more assertive about requesting an alternate enroute. I do not believe we could have forecasted such bad weather; which is why we did not ask to remove passengers to add fuel in ZZZ. As we could not find a suitable alternate; we had little choice once we were low on fuel than to attempt to land on any runway. A third go around would have likely had us considering an off field landing.

Air Carrier pilots reported they could not program the SID correctly and flew off course. The reporters referenced a fix with the same name but starts with a different letter exists in the NAS.

On the ORCKA 5 Departure; after passing the 160 SMO radial and DOCKR below 3;000 feet. We were given heading of 030 and climb to 12;000 feet as prescribed by the SID (expect vectors). As we were climbing and turning he gave us direct 'KLIPR at or above 10;000; climb to 15;000.' I could not find KLIPR on the legs pages. I checked several downline pages; went back to page 1/9 and then checked the route page to verify the ORCKA 5. It was loaded but still no KLIPR. I told the controller it isn't apparently on our route. He spelled it out. I was moving too slow. He gave us 030 heading and told us to let us know when we are heading there. I though we were heading in the right direction but the intersection is now behind us. As I was jamming the box; perhaps KLIPR got eaten or dropped out as we passed it. It's location is right by DOCKR. I can't figure out why it wasn't there initially as we turned. We were going through 10;000 feet easily so he then gave us direct KEGGS and to go to next frequency. The next controller gave us direct NNAVY. Altitudes were no issue; if anything our climb rate was quicker than my cumbersome effort towards KLIPR. What could we have done better. I had expectation bias from the old Loop departure. If I remember after DOCKR you loop back to LAX at or above 10;000 feet. With this departure giving an initial vector and our climb rate much better than my 737 experience. I was looking for KLIPR to be farther down the road than between LAX and DOCKR. I still don't know why I didn't see it because I was looking at the' top of the flight plan' legs page. I was just too slow for the expectation of the controller so he vectored us on down the line. Although I haven't been to LAX in two years I am comfortable there and fell behind unexpectedly during this event. Errors were automation Management; FMC / CDU and similarly spelled waypoints.

The following narrative describes events that occurred over a very short period of time; perhaps only a few minutes in total. It is my sincere intention not to cast blame; but to offer an explanation for what happened from my biased point of view as the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X. Our flight began normally from LAX; with the exception that we were pushing back about 45 minutes late due our aircraft's late arrival into Gate 77. Preflight duties were performed fairly routine; but under some time pressure to complete everything thoroughly but as quickly as we could in an attempt to make up some of our delay. This time pressure was self-induced; as no other employee was pushing us for an on time arrival in ZZZ. Red flag #1. During the pre-departure cockpit preparations; we received notice that the passenger boarding was complete; followed shortly by ramp informing us that they were ready for the parking brake release and pushback. At this point I gave a cursory PF brief from the briefing card we all carry - too cursory. Red flag #2. Taxi and takeoff were normal from Runway 25R on the ORCKA5 Departure. I was manually flying; enjoying only my second flight as PF in over a month. We switched from Tower frequency over to SOCAL Departure; and shortly after checking in we received instructions to continue climb I believe to 5;000 feet and turn left to a heading of 030 degrees. Quickly after that we were given further climb to 12;000 and direct to KLIPR. At this point things went wrong; rapidly. The Captain; as PM (Pilot Monitoring); couldn't find the KLIPR intersection on the legs page; and informed ATC that it did not appear to be on our departure. SOCAL spelled out the intersection phonetically; and then I think confirmed that we were on the ORCKA5. Things were happening fast. While hand-flying; in the turning climb; I tried to locate (unsuccessfully) KLIPR on the 10-3 page displayed on the iPad. Red flag #3.At this point; I should have turned on the autopilot to assist with the FMC and MCP inputs; as I could detect the stress and frustration in the Captain's voice in being unable to find KLIPR on the legs page; or on the departure plan view. Red flag #4. In my divided attention between flying the aircraft and searching for KLIPR on my iPad; I failed to find it as well. I was looking too far down the flight segment to see that the this waypoint is located right off the departure end of the 25s at LAX. This was the key moment; I think; and the last opportunity to correct the error. All I needed to do was put on the AP (autopilot); join the Captain and assist with the repair. But I did not; at least not immediately. The Captain inserted KLIPR on the legs page; got my confirmation; and executed the entry. When I had looked at the route modification; I thought it was correct. The waypoint showed in the correct direction (I thought) but much further down line than it should have; off the scale of my selected range on the navigation display. Red flag #5. Passing around 10;000 feet I engaged the autopilot at the Captain's urging to finally get back in the cockpit as a crew and together correct the problem. I engaged LNAV; but we were not turning fast enough for ATC and the controller gave us a new heading of 010. I'd like to add at this point that our controller was patient; helpful and professional throughout our fiasco. The only way he could have helped us more is if he teleported into the cockpit and handed us our crew meals. Somewhere in the fray I had suggested that we reload the departure and that would bring KLIPR up; and now the legs page had a discontinuity and we had lost the LAS transition. Also we were given further climb; and now the KEGGS intersection to get us back on the departure. It was at this point I saw we had not been heading to KLIPR at all; but to 'CLIPR'! How did I miss that?! I had set up that problem by not giving proper confirmation of the legs page entry; having not used proper procedures (see Red flag #5). Further climb; and now direct to NNAVY were issued; but we first had to reload the lost LAS transition. After that was competently accomplished; our 'helmet fire' was apparently extinguished; and we were switched to the next Departure Controller. He gave us direct Las Vegas; and kindly spelled 'LAS' in the clearance for the lost crew.What followed was probably a good 2 hours of discussion and self-examination of what went wrong and why. I believe that two primary factors set us up for these errors. The first was my too-brief departure review. This was the first time the Captain had been on this departure; and only my second. Although we both verified the FMC route and legs page; and had confirmed the proper altitudes; we were not familiar with all the new (to us) waypoints; such as KLIPR. A more thorough review on the ground was paramount; and I failed to do it. The second was my desire to manually fly the aircraft during what rapidly became a complex departure. At the first sign of things getting too busy; it became mandatory for me to engage the autopilot; and thereby engage my brain in helping eliminate the threat. I failed in that regard. Adding mistakes such as 'CLIPR' vs. 'KLIPR'; was due to my attention being more in the HUD than on performing proper FMC verification procedures. That was entirely on me. I still have no explanation for why KLIPR was not on the legs page. I had displayed on my CDU the Takeoff Ref page; and did not give due diligence to the ND or the legs page on the Captain's side. What I saw was '_ _ IPR'; and a magenta line in the direction I wanted to go. Not good enough! Additionally; in my attempt to find KLIPR on the Jepps I zoomed in and slid the page right-to-left; taking the desired waypoint right out of sight. Using the autopilot undoubtedly would have enabled me to do this search more thoroughly. We had only seconds; it seemed; to prevent this entire undesired event.

A319 Captain reported a fume event during preflight that resulted in physiological symptoms in flight and cabin crew members.

The five of us crew members boarded Aircraft X at ZZZ just as soon as the inbound flight fully deplaned. The inbound flight crew left the APU and APU Bleed ON. Upon stepping aboard and entering the Flight Deck (FD); I noticed an odor that wasn't quite normal. As I was setting up; one of the flight attendants (FAs) called me to the back to check on something. She was standing approximately halfway between first class and the emergency exit row; and as I walked towards her the odor became readily noticeable and more intense. I recognized it as an odor I haven't smelt in many years; that of burning oil coming through the APU driven pack. She asked; 'do you smell that?' which confirmed my thought. I said I certainly did and that we were not going to take this aircraft. She said 'it's that old dirty sock smell' referring to a common term used many years ago (6-8?) pertaining to a period when there were many bad and noxious odors on the Airbus 320 fleet. I told her I agreed and explained it was likely APU oil that was getting into the air conditioning system. I took a few steps further aft and noticed the odor intensified the further back I went. I believe she went to the back of the aircraft to tell another FA as I made my way to the FD to turn the APU Bleed OFF. I briefly explained the situation to the FA in the fwd galley; and told her we were not taking this aircraft. After turning the APU Bleed OFF; I called Maintenance and informed them of the situation. I grabbed the AML and my iPad and headed out to the jetway to fill out the forms. All 3 FAs were now in the jetway and my FO (First Officer) was outside doing his walk-around; preflight inspection. I advised the cleaning crew they should also exit the aircraft; though 2 of them remained aboard as they wanted to finish as they were almost done. The odor dissipated within a few minutes of turning the bleed OFF. I then called my Dispatcher and advised her of the situation; explaining the noxious odor we just experienced; and that some of us already had noticeable symptoms. Per the first items of the online Smoke/Odor/Fume Report in [the] checklist; I asked how everyone was feeling. The 3 FAs and myself had throat irritation; a foul taste in our mouths; and varying degrees of a headache. Mine was slight at that time; hardly worth noting as I began filling out the S/O/F form. My FO had been outside; therefore had minimal exposure and no ill affects. The 4 of them then went up to wait in the terminal while I remained in the jetway to fill out the S/O/F form and AML. A few minutes later; an FA came down to inform me that another FA was feeling light headed and nauseous and that they were contacting their Inflight Coordinator to seek medical assistance. A few minutes later; my FO came down to inform me that FA was now looking faint and had vomited. I gave him the number to Med-Air to give to the FAs. After completing the S/O/F report and making an AML entry; I put the AML back in the FD; shutdown the aircraft and left; intending to go with my FO to another gate (D3?) for a replacement aircraft to complete the flight to ZZZ1. As I was walking up the jetway my symptoms intensified; particularly the headache; and upon entering the terminal it was strongly suggested I have my condition assessed. I called the Chief Pilots [office] to confer and advise them of the situation; then I went with the FAs to [the] hospital. The 4 of us each had POC Blood Gas; arterial tests done; and were monitored. We were discharged shortly after midnight. I contacted an FA to see how she and the rest of the FAs were doing. She reported a new symptom of watery eyes; still with sore throat and headache. Another FA still had a dull headache; and the one who vomited was still not feeling well. The first FA contacted me again later in the day for an update stating no change with her; the other one was now down to a dull headache; and the one suffering the worst now reports body aches. My own symptoms have improved but not yet gone away; still with a mild throat irritation; a nasty taste in my mouth; and almost negligible headache. I have been on the A320 fleet for overall XX years and have experienced many of these events; particularly during that long ago time period when there was a rash of these incidents; many before the cause was determined or rectified. I was rather surprised at how quickly and intensely the symptoms came on during this event. This was by far the most intense experience I've had. As mentioned above; I haven't experienced this in many years. It is my understanding that maintenance procedures had been put in place to prevent these from occurring. I recently read a bulletin message regarding recent events occurring and a new operational procedure to remedy the situation. I am curious as to what may have changed to cause the recent events; as it seemed to me this had been under control. If it is a design flaw it must be fixed. If it is a procedural matter; we must figure out what works for the health and safety of our passengers; and particularly the crew who have potential exposure many times per work day.

Flight Crew reported an air turn back after the left pack failed after takeoff with the right pack on MEL.

This was a FFOD flight. While completing the hydraulic test; Hydraulic Pump 3B would not work. While writing this up; cabin boarding commenced. The associated circuit breaker 1A2 remained set in. Because of this problem; along with the emergency lights not working; and in consultation with Maintenance Control; it was determined that the airplane would be deplaned because it was unknown how long the flight would be delayed in getting maintenance personnel to the airplane to resolve the maintenance issues with the aircraft. I left the aircraft; still prior to the original departure time; and notified the ramp agents and gate agents. The passenger gate checked bags were brought back on the cart to the front of the plane so passengers would be able to have their things in the terminal. I made the announcement to the passengers face-to-face via the Flight Attendant's (FA) inter-phone explaining that we would be deplaning due to the aircraft needing maintenance and the time required for them to complete their job to ensure the airplane was safe for flight. It was also due to the hot temperatures making it uncomfortable in the cabin of the aircraft.As the passengers deplaned; there were a number of passengers saying that they would rather be late; but fly in a safe airplane. I kept assuring them their safety is our top priority. A couple expressed discontentment due to the strain placed on their travel plans and possibility missing their connections. I told them I that I apologized for the inconvenience; but that I needed to make sure they were completely safe on our flight and directed them to the gate agent to see what could be done to help them. I did not see anyone making a video or taking pictures with their phone. There were a couple of people talking on the phone.While I was greeting the passengers as they deplaned; the first officer notified me that the R PACK HI TEMP caution message came on and shut the PACK down by itself. This was then written up in the ELB.During the approximately 1 hour and 55 minutes delay; I made several trips into the terminal (about every 15-20 minutes) to make announcements to the passengers providing up-to-date information regarding the time frame of the delay; the status of the maintenance process; and to express sympathy for the inconvenience and disruption to their travel; but that their safety is our first priority.Maintenance came out to the airplane and resolved the hydraulic pump issue and verified the emergency lights had been charged long enough by the APU and the R PACK was deferred.By the time Maintenance had completed their items; several passengers had rebooked to a flight leaving for ZZZ just an hour or two later. Some that were just flying to ZZZ opted to drive instead saying the trip would be quicker. Again; I did not see anyone appearing to be making a scene or social media post; video; or taking photos. There was one man who expressed his displeasure at not making his connection in ZZZ. I expressed my apologies for his inconvenience; but told him that his safety was our top priority.As Maintenance had returned the airplane to service on their part; we elected to board the airplane while waiting for Dispatch to return the airplane to service. I made the announcement in the terminal that the maintenance issues had been resolved; again expressing apologies for the inconvenience; but telling them that their safety is our top priority. At that point; boarding commenced. I called Dispatch and verified that I had the the amended release; with its associated limitations on the cruise altitude. They then returned the airplane to service; which we saw verified in the ELB.After boarding; the flight deck crew and cabin crew complied with all procedures and we pushed out of the gate for taxi. After contacting ATC; we had a 5 minute wait for our flow time at the end of the runway. After waiting; we departed climbing on departure; with me acting as Pilot Flying (PF).As we climbed throughabout 7;000 feet; the L PACK HI TEMP caution message illuminated. A couple seconds later; the PACK fault light illuminated and the cabin depressurized slowly. I told my First Officer that we were going to level off at 9;000 feet; which we did.I verbalized that this was an unanticipated threat and that I was flying the airplane. I stated that there were no QRC procedures or memory items. I then told him that I was going to have him fly the airplane; holding a general orbit over the airport within the confines of the airport. I made the radio call at that point to ATC that we were leveling off at 9;000 feet and would be making turns over the top of the ZZZ1 airport for what I approximated to be about 15 minutes. ATC asked if we were declaring an emergency. I declined declaring an emergency and told him that when I got back with Center; that I would want vectors back for the approach. Center responded with 'roger.'I then proceeded with the QRH abnormal L PACK HI TEMP (Bleed source is engine) procedure. The procedure did not resolve the problem and the caution message remained illuminated. Because I did not have any operative PACKS that negated the ability to transfer the bleeds from the engines to the APU.I contacted Ops on COM 2 and notified them of the problem and that we would be coming back to the airport. They responded and understood. I called the Flight Attendant and notified her of the problem; but that this was not an emergency; just to clean up the cabin and configure for landing. I told her that she had 10 minutes.I then made a PA announcement that we had lost pressure in the cabin and that we would be returning to ZZZ1 after I had completed a couple of procedures. I expressed my apologies of the continued problems and the inconvenience to them.Because of the slow depressurization of the aircraft; the CABIN ALT caution message came on while I was running the L PACK HI TEMP QRH procedure. This was expected and I ran the abnormal QRH procedure for CABIN ALT after finishing the procedure for the L PACK HI TEMP. The CABIN ALT caution message persisted; as expected. My next procedure to run was the abnormal QRH for Unpressurized Flight Procedure (PACKs off). I completed this procedure; confirming the guarded switches with my First Officer. During this entire time; my First Officer had been making CTAF radio position calls. Another airplane had flown up underneath us and was staying 1;000 feet below us. Because of this; the other airplane would get within 800-900 feet below us and kept tripping TCAS traffic alerts. My previous instructions to my First Officer were to orbit the airport; which he was doing. I had to stop the QRH procedures and redirect where to put the airplane to avoid the continued TAs. I changed my instructions to him that he could outline the geographic exterior of the valley to avoid the other airplane. We never heard any radio calls on CTAF from the other airplane of what they were doing or any intentions. These radio calls are not required in the ZZZ1 area.I finished the QRH procedures.I called the passengers again and attempted to assure them that; although we had lost pressure; the airplane was still flying fine and the flight crew was working to get the airplane on the ground safely and we should be on the ground within 10 minutes.I contacted ATC and they told me that unless I could climb higher than 10;000 feet; I would not be able to get vectors. Because the weather visibility was virtually unlimited and there were no clouds; I called the airport insight and cancelled IFR. In hindsight; I should not have canceled IFR; but I was still given traffic advisories from Center until we were clear of the conflicting targets.I directed the FO to fly east over the desert area that had lower terrain obstacles that would allow us to descend to land on Runway XX.I explained to my First Officer that we didn't have cabin pressure and that we would need to plan a slow descent rate.I heard the FA's jumpseat click and I called her to verify that she had been able to complete her duties; which she affirmed. I then made a PA announcement attempting to assure the passengers that the procedures were complete and we would be landing in about 5 or so minutes. I went on to explain that because the airplane was not compensating for the lack of pressure that they would feel the pressure change in their ears.Inside the airplane; it did get very hot. Even with the RAM AIR open; we were not able to cool it off. I did have concern about some of the elderly passengers we had onboard. The ECS page said the cabin temperature was 34 degrees C; but it felt hotter. The QRH procedure talks about keeping the speed up to 250 knots for cabin cooling; but that was not possible due to landing and having to keep the airplane confined in the valley and maneuvering for landing.We landed normally; besides the pressure; and taxied into parking at the terminal. We opened the door; which immediately allowed cooler air into the cabin; and I made another passenger announcement; again expressing apologies for the problems and that they could talk to the gate agent to make further arrangements.I wrote up the L PACK HI TEMP caution message in the ELB; called maintenance control and finished up with them. Operations then wanted to move the airplane to an adjacent FBO to open up gate space for flights expected later. Maintenance Control made a note in their record of the location of the airplane being moved to the FBO and stated that they were fine with the airplane being relocated.As passengers deplaned; they were frustrated with the return of the flight.After everyone was deplaned and safe in the terminal; the plane was pushed back and we repositioned it to the FBO. I called Dispatch and had them close out the ELB; as the program had locked me out from being able to close out myself. Old equipment on a hot day.I cannot entirely control the effectiveness or reliability of an airplane or its systems.

The Captain was flying out of ZZZ1 on the ZZZZZ departure; Runway XX. With the right pack deferred already; we received a left pack hi temp on the right; climbing turn. Upon receiving the caution message; we established a benign flight regime at 200kts; 9;000 feet in a right-hand orbit atop ZZZ1. The Captain then assigned duties amongst the crew per [company guidelines]; specifically I flew the aircraft and the captain ran the appropriate checklists and assumed pilot monitoring duties. Concurrently; we notified ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 OPS and Dispatch of our situation and intentions. While completing checklists we received a traffic advisory from ZZZ Center and TCAS advisory. We were able to visually acquire the other aircraft quickly and adjust our flight path to continue our response to the situation. After completing all required checklists; we notified the FA and passengers about the situation and reengaged with ZZZ Center about our intentions to return into ZZZ1. We conducted a standard descent/approach briefing; set up a left-hand intercept onto the final approach course and established a slow; deliberate descent profile on the approach [Runway] XX into ZZZ1 and landed/taxied to the terminal without incident. The left pack hi temp caution message caused the crew to conduct the actions as described in the narrative.Issues with aircraft cannot be completely avoided; the crew acted and responded to the situation in compliance with our directives and in a safe manner.

A Center Controller and Supervisor reported Military Special Use airspace was implemented in their and adjoining facility airspace without complete coordination or established procedures being followed. The Controller unknowingly allowed an aircraft to fly through airspace which was being used by military aircraft not under his control.

This is once again another report about the Steelhead MOA/ATCAA. Area X Controllers were briefed that the Steelhead ATCAA (Air Traffic Control Assigned Airspace) was going to be active from 29;000 feet to 31;000 feet from XA:00-XD:00. There would be numerous military aircraft in the MOA (Military Operations Area) due to the VIP being in TVC. When I sat down at the sector; there was already confusion. There were 3 tanker aircraft wanting a clearance into the MOA but it was not yet active. I tried to call the Minneapolis Center military desk and Black Talon (as I've repeatedly been told to do after these reports). Cleveland Center's 'fix' is to call those two facilities. There was no answer at either line. I tried having my Assist call. No answer. I had the Supervisor call. No answer. I called the Minneapolis Center controller at TVC high sector to try to coordinate a new altitude block of 25;000 to 31;000 feet and was denied. The tankers were given vectors until the airspace went active. At that time; I cleared the tankers into the MOA. During this live operation; the tankers repeatedly asked for more vertical airspace. The supervisor coordinated it and it was granted.I told the Operations Manager (OM) that a dangerous situation was occurring and has been occurring with the Steelhead MOA/ATCAA. He stated that he didn't really know how it worked; but the aircraft controlled the airspace and that he did not think there was an air traffic controller working the airspace. Later on; the OM talked to my supervisor who spoke to me. The supervisor said that Black Talon is only the coordinating agency and they simply schedule the airspace but are not controllers. As the day went on; the tankers were asking to join up and were asking for permission to climb and descend. This is not the procedure for military airspace. In MOA/ATCAA; the aircraft are not under the FAA's control. Whose control are they under? I am still unclear. However; they were soliciting separation services. I didn't even have flight plans for these aircraft any longer. Their radar services had been terminated. I advised them that they are responsible for separating themselves and I was not providing separation services. They informed me that Aircraft Y told them that they had to ask my permission for altitude changes inside the Steelhead ATCAA. There were also several spillouts involving these aircraft. At least 2; I personally saw.After another break I came back to a cap and anchor drawn on the screen. Cleveland Center's military guy had come in and drawn a cap and anchor but had told the controllers it 'wasn't official'. Basically; what it seems happened is someone made a cap and anchor in the Steelhead MOA at 29;000 to 31;000 feet. Cap and anchors are typically inclusive vertical altitudes. The cap and anchor; however; were not in the confines of the Steelhead MOA hence the spillouts. To be clear; the Steelhead ATCAA was active just apparently with a cap and anchor that no one forwarded down the line. The aircraft were making altitude and time adjustments real time; not in advance. It went from FL290B310 to FL200B310 and from XA:00-XD:00 to now XA:00-XG:00. Very last minute changes.To make this matter even worse was that I was controlling the VIP aircraft. I had sent the VIP aircraft through this (at the time) unknown cap and anchor because I wasn't told about it. Every pilot and every aircraft is important to me; but the VIP aircraft was placed in an unsafe proximity to randomly maneuvering military aircraft that were not radar identified; who I no longer had flight plan information on; and who were not on my frequency. It was only after the VIP aircraft flew through that a 'not official' cap and anchor was drawn which not only penetrated Cleveland; but Minneapolis and Toronto Centers as well.The Steelhead MOA/ATCAA seems strangely still very confusing. My supervisor and Operations Manager were unclear; and still are unclear; about it. Does Black Talon coordinate it through the Minneapolis military desk? Does Aircraft Y control it? I give pilots a frequency for Black Talon so maybe there is a controller there? Someone needs to find this stuff out. I personally volunteer for the mission. I will be medically disqualified for weeks and I would spend that time and my own money to travel to wherever or Zoom meeting whoever to figure this out. This has been an on-going issue that was especially perverse today. I have been raising the alarm for quite some time and am passionate about it and would like to personally get/set the record straight so that all aircraft and pilots or safe. I hope this will be met with the serious spirit with which it's written.

As a Supervisor in Area X at Cleveland Center; I spent my morning attempting to coordinate and discover why the aircraft were not following what we were briefed on. Area X was briefed that due to the TFR for VIP at Traverse City; Steelhead ATCAA would be activated from 29;000 to 31;000 feet for tanker and E3 activity. These altitudes and ATCAA (Air Traffic Control Assigned Airspace) were supposed to encompass all AEW (airborne early warning) and supporting activity. The ATCAA was activated from approximately XA:45Z to XE:00Z; however aircraft showed up before it was active and then requested it to remain active past it's finish time.From the start; every single aircraft requested different altitudes than what was coordinated. I attempted to get information from Minneapolis Center; our military desk and Black Talon and was unable to get any answers. Eventually; we extended the Steelhead ATCAA from 23;000 to 31;000 feet to accommodate. Later; a tanker aircraft requested a block altitude of 20;000 to 22;000 feet and a controller gave him those until established in the lateral boundaries of Steelhead; at which point the controller understood the aircraft would climb to within the altitude limits of Steelhead (FL230-FL310). The aircraft never climbed. The controller then coordinated with Minneapolis Center blocking 20;000 to 23;000 feet to accommodate the aircraft. I then coordinated with our military coordinator to extend Steelhead to include these altitudes.When any aircraft are cleared into the Steelhead complex; radar service is terminated and the aircraft track gets dropped. This occurred during this session; as we were briefed to treat the aircraft as we normally would with Steelhead. However; while Steelhead was active; we had multiple occasions where an aircraft went outside of the lateral bounds of the Steelhead complex. After trying repeatedly to find out why this was happening; we discovered that the Sentry track was not fully inside of the Steelhead complex as we were briefed. At this point I called on the phone to Minneapolis Center supervisors desk; Toronto Center sectors Hamilton and Centralia to warn and pass along that we discovered that our information was incorrect. VIP Aircraft traveled through our airspace around XB:00 Local time estimated. Having no Controller in Charges on the entire day shift; I asked the Operations Manager to cover the Supervisor position while I plugged in and monitored the VIP movement. VIP Aircraft's course traveled about 4 to 5 miles west of the Steelhead ATCAA. During this time we kept a close eye on any tracks within Steelhead due to their previous spillover events (We were not aware at this point that the Sentry was not fully enclosed within Steelhead). All tracks were on the East side of Steelhead and not in conflct with the VIP aircraft; however that potential did exist due to the Sentry course that we were not aware of.In addition; multiple aircraft called at the Peck sector to request join ups and altitude changes while within the Steelhead ATCAA. The aircraft stated that Aircraft Y told them to do so. I had the controller inform the aircraft calling that Cleveland Center could not provide control instructions within Steelhead ATCAA. I also told the controller to state that they were not providing any separation services within Steelhead and that it was Aircraft control. At this point the floor walker was involved as well and verified that what we were doing was correct and was able to inform us why aircraft were spilling out of Steelhead.
